questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Counting microtubules in the axoneme of a cilium or flagellum, in a centriole and in a centrosome, and the functions of the cytoskeleton
questions.question: How many microtubules are present in the axoneme of a eukaryotic flagellum, in one centriole, and in one centrosome, and which statement about these structures is correct?
options: A) 18, 18 and 36; centrioles have a 9 + 2 arrangement

B) 20 (9 peripheral doublets + 2 central singlets, the 9 + 2 array), 27 (9 peripheral triplets) and 54 (two centrioles); the basal bodies of cilia and flagella are centriole-like, the central part of a centriole has a proteinaceous hub joined to the peripheral triplets by radial spokes, centrioles form the basal bodies and the spindle apparatus in animal cells, and the cytoskeleton of microtubules, microfilaments and intermediate filaments gives mechanical support, motility and shape to the cell
C) 11, 9 and 18; prokaryotic flagella have the same 9 + 2 structure
D) 20, 27 and 27; the cytoskeleton is found only in plant cells
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 20, 27 and 54 microtubules; centrioles form basal bodies and the spindle; cytoskeleton functions.
Concept: An elaborate network of filamentous proteinaceous structures consisting of microtubules, microfilaments and intermediate filaments present in the cytoplasm is collectively referred to as the cytoskeleton; the cytoskeleton in a cell is involved in many functions such as mechanical support, motility and maintenance of the shape of the cell. Cilia (sing.: cilium) and flagella (sing.: flagellum) are hair-like outgrowths of the cell membrane; cilia are small structures which work like oars, causing the movement of either the cell or the surrounding fluid; flagella are comparatively longer and responsible for cell movement; the prokaryotic bacteria also possess flagella but these are structurally different from those of the eukaryotic flagella. The electron microscopic study of a cilium or the flagellum shows that they are covered with plasma membrane; their core, called the axoneme, possesses a number of microtubules running parallel to the long axis; the axoneme usually has nine pairs of doublets of radially arranged peripheral microtubules and a pair of centrally located microtubules; such an arrangement of axonemal microtubules is referred to as the 9 + 2 array; both the cilium and flagellum emerge from centriole-like structures called the basal bodies. Centrosome is an organelle usually containing two cylindrical structures called centrioles; they are surrounded by amorphous pericentriolar materials; both the centrioles in a centrosome lie perpendicular to each other, in which each has an organisation like the cartwheel; they are made up of nine evenly spaced peripheral fibrils of tubulin protein; each of the peripheral fibrils is a triplet; the adjacent triplets are also linked; the central part of the proximal region of the centriole is also proteinaceous and called the hub, which is connected with tubules of the peripheral triplets by radial spokes made of protein; the centrioles form the basal body of cilia or flagella, and spindle fibres that give rise to the spindle apparatus during cell division in animal cells.
Given: Axoneme 9 + 2; centriole 9 triplets; centrosome = 2 centrioles.
Formula/Principle: Count microtubules = (number of units) × (tubules per unit) + central tubules.
Step 1: Axoneme: 9 × 2 + 2 = 20.
Step 2: Centriole: 9 × 3 = 27.
Step 3: Centrosome: 2 × 27 = 54.
Why: The doublet and triplet organisation of tubulin gives each structure a fixed count, linking cilia and flagella to their centriole-like basal bodies.
Why not the others: (A) Omits the central pair and treats triplets as doublets; centrioles are 9 + 0 triplets. (C) Wrong counts; bacterial flagella differ. (D) A centrosome has two centrioles; animal cells have a cytoskeleton.
Key point: Axoneme 9 + 2 (20 microtubules); centriole 9 triplets (27); centrosome two centrioles.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: The order in which bonds form when nucleotides are assembled into a DNA double helix, and the dimensions and base-pairing rules of the Watson–Crick model
questions.question: Which sequence and description of building DNA is correct?
options: A) A phosphate joins the base first; then sugar is added by a peptide bond; strands are parallel

B) A nitrogenous base joins the 1′ carbon of a pentose sugar through an N-glycosidic linkage to form a nucleoside; a phosphate attaches to the 5′-OH of the sugar through a phosphoester linkage to form a nucleotide; nucleotides are joined by 3′–5′ phosphodiester linkages into a polynucleotide; two antiparallel chains pair through hydrogen bonds (A=T with two, G≡C with three), as predicted by Chargaff's rules (A = T, G = C); the helix is right-handed with a pitch of 3.4 nm and about 10 base pairs per turn, so the distance between base pairs is about 0.34 nm
C) Nucleosides are joined by peptide bonds; there are 3.4 base pairs per turn
D) Purines pair with purines, so the helix width varies along its length
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) N-glycosidic → phosphoester → 3′–5′ phosphodiester; antiparallel chains; A=T, G≡C; pitch 3.4 nm, 10 bp per turn, 0.34 nm per bp.
Concept: A nucleotide has three components — a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar (ribose in the case of RNA, and deoxyribose for DNA) and a phosphate group; there are two types of nitrogenous bases — purines (adenine and guanine) and pyrimidines (cytosine, uracil and thymine). A nitrogenous base is linked to the pentose sugar through an N-glycosidic linkage to form a nucleoside, such as adenosine or deoxyadenosine; when a phosphate group is linked to the 5′-OH of a nucleoside through a phosphoester linkage, a corresponding nucleotide (or deoxynucleotide depending upon the type of sugar present) is formed; two nucleotides are linked through a 3′–5′ phosphodiester linkage to form a dinucleotide; more nucleotides can be joined in such a manner to form a polynucleotide chain. Based on the X-ray diffraction data produced by Maurice Wilkins and Rosalind Franklin, James Watson and Francis Crick proposed a very simple but famous double helix model for the structure of DNA; one of the hallmarks of their proposition was base pairing between the two strands of polynucleotide chains; however, this proposition was also based on the observation of Erwin Chargaff that for a double stranded DNA, the ratios between adenine and thymine and guanine and cytosine are constant and equal one. The salient features are: (i) it is made of two polynucleotide chains, where the backbone is constituted by sugar-phosphate, and the bases project inside; (ii) the two chains have anti-parallel polarity; (iii) the bases in two strands are paired through hydrogen bonds (H-bonds) forming base pairs; adenine forms two hydrogen bonds with thymine from the opposite strand and vice-versa, and guanine is bonded with cytosine with three H-bonds; as a result, always a purine comes opposite to a pyrimidine, which generates approximately uniform distance between the two strands of the helix; (iv) the two chains are coiled in a right-handed fashion; the pitch of the helix is 3.4 nm and there are roughly 10 bp in each turn; consequently, the distance between a bp in a helix is approximately 0.34 nm.
Step 1: Base + sugar (N-glycosidic) ⇒ nucleoside.
Step 2: Nucleoside + phosphate at 5′ (phosphoester) ⇒ nucleotide.
Step 3: Nucleotides joined 3′–5′ (phosphodiester) ⇒ strand; two antiparallel strands pair.
Why: Purine–pyrimidine pairing keeps the helix width uniform and complementary pairing allows each strand to template the other.
Why not the others: (A) Order and bond types wrong; strands are antiparallel. (C) Peptide bonds join amino acids; about 10 bp per turn. (D) Purines pair with pyrimidines.
Key point: Base–sugar (N-glycosidic), sugar–phosphate (phosphoester), nucleotide–nucleotide (3′–5′ phosphodiester).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Explaining enzyme action through the enzyme–substrate complex and lowering of activation energy, competitive inhibition, and the classes of enzymes and their cofactors
questions.question: Which explanation of enzyme function is correct?
options: A) Enzymes raise the activation energy so that reactions occur more slowly and safely
B) A competitive inhibitor binds to a site other than the active site and changes the enzyme's shape permanently
C) All enzymes are made only of protein and never need non-protein partners

D) The substrate binds the active site to form a transient enzyme–substrate complex, which induces the enzyme to fit more tightly and lowers the activation energy, so the reaction is faster; a competitive inhibitor resembles the substrate and competes for the active site, as malonate inhibits succinic dehydrogenase; enzymes are classed as oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases and ligases; cofactors include prosthetic groups tightly bound to the apoenzyme (haem in peroxidase and catalase), coenzymes (NAD and NADP, containing the vitamin niacin) and metal ions (zinc for carboxypeptidase)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ES complex, induced fit, lowered activation energy; competitive inhibition by malonate; six classes; prosthetic groups, coenzymes, metal ions.
Concept: Almost all enzymes are proteins; there are some nucleic acids that behave like enzymes, called ribozymes. The active site of an enzyme is a crevice or pocket into which the substrate fits; thus enzymes, through their active site, catalyse reactions at a high rate. The substrate binds to the active site of the enzyme, fitting into the active site; the binding of the substrate induces the enzyme to alter its shape, fitting more tightly around the substrate; the active site of the enzyme, now in close proximity of the substrate, breaks the chemical bonds of the substrate and the new enzyme–product complex is formed; the enzyme releases the products of the reaction and the free enzyme is ready to bind to another molecule of the substrate and run through the catalytic cycle once again. The difference in average energy content of S from that of the transition state is called activation energy; enzymes eventually bring down this energy barrier, making the transition of S to P more easy. When the binding of the chemical shuts off enzyme activity, the process is called inhibition and the chemical is called an inhibitor; when the inhibitor closely resembles the substrate in its molecular structure and inhibits the activity of the enzyme, it is known as a competitive inhibitor; due to its close structural similarity with the substrate, the inhibitor competes with the substrate for the substrate-binding site of the enzyme; e.g. inhibition of succinic dehydrogenase by malonate, which closely resembles the substrate succinate in structure; such competitive inhibitors are often used in the control of bacterial pathogens. Enzymes are divided into 6 classes each with 4–13 subclasses: oxidoreductases/dehydrogenases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases and ligases. Enzymes are composed of one or several polypeptide chains; however, there are a number of cases in which non-protein constituents called cofactors are bound to the enzyme to make it catalytically active; in these instances the protein portion of the enzyme is called the apoenzyme; three kinds of cofactors may be identified: prosthetic groups, co-enzymes and metal ions; prosthetic groups are organic compounds distinguished from other cofactors in that they are tightly bound to the apoenzyme, e.g. in peroxidase and catalase, haem is the prosthetic group; co-enzymes are also organic compounds, but their association with the apoenzyme is only transient; the essential chemical components of many coenzymes are vitamins, e.g. coenzyme nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and NADP contain the vitamin niacin; a number of enzymes require metal ions for their activity which form coordination bonds with side chains at the active site, e.g. zinc is a cofactor for the proteolytic enzyme carboxypeptidase.
Why: An enzyme speeds a reaction by stabilising the transition state through specific binding, so anything that blocks the active site competes with the substrate.
Why not the others: (A) Enzymes lower activation energy. (B) That describes a non-competitive effect, not competitive inhibition. (C) Many enzymes need cofactors, and ribozymes are RNA.
Key point: Enzymes lower activation energy via ES complex; competitive inhibitors mimic substrate; cofactors: prosthetic group, coenzyme, metal ion.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Calculating Rf values of leaf pigments from paper chromatography and relating their order to pigment colour and role in light absorption
questions.question: Leaf pigments are separated by paper chromatography. The solvent front travels 10.0 cm; spots appear at 9.5 cm (orange-yellow), 7.0 cm (yellow), 5.0 cm (blue-green) and 3.5 cm (yellow-green). What are the Rf values and identities, and which statement is correct?
options: A) Rf 0.95 carotene, 0.70 xanthophyll, 0.50 chlorophyll a, 0.35 chlorophyll b; chlorophyll a is the chief pigment associated with photosynthesis, with absorption maxima in the blue and red regions, while chlorophyll b, xanthophylls and carotenoids are accessory pigments that absorb other wavelengths, pass the energy to chlorophyll a and protect it from photo-oxidation
B) Rf 9.5, 7.0, 5.0, 3.5; chlorophyll b is the chief pigment
C) Rf 0.95 chlorophyll a, 0.35 carotene; carotenoids absorb mainly green light
D) Rf 0.05, 0.30, 0.50, 0.65; xanthophyll is blue-green
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Rf 0.95, 0.70, 0.50, 0.35 = carotene, xanthophyll, chl a, chl b; chl a chief pigment; accessory pigments widen absorption and protect chl a.
Concept: Paper chromatography of a leaf extract shows that the colour we see in leaves is not due to a single pigment but due to four pigments: chlorophyll a (bright or blue green in the chromatograph), chlorophyll b (yellow green), xanthophylls (yellow) and carotenoids (yellow to yellow-orange). Pigments are substances that have an ability to absorb light at specific wavelengths; the graph showing the ability of chlorophyll a to absorb lights of different wavelengths (absorption spectrum) shows maxima in the blue and red regions; the action spectrum of photosynthesis — the rate of photosynthesis at different wavelengths — closely coincides with the absorption spectrum of chlorophyll a, indicating that chlorophyll a is the chief pigment associated with photosynthesis. Though chlorophyll is the major pigment responsible for trapping light, other thylakoid pigments like chlorophyll b, xanthophylls and carotenoids, which are called accessory pigments, also absorb light and transfer the energy to chlorophyll a; indeed, they not only enable a wider range of wavelengths of incoming light to be utilised for photosynthesis but also protect chlorophyll a from photo-oxidation. The retention factor Rf = distance moved by the pigment/distance moved by the solvent front; less polar pigments move farther with the non-polar solvent.
Given: Solvent front 10.0 cm; spots at 9.5, 7.0, 5.0, 3.5 cm.
Formula/Principle: Rf = distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent front.
Step 1: Rf = 9.5/10 = 0.95; 7.0/10 = 0.70.
Step 2: Rf = 5.0/10 = 0.50; 3.5/10 = 0.35.
Step 3: Match colours: orange-yellow carotene, yellow xanthophyll, blue-green chl a, yellow-green chl b.
Why: Each pigment partitions differently between the paper and the solvent, so it moves a characteristic fraction of the solvent distance.
Why not the others: (B) Rf is a ratio, not a distance; chl a is the chief pigment. (C) Wrong identities; carotenoids absorb blue-violet light. (D) Subtracts from 1; xanthophyll is yellow.
Key point: Rf = d(spot)/d(solvent); carotene fastest, chl b slowest; chl a chief pigment.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting experiments on fruit ripening, stomatal closure and seed dormancy in terms of the actions of ethylene and abscisic acid
questions.question: (i) Unripe bananas kept in a closed box with a few ripe ones ripen faster than bananas kept alone. (ii) Leaves of a water-stressed plant close their stomata, and the same happens when a well-watered leaf is sprayed with a hormone from stressed leaves. (iii) Seeds of a plant fail to germinate until the hormone level in them falls. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) (i) Ethylene, a gaseous hormone released by ripening fruits, hastens fruit ripening (with a rise in respiration rate, the respiratory climacteric), and ethephon, which releases ethylene, is used for this; (ii) abscisic acid (ABA), the 'stress hormone', stimulates stomatal closure, increasing tolerance to stresses; (iii) ABA induces seed dormancy and inhibits germination, so seeds germinate when ABA falls; ABA and gibberellins generally act as antagonists
B) (i) Gibberellin from ripe fruits causes ripening; (ii) cytokinin closes stomata; (iii) auxin causes dormancy
C) (i) Abscisic acid ripens fruits; (iii) ethylene induces seed dormancy
D) The effects are caused by temperature differences, not hormones
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Ethylene hastens ripening (climacteric; ethephon); ABA closes stomata and induces dormancy; ABA antagonises gibberellins.
Concept: Ethylene is a simple gaseous PGR; it is synthesised in large amounts by tissues undergoing senescence and ripening fruits; influences of ethylene on plants include horizontal growth of seedlings, swelling of the axis and apical hook formation in dicot seedlings; ethylene promotes senescence and abscission of plant organs, especially of leaves and flowers; ethylene is highly effective in fruit ripening; it enhances the respiration rate during ripening of the fruits; this rise in rate of respiration is called respiratory climacteric; ethylene breaks seed and bud dormancy, initiates germination in peanut seeds and sprouting of potato tubers; it promotes rapid internode/petiole elongation in deep water rice plants; it also promotes root growth and root hair formation, thus helping the plants to increase their absorption surface; ethylene is used to initiate flowering and for synchronising fruit-set in pineapples, and it also induces flowering in mango; the most widely used compound as a source of ethylene is ethephon, which in aqueous solution is readily absorbed and transported within the plant and releases ethylene slowly; ethephon hastens fruit ripening in tomatoes and apples and accelerates abscission in flowers and fruits; it promotes female flowers in cucumbers, thereby increasing the yield. Abscisic acid (ABA) was discovered for its role in regulating abscission and dormancy; but like other PGRs, it also has other wide ranging effects on plant growth and development; it acts as a general plant growth inhibitor and an inhibitor of plant metabolism; ABA inhibits seed germination; ABA stimulates the closure of stomata and increases the tolerance of plants to various kinds of stresses; therefore, it is also called the stress hormone; ABA plays an important role in seed development, maturation and dormancy; by inducing dormancy, ABA helps seeds to withstand desiccation and other factors unfavourable for growth; in most situations, ABA acts as an antagonist to GAs.
Step 1: Ripe fruit speeds ripening of neighbours in a closed box ⇒ a gas ⇒ ethylene.
Step 2: Stress hormone transferable by spray closes stomata ⇒ ABA.
Step 3: Germination only after hormone falls ⇒ ABA-induced dormancy.
Why: Ethylene diffuses as a gas and acts at low concentration, while ABA signals water stress and keeps seeds dormant under unfavourable conditions.
Why not the others: (B) Hormones mismatched. (C) Roles of ABA and ethylene swapped. (D) The transfer experiments show chemical signals.
Key point: Ethylene: ripening, climacteric; ABA: stomatal closure, dormancy, stress hormone.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Reading a table of respiratory disorders and of the centres and receptors regulating breathing
questions.question:
A table summarises observations.

Condition or structure | Observation
Disorder X | difficulty in breathing with wheezing due to inflammation of bronchi and bronchioles
Disorder Y | alveolar walls damaged, respiratory surface decreased; major cause cigarette smoking
Disorder Z | inflammation and fibrosis of lungs in stone-grinding or breaking workers
Centre in medulla | primarily responsible for respiratory rhythm
Centre in pons | can moderate the rhythm and reduce inspiration duration
Area beside rhythm centre | highly sensitive to CO₂ and H⁺

Which reading of the table is correct?
options: A) X is emphysema, Y is asthma, Z is pneumonia

B) X is asthma, Y is emphysema and Z an occupational respiratory disorder caused by long exposure to dust, preventable by wearing protective masks; the respiratory rhythm centre lies in the medulla, the pneumotaxic centre in the pons, and the chemosensitive area next to the rhythm centre responds to increased CO₂ and H⁺, signalling changes in breathing; receptors in the aortic arch and carotid artery also detect these changes, while the role of oxygen in regulating the rhythm is quite insignificant
C) Oxygen concentration is the main regulator of the respiratory rhythm
D) The pneumotaxic centre is in the medulla and the rhythm centre in the pons
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) X asthma, Y emphysema, Z occupational disorder; rhythm centre in medulla, pneumotaxic centre in pons; chemosensitive area responds to CO₂ and H⁺; O₂'s role insignificant.
Concept: Human beings have a significant ability to maintain and moderate the respiratory rhythm to suit the demands of the body tissues; this is done by the neural system. A specialised centre present in the medulla region of the brain, called the respiratory rhythm centre, is primarily responsible for this regulation; another centre present in the pons region of the brain, called the pneumotaxic centre, can moderate the functions of the respiratory rhythm centre; neural signals from this centre can reduce the duration of inspiration and thereby alter the respiratory rate. A chemosensitive area is situated adjacent to the rhythm centre which is highly sensitive to CO₂ and hydrogen ions; increase in these substances can activate this centre, which in turn can signal the rhythm centre to make necessary adjustments in the respiratory process by which these substances can be eliminated; receptors associated with the aortic arch and carotid artery also can recognise changes in CO₂ and H⁺ concentration and send necessary signals to the rhythm centre for remedial actions; the role of oxygen in the regulation of respiratory rhythm is quite insignificant. Asthma is a difficulty in breathing causing wheezing due to inflammation of bronchi and bronchioles. Emphysema is a chronic disorder in which alveolar walls are damaged due to which the respiratory surface is decreased; one of the major causes of this is cigarette smoking. Occupational respiratory disorders: in certain industries, especially those involving grinding or stone-breaking, so much dust is produced that the defence mechanism of the body cannot fully cope with the situation; long exposure can give rise to inflammation leading to fibrosis (proliferation of fibrous tissues) and thus causing serious lung damage; workers in such industries should wear protective masks.
Step 1: Bronchial inflammation, wheezing ⇒ asthma (X).
Step 2: Alveolar damage, smoking ⇒ emphysema (Y).
Step 3: Dust, fibrosis in stone workers ⇒ occupational disorder (Z).
Why: Breathing is driven mainly by CO₂ and H⁺ levels sensed centrally and peripherally, because these change most with metabolic activity.
Why not the others: (A) Labels swapped. (C) O₂ plays an insignificant role. (D) Locations swapped.
Key point: Rhythm centre (medulla), pneumotaxic (pons); chemosensitive area: CO₂, H⁺.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Reading data on heart rate and stroke volume to calculate cardiac output and duration of a cardiac cycle, and the events of the cycle
questions.question:
A table compares two people.

Person | Heart rate (beats min⁻¹) | Stroke volume (mL)
Untrained adult | 70 | 75
Trained athlete at rest | 50 | 105

Which reading of these data is correct?
options: A) The untrained adult has a higher cardiac output because the heart beats faster
B) Cardiac output equals stroke volume divided by heart rate

C) Both have a cardiac output of 5.25 L min⁻¹ (70 × 75 = 50 × 105 = 5250 mL); the athlete's cardiac cycle lasts 60/50 = 1.2 s compared with about 0.86 s for the untrained adult; in each cycle, joint diastole lets blood flow into the ventricles, atrial systole adds about 30 per cent more, ventricular systole closes the AV valves (first heart sound, 'lub') and opens the semilunar valves, and closure of the semilunar valves at the start of ventricular diastole gives the second sound ('dub'); athletes can raise cardiac output far more than ordinary people
D) The athlete pumps 5.25 L per beat
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Both 5.25 L min⁻¹; cycle 1.2 s vs 0.86 s; events and heart sounds as described.
Concept: The cardiac events that occur from the beginning of one heartbeat to the beginning of the next constitute a cardiac cycle; the heart beats 72 times per minute, i.e. that many cardiac cycles are performed per minute; from this it could be deduced that the duration of a cardiac cycle is 0.8 seconds. To begin with, all the four chambers of heart are in a relaxed state, i.e. they are in joint diastole; as the tricuspid and bicuspid valves are open, blood from the pulmonary veins and vena cava flows into the left and the right ventricle respectively through the left and right atria; the SAN now generates an action potential which stimulates both the atria to undergo a simultaneous contraction — the atrial systole; this increases the flow of blood into the ventricles by about 30 per cent. The ventricular pressure increases, causing the closure of tricuspid and bicuspid valves due to attempted backflow of blood into the atria; as the ventricular pressure increases further, the semilunar valves guarding the pulmonary artery (right side) and the aorta (left side) are forced open, allowing the blood in the ventricles to flow through these vessels into the circulatory pathways; the ventricles now relax (ventricular diastole) and the ventricular pressure falls, causing the closing of semilunar valves which prevents the backflow of blood into the ventricles. During a cardiac cycle, each ventricle pumps out approximately 70 mL of blood, which is called the stroke volume; the stroke volume multiplied by the heart rate (number of beats per min) gives the cardiac output; therefore, the cardiac output can be defined as the volume of blood pumped out by each ventricle per minute and averages 5000 mL or 5 litres in a healthy individual; the body has the ability to alter the stroke volume as well as the heart rate and thereby the cardiac output; for example, the cardiac output of an athlete will be much higher than that of an ordinary man. During each cardiac cycle two prominent sounds are produced which can be easily heard through a stethoscope; the first heart sound (lub) is associated with the closure of the tricuspid and bicuspid valves, whereas the second heart sound (dub) is associated with the closure of the semilunar valves.
Given: Untrained: 70 min⁻¹, 75 mL; athlete: 50 min⁻¹, 105 mL.
Formula/Principle: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate; cycle duration = 60/heart rate.
Step 1: Untrained: 75 × 70 = 5250 mL min⁻¹.
Step 2: Athlete: 105 × 50 = 5250 mL min⁻¹.
Step 3: Cycle: 60/70 = 0.86 s; 60/50 = 1.2 s.
Why: A larger, stronger heart pumps more per beat, so the same resting output is achieved with fewer beats.
Why not the others: (A) Outputs are equal. (B) Output is the product. (D) 5.25 L is per minute.
Key point: Cardiac output = SV × HR ≈ 5 L min⁻¹; lub = AV valves close, dub = semilunar valves close.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Predicting the effects of blocking NaCl transport in Henle's loop or lacking ADH on the medullary gradient and urine concentration, using the counter-current mechanism
questions.question: Patient P takes a drug that blocks active transport of NaCl out of the ascending limb of Henle's loop. Patient Q cannot release ADH. Which prediction is correct?
options: A) Both patients produce highly concentrated urine
B) P's urine becomes more concentrated because more NaCl stays in the filtrate
C) Q's collecting duct becomes more permeable to water

D) In P, the medullary interstitial osmolarity, which normally rises from about 300 mOsmol L⁻¹ in the cortex to about 1200 mOsmol L⁻¹ in the inner medulla, is no longer built up, so water is not drawn out of the collecting duct and the urine is dilute; in Q, without ADH the collecting duct stays relatively impermeable to water, so large volumes of dilute urine are passed (diabetes insipidus); the gradient is created by the counter-current flow in the two limbs of Henle's loop and in the vasa recta, with NaCl transported by the ascending limb and urea also contributing
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) P loses the medullary gradient → dilute urine; Q has diabetes insipidus; gradient from counter-current in Henle's loop and vasa recta, with NaCl and urea.
Concept: Mammals have the ability to produce a concentrated urine; Henle's loop and vasa recta play a significant role in this; the flow of filtrate in the two limbs of Henle's loop is in opposite directions and thus forms a counter current; the flow of blood through the two limbs of vasa recta is also in a counter-current pattern; the proximity between the Henle's loop and vasa recta, as well as the counter current in them, help in maintaining an increasing osmolarity towards the inner medullary interstitium, i.e. from 300 mOsmolL⁻¹ in the cortex to about 1200 mOsmolL⁻¹ in the inner medulla. This gradient is mainly caused by NaCl and urea: NaCl is transported by the ascending limb of Henle's loop which is exchanged with the descending limb of vasa recta; NaCl is returned to the interstitium by the ascending portion of vasa recta; similarly, small amounts of urea enter the thin segment of the ascending limb of Henle's loop, which is transported back to the interstitium by the collecting tubule; the above described transport of substances facilitated by the special arrangement of Henle's loop and vasa recta is called the counter current mechanism; this mechanism helps to maintain a concentration gradient in the medullary interstitium; presence of such interstitial gradient helps in an easy passage of water from the collecting tubule, thereby concentrating the filtrate (urine); human kidneys can produce urine nearly four times concentrated than the initial filtrate formed. Osmoreceptors in the body are activated by changes in blood volume, body fluid volume and ionic concentration; an excessive loss of fluid from the body can activate these receptors, which stimulate the hypothalamus to release antidiuretic hormone (ADH) or vasopressin from the neurohypophysis; ADH facilitates water reabsorption from latter parts of the tubule, thereby preventing diuresis; defects in ADH receptors or inability to secrete ADH lead to diabetes insipidus.
Step 1: Blocked NaCl transport ⇒ no medullary gradient.
Step 2: No gradient ⇒ little water leaves collecting duct ⇒ dilute urine (P).
Step 3: No ADH ⇒ collecting duct impermeable to water ⇒ diabetes insipidus (Q).
Why: Concentrating urine needs both a hypertonic medulla (built by the loop) and water-permeable collecting ducts (controlled by ADH).
Why not the others: (A) Both produce dilute urine. (B) Without the gradient urine cannot be concentrated. (C) ADH is needed to raise water permeability.
Key point: Counter-current mechanism builds 300 → 1200 mOsmol L⁻¹; ADH makes collecting duct permeable to water.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: The sequence of hormonal events controlling thyroid hormone release and blood calcium, and the roles of the thyroid, parathyroid and pineal glands
questions.question: Which sequence and description of hormonal control is correct?
options: A) Hypothalamus releases TRH → anterior pituitary releases TSH → thyroid follicles secrete T₃ and T₄ (which need iodine) → these regulate basal metabolic rate, RBC formation and the metabolism of carbohydrates, proteins and fats; when blood Ca²⁺ falls, the parathyroid glands secrete parathyroid hormone (PTH), which stimulates bone resorption, reabsorption of Ca²⁺ by renal tubules and absorption of Ca²⁺ from digested food, raising blood Ca²⁺, while thyrocalcitonin from the thyroid lowers it; the pineal gland secretes melatonin, which regulates the 24-hour (diurnal) rhythm of the body
B) PTH lowers blood Ca²⁺, and thyrocalcitonin raises it
C) Iodine deficiency causes Graves' disease, an enlargement due to excess hormone
D) Melatonin is secreted by the parathyroid glands to control calcium
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) TRH → TSH → T₃/T₄; low Ca²⁺ → PTH (bone resorption, renal reabsorption, intestinal absorption); TCT lowers Ca²⁺; pineal melatonin controls diurnal rhythm.
Concept: The thyroid gland is composed of two lobes located on either side of the trachea; both lobes are interconnected with a thin flap of connective tissue called isthmus; the thyroid gland is composed of follicles and stromal tissues; each thyroid follicle is composed of follicular cells enclosing a cavity; these follicular cells synthesise two hormones, tetraiodothyronine or thyroxine (T₄) and triiodothyronine (T₃); iodine is essential for the normal rate of hormone synthesis in the thyroid; deficiency of iodine in our diet results in hypothyroidism and enlargement of the thyroid gland, commonly called goitre; hypothyroidism during pregnancy causes defective development and maturation of the growing baby, leading to stunted growth (cretinism), mental retardation, low intelligence quotient, abnormal skin, deaf-mutism, etc.; cancer of the thyroid gland or development of nodules of the thyroid glands may lead to an abnormally high rate of synthesis and secretion of the thyroid hormones, leading to hyperthyroidism; exophthalmic goitre (Graves' disease) is a form of hyperthyroidism. Thyroid hormones play an important role in the regulation of the basal metabolic rate; these hormones also support the process of red blood cell formation; thyroid hormones control the metabolism of carbohydrates, proteins and fats; maintenance of water and electrolyte balance is also influenced by thyroid hormones; the thyroid gland also secretes a protein hormone called thyrocalcitonin (TCT), which regulates the blood calcium levels. In humans, four parathyroid glands are present on the back side of the thyroid gland; the parathyroid glands secrete a peptide hormone called parathyroid hormone (PTH); the secretion of PTH is regulated by the circulating levels of calcium ions; PTH increases the Ca²⁺ levels in the blood; PTH acts on bones and stimulates the process of bone resorption (dissolution/demineralisation); PTH also stimulates reabsorption of Ca²⁺ by the renal tubules and increases Ca²⁺ absorption from the digested food; it is thus clear that PTH is a hypercalcemic hormone, i.e. it increases the blood Ca²⁺ levels; along with TCT, it plays a significant role in calcium balance in the body. The pineal gland is located on the dorsal side of the forebrain; the pineal gland secretes a hormone called melatonin; melatonin plays a very important role in the regulation of a 24-hour (diurnal) rhythm of our body; for example, it helps in maintaining the normal rhythms of sleep–wake cycle and body temperature; in addition, melatonin also influences metabolism, pigmentation, the menstrual cycle as well as our defence capability.
Step 1: TRH (hypothalamus) → TSH (anterior pituitary) → T₃/T₄ (thyroid).
Step 2: Low blood Ca²⁺ → PTH → bone, kidney and gut raise Ca²⁺.
Step 3: TCT opposes PTH; melatonin (pineal) sets diurnal rhythms.
Why: Hormone cascades amplify signals, and opposing hormones (PTH and TCT) hold blood calcium within narrow limits.
Why not the others: (B) Roles reversed. (C) Iodine deficiency causes goitre with hypothyroidism; Graves' disease is hyperthyroidism. (D) Melatonin is from the pineal gland.
Key point: TRH → TSH → T₃/T₄; PTH raises Ca²⁺, TCT lowers it; melatonin → diurnal rhythm.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Explaining megasporogenesis and the development of the 7-celled, 8-nucleate embryo sac, and the reasons for monosporic development and the role of the filiform apparatus
questions.question: Which explanation of megasporogenesis and the embryo sac is correct?
options: A) The megaspore mother cell divides by mitosis, so the embryo sac is diploid
B) All four megaspores develop into embryo sacs
C) The embryo sac has 8 cells and 7 nuclei

D) A single megaspore mother cell (MMC) in the micropylar region of the nucellus divides by meiosis to form four megaspores; in most flowering plants three degenerate and one functional megaspore develops into the female gametophyte (monosporic development); its nucleus divides mitotically three times without immediate wall formation (free nuclear divisions), giving 8 nuclei, after which walls form to give a 7-celled, 8-nucleate embryo sac: an egg apparatus (egg + two synergids, whose filiform apparatus guides the pollen tube) at the micropylar end, three antipodals at the chalazal end and a large central cell with two polar nuclei
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) MMC meiosis → 4 megaspores, 1 functional (monosporic) → 3 free nuclear mitoses → 7 cells, 8 nuclei; egg apparatus with filiform apparatus.
Concept: The process of formation of megaspores from the megaspore mother cell is called megasporogenesis; ovules generally differentiate a single megaspore mother cell (MMC) in the micropylar region of the nucellus; it is a large cell containing dense cytoplasm and a prominent nucleus; the MMC undergoes meiotic division; meiosis results in the production of four megaspores. In a majority of flowering plants, one of the megaspores is functional while the other three degenerate; only the functional megaspore develops into the female gametophyte (embryo sac); this method of embryo sac formation from a single megaspore is termed monosporic development. The nucleus of the functional megaspore divides mitotically to form two nuclei which move to the opposite poles, forming the 2-nucleate embryo sac; two more sequential mitotic nuclear divisions result in the formation of the 4-nucleate and later the 8-nucleate stages of the embryo sac; it is of interest to note that these mitotic divisions are strictly free nuclear, that is, nuclear divisions are not followed immediately by cell wall formation; after the 8-nucleate stage, cell walls are laid down leading to the organisation of the typical female gametophyte or embryo sac. Six of the eight nuclei are surrounded by cell walls and organised into cells; the remaining two nuclei, called polar nuclei, are situated below the egg apparatus in the large central cell; there is a characteristic distribution of the cells within the embryo sac: three cells are grouped together at the micropylar end and constitute the egg apparatus; the egg apparatus, in turn, consists of two synergids and one egg cell; the synergids have special cellular thickenings at the micropylar tip called filiform apparatus, which play an important role in guiding the pollen tubes into the synergid; three cells are at the chalazal end and are called the antipodals; the large central cell, as mentioned earlier, has two polar nuclei; thus, a typical angiosperm embryo sac, at maturity, though 8-nucleate is 7-celled.
Step 1: MMC (2n) → meiosis → four haploid megaspores.
Step 2: One functional megaspore → three free nuclear mitoses → 8 nuclei.
Step 3: Wall formation → 3 antipodals + 2 synergids + egg + central cell (2 polar nuclei) = 7 cells.
Why: Meiosis makes the gametophyte haploid; free nuclear divisions followed by wall formation produce the specific arrangement needed for double fertilisation.
Why not the others: (A) The MMC divides by meiosis; the embryo sac is haploid. (B) Usually three megaspores degenerate. (C) It is 7-celled and 8-nucleate.
Key point: Monosporic; 3 mitoses; 7 cells, 8 nuclei; filiform apparatus guides pollen tube.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Reading hormone levels across a 28-day menstrual cycle to identify phases, the trigger for ovulation and the fate of the corpus luteum
questions.question:
Hormone levels (relative) during a 28-day cycle with no pregnancy:

Day | LH | FSH | Oestrogen | Progesterone
3 | low | moderate | low | low
12 | rising | rising | peak | low
14 | surge | peak | falling | low
21 | low | low | moderate | peak
27 | low | low | low | falling

Which reading of this table is correct?
options: A) The LH surge on day 14 is caused by progesterone and follows ovulation
B) Progesterone peaks before ovulation and stimulates follicle growth

C) The follicular phase (days 6–13) is marked by rising FSH and LH and oestrogen from the growing follicles; both LH and FSH peak about mid-cycle, and the rapid LH surge induces rupture of the Graafian follicle and ovulation on about day 14; in the luteal phase the corpus luteum secretes large amounts of progesterone, essential for maintaining the endometrium; with no fertilisation the corpus luteum degenerates, progesterone falls, and the endometrium disintegrates, starting menstruation (days 1–5) of the next cycle
D) Menstruation begins because the LH surge destroys the endometrium
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Follicular phase with rising FSH, LH and oestrogen; LH surge → ovulation (day 14); luteal phase progesterone from corpus luteum; its degeneration → menstruation.
Concept: The reproductive cycle in the female primates (e.g. monkeys, apes and human beings) is called the menstrual cycle; the first menstruation begins at puberty and is called menarche; in human females, menstruation is repeated at an average interval of about 28/29 days, and the cycle of events starting from one menstruation till the next one is called the menstrual cycle; one ovum is released (ovulation) during the middle of each menstrual cycle. The cycle starts with the menstrual phase, when menstrual flow occurs, and it lasts for 3–5 days; the menstrual flow results due to breakdown of the endometrial lining of the uterus and its blood vessels, which forms liquid that comes out through vagina; menstruation only occurs if the released ovum is not fertilised. The menstrual phase is followed by the follicular phase; during this phase, the primary follicles in the ovary grow to become a fully mature Graafian follicle, and simultaneously the endometrium of the uterus regenerates through proliferation; these changes in the ovary and the uterus are induced by changes in the levels of pituitary and ovarian hormones; the secretion of gonadotropins (LH and FSH) increases gradually during the follicular phase and stimulates follicular development as well as secretion of oestrogens by the growing follicles. Both LH and FSH attain a peak level in the middle of the cycle (about the 14th day); the rapid secretion of LH leading to its maximum level during the mid-cycle, called the LH surge, induces rupture of the Graafian follicle and thereby the release of ovum (ovulation). The ovulation (ovulatory phase) is followed by the luteal phase, during which the remaining parts of the Graafian follicle transform as the corpus luteum; the corpus luteum secretes large amounts of progesterone, which is essential for maintenance of the endometrium; such an endometrium is necessary for implantation of the fertilised ovum and other events of pregnancy; during pregnancy all events of the menstrual cycle stop and there is no menstruation; in the absence of fertilisation, the corpus luteum degenerates; this causes disintegration of the endometrium leading to menstruation, marking a new cycle.
Given: Table of hormone levels.
Step 1: Days 3–12: FSH, LH, oestrogen rising ⇒ follicular phase.
Step 2: Day 14: LH surge ⇒ ovulation.
Step 3: Day 21 progesterone peak (corpus luteum); day 27 fall ⇒ menstruation follows.
Why: The pituitary gonadotropins drive follicle growth and ovulation, while progesterone from the corpus luteum keeps the endometrium ready; its withdrawal triggers menstruation.
Why not the others: (A) The LH surge precedes and causes ovulation. (B) Progesterone peaks after ovulation. (D) Menstruation follows progesterone withdrawal.
Key point: LH surge → ovulation; corpus luteum → progesterone; its decline → menstruation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Comparing pedigree patterns of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive and X-linked recessive traits, with human examples
questions.question: Which comparison of pedigree patterns is correct?
options: A) An autosomal recessive trait appears in every generation, and affected children always have an affected parent
B) An X-linked recessive trait affects females more often than males and passes from father to son

C) An autosomal dominant trait such as myotonic dystrophy usually appears in every generation, with an affected child having at least one affected parent and both sexes affected equally; an autosomal recessive trait such as sickle-cell anaemia or phenylketonuria can skip generations, appearing in children of two unaffected carrier parents (often seen with consanguineous marriage), again in both sexes; an X-linked recessive trait such as haemophilia or colour blindness affects mainly males, is passed from a carrier mother to half her sons, and is never passed from father to son
D) All three patterns are indistinguishable in pedigrees
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Dominant: every generation; recessive: skips, carrier parents; X-linked recessive: mainly males, carrier mother, no father-to-son transmission.
Concept: The idea that disorders are inherited has prevailed in human society since long; this was based on the heritability of certain characteristic features in families; after the rediscovery of Mendel's work, the practice of analysing inheritance patterns of traits in human beings began; since it is evident that control crosses cannot be performed in human beings, the study of the family history about inheritance of a particular trait provides an alternative; such an analysis of traits in several generations of a family is called pedigree analysis. Mendelian disorders are mainly determined by alteration or mutation in a single gene; these disorders are transmitted to the offspring on the same lines as studied in the principle of inheritance; the pattern of inheritance of such Mendelian disorders can be traced in a family by pedigree analysis; it is evident that the trait in question can be dominant or recessive; similarly, the trait may also be linked to the sex chromosome as in the case of haemophilia; it is evident that this X-linked recessive trait shows transmission from carrier female to male progeny. Haemophilia: a single protein that is a part of the cascade of proteins involved in the clotting of blood is affected; the possibility of a female becoming a haemophiliac is extremely rare because the mother of such a female has to be at least a carrier and the father should be haemophilic. Sickle-cell anaemia is an autosome-linked recessive trait that can be transmitted from parents to the offspring when both the partners are carriers for the gene (heterozygous); phenylketonuria is also an autosomal recessive trait; myotonic dystrophy is an autosomal dominant trait. Colour blindness is a sex-linked recessive disorder due to defect in either the red or green cone of the eye; it occurs in about 8 per cent of males and only about 0.4 per cent of females.
Why: Each pattern follows from where the gene sits and whether one copy suffices: one dominant copy shows; recessive needs two; X-linked recessive shows in hemizygous males.
Why not the others: (A) That describes a dominant pattern. (B) X-linked recessive traits mostly affect males, and fathers give sons a Y, not an X. (D) The patterns differ characteristically.
Key point: AD every generation; AR skips (carrier parents); XR mainly males, never father → son.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Comparing transcription with translation, and the roles of tRNA charging, ribosomal RNA as a ribozyme, untranslated regions and release factors in translation
questions.question: Which comparison of transcription and translation is correct?
options: A) Translation uses DNA as a template and occurs in the nucleus of eukaryotes

B) Transcription copies a DNA template into RNA using RNA polymerase, while translation polymerises amino acids into a polypeptide on ribosomes using mRNA codons; before translation, amino acids are activated with ATP and linked to their cognate tRNA (charging or aminoacylation); the ribosome's large subunit has peptidyl transferase activity, and in bacteria the 23S rRNA acts as this catalyst (a ribozyme); translation begins at the start codon AUG, the mRNA has untranslated regions (UTRs) before the start codon and after the stop codon, and a release factor binds the stop codon to end translation and release the polypeptide
C) Peptide bonds are formed by tRNA acting as an enzyme without the ribosome
D) Translation starts at the first nucleotide of the mRNA and ends at the last, with no untranslated regions
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Transcription DNA → RNA; translation mRNA → polypeptide on ribosomes; tRNA charging; 23S rRNA ribozyme; AUG start, UTRs, release factor.
Concept: Translation refers to the process of polymerisation of amino acids to form a polypeptide; the order and sequence of amino acids are defined by the sequence of bases in the mRNA; the amino acids are joined by a bond known as a peptide bond; formation of a peptide bond requires energy; therefore, in the first phase itself amino acids are activated in the presence of ATP and linked to their cognate tRNA — a process commonly called charging of tRNA or aminoacylation of tRNA, to be more specific; if two such charged tRNAs are brought close enough, the formation of a peptide bond between them would be favoured energetically; the presence of a catalyst would enhance the rate of peptide bond formation. The cellular factory responsible for synthesising proteins is the ribosome; the ribosome consists of structural RNAs and about 80 different proteins; in its inactive state, it exists as two subunits, a large subunit and a small subunit; when the small subunit encounters an mRNA, the process of translation of the mRNA to protein begins; there are two sites in the large subunit for subsequent amino acids to bind to and thus be close enough to each other for the formation of a peptide bond; the ribosome also acts as a catalyst (23S rRNA in bacteria is the enzyme — ribozyme) for the formation of the peptide bond. A translational unit in mRNA is the sequence of RNA that is flanked by the start codon (AUG) and the stop codon and codes for a polypeptide; an mRNA also has some additional sequences that are not translated and are referred to as untranslated regions (UTR); the UTRs are present at both the 5′-end (before the start codon) and at the 3′-end (after the stop codon); they are required for an efficient translation process. For initiation, the ribosome binds to the mRNA at the start codon (AUG) that is recognised only by the initiator tRNA; the ribosome proceeds to the elongation phase of protein synthesis; at the end, a release factor binds to the stop codon, terminating translation and releasing the complete polypeptide from the ribosome. In transcription, RNA polymerase copies the template strand of DNA into RNA.
Why: Transcription and translation differ in template, product, enzyme machinery and location, but both have defined start and stop signals.
Why not the others: (A) Translation reads mRNA on ribosomes in the cytoplasm. (C) The ribosome, specifically rRNA, catalyses peptide bonds. (D) UTRs flank the coding region.
Key point: tRNA charging; ribosome (23S rRNA ribozyme) forms peptide bonds; AUG start, UTRs, release factor.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Predicting expression of lac operon genes in mutants of the repressor gene or the operator, and in the presence or absence of lactose
questions.question: E. coli strains are grown with and without lactose. Strain 1 has a mutation making the i gene product non-functional. Strain 2 has an operator mutation so the repressor cannot bind. Strain 3 has a mutation inactivating the z gene. Which prediction is correct?
options: A) Strains 1 and 2 make β-galactosidase only when lactose is present
B) In strain 3, β-galactosidase is made normally because the operator is intact
C) Strain 1 cannot make any lac enzymes because the repressor is needed to switch genes on

D) In the normal lac operon the repressor from the i gene binds the operator and blocks RNA polymerase; lactose (or allolactose), the inducer, inactivates the repressor so z (β-galactosidase), y (permease) and a (transacetylase) are transcribed; strains 1 and 2 cannot block transcription, so they make the enzymes even without lactose (constitutive expression); strain 3 is induced by lactose but makes no functional β-galactosidase, so it cannot hydrolyse lactose into glucose and galactose; the lac operon is thus under negative regulation
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Strains 1 and 2 constitutive; strain 3 lacks β-galactosidase; negative regulation by the repressor.
Concept: The elucidation of the lac operon was also a result of a close association between a geneticist, Francois Jacob, and a biochemist, Jacque Monod; they were the first to elucidate a transcriptionally regulated system. In lac operon (here lac refers to lactose), a polycistronic structural gene is regulated by a common promoter and regulatory genes; such arrangement is very common in bacteria and is referred to as an operon. The lac operon consists of one regulatory gene (the i gene — here the term i does not refer to inducer, rather it is derived from the word inhibitor) and three structural genes (z, y and a); the i gene codes for the repressor of the lac operon; the z gene codes for β-galactosidase (β-gal), which is primarily responsible for the hydrolysis of the disaccharide lactose into its monomeric units, galactose and glucose; the y gene codes for permease, which increases permeability of the cell to β-galactosides; the a gene encodes a transacetylase. Lactose is the substrate for the enzyme β-galactosidase and it regulates switching on and off of the operon; hence, it is termed the inducer. In the absence of a preferred carbon source such as glucose, if lactose is provided in the growth medium of the bacteria, the lactose is transported into the cells through the action of permease; the lactose then induces the operon. The repressor of the operon is synthesised (all the time — constitutively) from the i gene; the repressor protein binds to the operator region of the operon and prevents RNA polymerase from transcribing the operon; in the presence of an inducer, such as lactose or allolactose, the repressor is inactivated by interaction with the inducer; this allows RNA polymerase access to the promoter and transcription proceeds; essentially, regulation of the lac operon can also be visualised as regulation of enzyme synthesis by its substrate; regulation of lac operon by repressor is referred to as negative regulation.
Step 1: Non-functional repressor (strain 1) or non-binding operator (strain 2) ⇒ operator never blocked ⇒ constitutive.
Step 2: z mutation (strain 3) ⇒ operon induced, but β-galactosidase inactive.
Step 3: Normal strain: lactose present ⇒ repressor inactivated ⇒ transcription.
Why: In negative regulation, gene expression occurs whenever the repressor fails to occupy the operator, whatever the reason.
Why not the others: (A) They cannot be repressed. (B) A z mutation destroys the enzyme. (C) The repressor switches genes off, not on.
Key point: Lac operon: repressor (i) binds operator; inducer inactivates repressor; z, y, a.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Reading genotype counts to calculate allele frequencies and expected Hardy–Weinberg proportions, testing equilibrium, and the factors that disturb it
questions.question:
Genotype counts in two populations of 1000 individuals each:

Population | AA | Aa | aa
P | 360 | 480 | 160
Q | 500 | 200 | 300

Which interpretation of these data is correct?
options: A) Both populations have p = 0.6 and are in equilibrium
B) Population Q has q = 0.3 and an excess of heterozygotes

C) In P, p = (2 × 360 + 480)/2000 = 0.6 and q = 0.4; expected frequencies p² = 0.36, 2pq = 0.48, q² = 0.16 match the observed 360 : 480 : 160, so P is in equilibrium; in Q, p = (1000 + 200)/2000 = 0.6 and q = 0.4 too, but observed heterozygotes (200) are far fewer than expected (480) and homozygotes more, so Q is not in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium; equilibrium can be disturbed by gene migration (gene flow), genetic drift, mutation, genetic recombination and natural selection
D) Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium requires a small population and frequent mutation
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) P: p = 0.6, in equilibrium; Q: same allele frequencies but heterozygote deficit, not in equilibrium; disturbing factors listed.
Concept: In a given population one can find out the frequency of occurrence of alleles of a gene or a locus; this frequency is supposed to remain fixed and even remain the same through generations; Hardy–Weinberg principle stated it using algebraic equations; this principle says that allele frequencies in a population are stable and are constant from generation to generation; the gene pool (total genes and their alleles in a population) remains a constant; this is called genetic equilibrium; the sum total of all the allelic frequencies is 1; individual frequencies, for example, can be named p, q, etc.; in a diploid, p and q represent the frequency of allele A and allele a; the frequency of AA individuals in a population is simply p², and similarly of aa is q², of Aa 2pq; hence p² + 2pq + q² = 1; this is a binomial expansion of (p + q)². When frequency measured differs from expected values, the difference (direction) indicates the extent of evolutionary change; disturbance in genetic equilibrium, or Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, i.e. change of frequency of alleles in a population, would then be interpreted as resulting in evolution. Five factors are known to affect Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium: gene migration or gene flow, genetic drift, mutation, genetic recombination and natural selection.
Given: P: 360, 480, 160; Q: 500, 200, 300; N = 1000 each.
Formula/Principle: p = (2·AA + Aa)/2N; expected AA : Aa : aa = p² : 2pq : q².
Step 1: P: p = 1200/2000 = 0.6, q = 0.4.
Step 2: Expected for N = 1000: 360 : 480 : 160 = observed ⇒ equilibrium.
Step 3: Q: p = 1200/2000 = 0.6; expected 360 : 480 : 160 vs observed 500 : 200 : 300 ⇒ not in equilibrium.
Why: Allele frequencies alone do not prove equilibrium; the genotype proportions must match p², 2pq and q².
Why not the others: (A) Q's genotypes depart from expectation. (B) Q has q = 0.4 and a heterozygote deficit. (D) Equilibrium assumes a large population and no mutation.
Key point: p² + 2pq + q² = 1; compare observed genotypes with expected to test equilibrium.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: The sequence of events from HIV infection to AIDS, and the causative agents and symptoms of some bacterial and viral diseases
questions.question: Which sequence and description of infectious diseases is correct?
options: A) HIV enters macrophages → its RNA genome is copied into viral DNA by reverse transcriptase → viral DNA is incorporated into the host cell's DNA → infected cells produce virus particles (macrophages act like an HIV factory) → HIV enters helper T-lymphocytes (TH), replicates and produces progeny viruses → the number of helper T cells falls progressively → the person suffers from infections they could otherwise fight, such as those caused by Mycobacterium and Toxoplasma; by contrast typhoid (Salmonella typhi) is confirmed by the Widal test, pneumonia (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae) fills alveoli with fluid, and the common cold (rhinoviruses) infects the nose and respiratory passage but not the lungs
B) HIV first destroys B cells, then copies its DNA into RNA
C) The common cold is caused by bacteria that infect the alveoli
D) Typhoid is a viral disease diagnosed by ELISA alone
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Macrophage infection → reverse transcription → integration → viral production → TH infection → TH decline → opportunistic infections; typhoid, pneumonia and common cold as described.
Concept: Acquired immuno deficiency syndrome (AIDS) means deficiency of the immune system, acquired during the lifetime of an individual, indicating that it is not a congenital disease; AIDS is caused by the human immuno deficiency virus (HIV), a member of a group of viruses called retroviruses, which have an envelope enclosing the RNA genome. After getting into the body of the person, the virus enters into macrophages where the RNA genome of the virus replicates to form viral DNA with the help of the enzyme reverse transcriptase; this viral DNA gets incorporated into the host cell's DNA and directs the infected cells to produce virus particles; the macrophages continue to produce virus and in this way act like an HIV factory; simultaneously, HIV enters into helper T-lymphocytes (TH), replicates and produces progeny viruses; the progeny viruses released in the blood attack other helper T-lymphocytes; this is repeated, leading to a progressive decrease in the number of helper T-lymphocytes in the body of the infected person; during this period, the person suffers from bouts of fever, diarrhoea and weight loss; due to decrease in the number of helper T lymphocytes, the person starts suffering from infections that could have been otherwise overcome, such as those due to bacteria especially Mycobacterium, viruses, fungi and even parasites like Toxoplasma; the patient becomes so immuno-deficient that he/she is unable to protect himself/herself against these infections; a widely used diagnostic test for AIDS is enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Salmonella typhi is a pathogenic bacterium which causes typhoid fever in human beings; these pathogens generally enter the small intestine through food and water contaminated with them and migrate to other organs through blood; sustained high fever (39° to 40 °C), weakness, stomach pain, constipation, headache and loss of appetite are some of the common symptoms; typhoid fever could be confirmed by the Widal test. Bacteria like Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae are responsible for the disease pneumonia in humans, which infects the alveoli (air-filled sacs) of the lungs; as a result of the infection, the alveoli get filled with fluid, leading to severe problems in respiration. The rhino viruses represent one such group of viruses which cause one of the most infectious human ailments — the common cold; they infect the nose and respiratory passage but not the lungs.
Step 1: Macrophage entry → reverse transcription → integration.
Step 2: Viral production; TH infection and destruction.
Step 3: Falling TH count → opportunistic infections (AIDS).
Why: HIV targets the helper T cells that coordinate immunity, so their progressive loss disables defence against many pathogens.
Why not the others: (B) HIV targets macrophages and TH cells, and copies RNA into DNA. (C) Common cold is viral and spares the lungs. (D) Typhoid is bacterial; Widal test confirms it.
Key point: HIV: macrophage → reverse transcription → TH decline → AIDS; typhoid (Widal), pneumonia (alveoli), common cold (rhinovirus).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Estimating how often a restriction enzyme cuts random DNA from the length of its recognition site, and the steps of isolating DNA and separating fragments by gel electrophoresis
questions.question: In a DNA molecule with all four bases equally frequent and randomly arranged, on average how often does an enzyme with a 4-base recognition site cut, how many sites would a 6-base cutter have in 1 million base pairs, and which statement about isolation and electrophoresis is correct?
options: A) Once every 16 bp; 1000 sites; DNA moves towards the cathode

B) Once every 4⁴ = 256 bp; about 10⁶/4⁶ = 10⁶/4096 ≈ 244 sites; to isolate DNA, cells are broken with enzymes (lysozyme for bacteria, cellulase for plants, chitinase for fungi), RNA is removed by ribonuclease and proteins by protease, and purified DNA is precipitated by chilled ethanol; in agarose gel electrophoresis the negatively charged DNA moves towards the anode, smaller fragments moving farther, and bands stained with ethidium bromide appear orange under UV light and can be cut out and eluted
C) Once every 1024 bp; 4096 sites; ethidium bromide makes DNA visible in ordinary light
D) Once every 256 bp; 4096 sites; larger fragments move farther
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Every 256 bp; ≈ 244 sites per Mb; isolation steps and electrophoresis principles as described.
Concept: Restriction endonucleases inspect the length of a DNA sequence; once they find a specific recognition sequence, they bind to the DNA and cut each of the two strands of the double helix at specific points in their sugar-phosphate backbones; each restriction endonuclease recognises a specific palindromic nucleotide sequence in the DNA. In order to cut the DNA with restriction enzymes, it needs to be in pure form, free from other macro-molecules; since the DNA is enclosed within the membranes, we have to break the cell open to release DNA along with other macromolecules such as RNA, proteins, polysaccharides and also lipids; this can be achieved by treating the bacterial cells/plant or animal tissue with enzymes such as lysozyme (bacteria), cellulase (plant cells) and chitinase (fungus); genes are located on long molecules of DNA intertwined with proteins such as histones; the RNA can be removed by treatment with ribonuclease, whereas proteins can be removed by treatment with protease; other molecules can be removed by appropriate treatments, and purified DNA ultimately precipitates out after the addition of chilled ethanol. The cutting of DNA by restriction endonucleases results in the fragments of DNA; these fragments can be separated by a technique known as gel electrophoresis; since DNA fragments are negatively charged molecules, they can be separated by forcing them to move towards the anode under an electric field through a medium/matrix; nowadays the most commonly used matrix is agarose, a natural polymer extracted from sea weeds; the DNA fragments separate (resolve) according to their size through the sieving effect provided by the agarose gel; hence, the smaller the fragment size, the farther it moves; the separated DNA fragments can be visualised only after staining the DNA with a compound known as ethidium bromide followed by exposure to UV radiation; you can see bright orange coloured bands of DNA in an ethidium bromide stained gel exposed to UV light; the separated bands of DNA are cut out from the agarose gel and extracted from the gel piece; this step is known as elution.
Given: Equal base frequency 1/4; 4-base and 6-base sites; 10⁶ bp.
Formula/Principle: Probability of a specific n-base sequence = (1/4)ⁿ; expected sites = length × (1/4)ⁿ.
Step 1: 4-base site: 4⁴ = 256 ⇒ one site per 256 bp.
Step 2: 6-base site: 4⁶ = 4096 ⇒ 10⁶/4096 ≈ 244 sites.
Step 3: Fragments separate by size; DNA (negative) moves to the anode.
Why: Each additional base in the recognition site makes a chance match four times rarer, so longer sites cut less often.
Why not the others: (A) Uses 4² and wrong pole. (C) Wrong power; staining needs UV. (D) Site count is per Mb, not 4⁶; smaller fragments move farther.
Key point: Site frequency (1/4)ⁿ; DNA moves to anode, smaller farther; EtBr + UV → orange bands.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Explaining competitive exclusion and the mechanisms by which competing species coexist or exclude each other, with field and laboratory examples
questions.question: Which explanation of interspecific competition is correct?
options: A) According to Gause's competitive exclusion principle, two closely related species competing for the same resources cannot coexist indefinitely and the competitively inferior one is eliminated; in Connell's field experiments the larger, competitively superior barnacle Balanus excluded the smaller Chthamalus from the rocky intertidal zone; competition can also occur between unrelated species, as between flamingoes and resident fishes for zooplankton in South American lakes, and through interference, as when goats introduced on a Galapagos island led to extinction of the Abingdon tortoise; species may coexist through resource partitioning, as MacArthur showed for five closely related warbler species feeding in different parts of the same tree
B) Competition occurs only between closely related species that share the same food
C) If two species compete, both must always become extinct
D) Resource partitioning means that two species eat each other's food in turns
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Gause's competitive exclusion; Balanus excluding Chthamalus; flamingoes vs fishes; goats vs Abingdon tortoise; MacArthur's warblers and resource partitioning.
Concept: When Darwin spoke of the struggle for existence and survival of the fittest in nature, he was convinced that interspecific competition is a potent force in organic evolution; it is generally believed that competition occurs when closely related species compete for the same resources that are limiting, but this is not entirely true; firstly, totally unrelated species could also compete for the same resource; for instance, in some shallow South American lakes visiting flamingoes and resident fishes compete for their common food, the zooplankton in the lake; secondly, resources need not be limiting for competition to occur; in interference competition, the feeding efficiency of one species might be reduced due to the interfering and inhibitory presence of the other species, even if resources (food and space) are abundant; therefore, competition is best defined as a process in which the fitness of one species (measured in terms of its 'r', the intrinsic rate of increase) is significantly lower in the presence of another species. It is relatively easy to demonstrate in laboratory experiments, as Gause and other experimental ecologists did, when resources are limited the competitively superior species will eventually eliminate the other species, but evidence for such competitive exclusion occurring in nature is not always conclusive; strong and persuasive circumstantial evidence does exist however in some cases; the Abingdon tortoise in Galapagos Islands became extinct within a decade after goats were introduced on the island, apparently due to the greater browsing efficiency of the goats; another evidence for the occurrence of competition in nature comes from what is called 'competitive release': a species whose distribution is restricted to a small geographical area because of the presence of a competitively superior species is found to expand its distributional range dramatically when the competing species is experimentally removed; Connell's elegant field experiments showed that on the rocky sea coasts of Scotland, the larger and competitively superior barnacle Balanus dominates the intertidal area and excludes the smaller barnacle Chthamalus from that zone. Gause's 'competitive exclusion principle' states that two closely related species competing for the same resources cannot co-exist indefinitely and the competitively inferior one will be eliminated eventually; this may be true if resources are limiting, but not otherwise; more recent studies do not support such gross generalisations about competition; while they do not rule out the occurrence of interspecific competition in nature, they point out that species facing competition might evolve mechanisms that promote co-existence rather than exclusion; one such mechanism is 'resource partitioning'; if two species compete for the same resource, they could avoid competition by choosing, for instance, different times for feeding or different foraging patterns; MacArthur showed that five closely related species of warblers living on the same tree were able to avoid competition and co-exist due to behavioural differences in their foraging activities.
Why: Competition lowers fitness; whether it leads to exclusion or coexistence depends on whether the species can divide the resource.
Why not the others: (B) Unrelated species can compete, and interference competition does not need shared food. (C) Usually only the inferior competitor is excluded. (D) Resource partitioning means using different parts, times or ways of feeding.
Key point: Competitive exclusion (Gause); competitive release (Connell); coexistence by resource partitioning (MacArthur).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Comparing taxonomic categories in the hierarchy, the rules of binomial nomenclature, and the three-domain system with the five-kingdom system
questions.question: Which comparison about classification and naming is correct?
options: A) In the name Mangifera indica, both words begin with capital letters and are printed in roman type
B) Family is a higher category than order, and class is lower than genus

C) The hierarchy in ascending order is species → genus → family → order → class → phylum (division for plants) → kingdom, with the number of shared characters decreasing as we go higher; in binomial nomenclature, proposed by Carolus Linnaeus, the first word is the genus (capitalised) and the second the specific epithet (small letter), both printed in italics or underlined separately when handwritten, and Latinised, often followed by the author's abbreviation (e.g. Mangifera indica Linn.); the three-domain system (Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya) divides the kingdom Monera into two domains, leaving the eukaryotic kingdoms in the third domain
D) The three-domain system places all prokaryotes and eukaryotes in a single domain
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Hierarchy species → kingdom; binomial rules; three domains (Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya).
Concept: Classification is not a single step process but involves a hierarchy of steps in which each step represents a rank or category; since the category is a part of overall taxonomic arrangement, it is called the taxonomic category, and all categories together constitute the taxonomic hierarchy; common categories are kingdom, phylum or division (for plants), class, order, family, genus and species; as we go higher from species to kingdom, the number of common characteristics goes on decreasing; the lower the taxa, the more are the characteristics that the members within the taxon share; the higher the category, the greater is the difficulty of determining the relationship to other taxa at the same level. Biologists follow universally accepted principles to provide scientific names to known organisms; each name has two components — the generic name and the specific epithet; this system of providing a name with two components is called binomial nomenclature; this naming system given by Carolus Linnaeus is being practised by biologists all over the world. The universal rules of nomenclature are as follows: biological names are generally in Latin and written in italics; they are Latinised or derived from Latin irrespective of their origin; the first word in a biological name represents the genus while the second component denotes the specific epithet; both the words in a biological name, when handwritten, are separately underlined, or printed in italics to indicate their Latin origin; the first word denoting the genus starts with a capital letter while the specific epithet starts with a small letter; it can be illustrated with the example of Mangifera indica; the name of the author appears after the specific epithet, i.e. at the end of the biological name, and is written in an abbreviated form, e.g. Mangifera indica Linn. indicates that this species was first described by Linnaeus. A three domain system has also been proposed that divides the Kingdom Monera into two domains, leaving the remaining eukaryotic kingdoms in the third domain and thereby a six kingdom classification.
Why: The hierarchy groups organisms by decreasing shared characters, and binomials give each species a unique, universal name.
Why not the others: (A) Specific epithet starts with a small letter; names are italicised. (B) Order is above family, and class above genus. (D) Three separate domains are recognised.
Key point: Species → genus → family → order → class → phylum/division → kingdom; Genus species in italics.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Counting phyla among Annelida, Arthropoda, Mollusca, Echinodermata and Hemichordata that show particular features — coelom, metamerism, radial symmetry in adults, water vascular system and open circulation
questions.question: Among Annelida, Arthropoda, Mollusca, Echinodermata and Hemichordata, how many phyla are coelomate and triploblastic, how many show true metameric segmentation, how many have radially symmetrical adults, and how many have a water vascular system?
options: D) 5 coelomate triploblastic; 2 metameric (Annelida and Arthropoda); 1 with radial adults (Echinodermata, whose larvae are bilateral); 1 with a water vascular system (Echinodermata, used for locomotion, capture and transport of food and respiration)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 5; 2; 1; 1.
Concept: Animals in which the body cavity, which is lined by mesoderm, is present are called coelomates — e.g. annelids, molluscs, arthropods, echinoderms, hemichordates and chordates; organisms in which the developing embryo has a third germinal layer, mesoderm, in between the ectoderm and endoderm are called triploblastic animals (platyhelminthes to chordates). In some animals the body is externally and internally divided into segments with a serial repetition of at least some organs; for example, in earthworm, the body shows this pattern, called metameric segmentation, and the phenomenon is known as metamerism. Annelida: they may be aquatic or terrestrial, free-living and sometimes parasitic; they exhibit organ-system level of body organisation and bilateral symmetry; they are triploblastic, metamerically segmented and coelomate animals; their body surface is distinctly marked out into segments or metameres, hence the phylum name Annelida. Arthropoda is the largest phylum of Animalia, which includes insects; over two-thirds of all named species on earth are arthropods; they have organ-system level of organisation; they are bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic, segmented and coelomate animals; the body of arthropods is covered by a chitinous exoskeleton; circulatory system is of open type. Mollusca is the second largest animal phylum; molluscs are terrestrial or aquatic (marine or fresh water), having an organ-system level of organisation; they are bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic and coelomate animals; body is covered by a calcareous shell and is unsegmented with a distinct head, muscular foot and visceral hump.
