Echinodermata: these animals have an endoskeleton of calcareous ossicles and, hence, the name Echinodermata (spiny bodied); all are marine with organ-system level of organisation; the adult echinoderms are radially symmetrical but larvae are bilaterally symmetrical; they are triploblastic and coelomate animals; the most distinctive feature of echinoderms is the presence of a water vascular system, which helps in locomotion, capture and transport of food and respiration. Hemichordata was earlier considered as a sub-phylum under phylum Chordata but now it is placed as a separate phylum under non-chordata; this phylum consists of a small group of worm-like marine animals with organ-system level of organisation; they are bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic and coelomate animals; the body is cylindrical and is composed of an anterior proboscis, a collar and a long trunk.
Given: Five phyla.
Formula/Principle: Tally each feature phylum by phylum.
Step 1: All five are triploblastic coelomates ⇒ 5.
Step 2: Metameric: Annelida, Arthropoda ⇒ 2.
Step 3: Radial adults and water vascular system: Echinodermata only ⇒ 1 and 1.
Why: These phyla share a true coelom, but segmentation, symmetry and the water vascular system distinguish them.
Why not the others: (A) Undercounts coelomates; overcounts radial and water vascular phyla. (B) Misses arthropod segmentation and echinoderm radial adults. (C) Undercounts coelomates; only echinoderms have radial adults.
Key point: All five coelomate; metamerism in annelids and arthropods; radial adults and water vascular system in echinoderms.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Calculating the degree of ionisation of acetic acid alone and in the presence of sodium acetate to show the common ion effect
questions.question: For acetic acid, Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵. What is the degree of ionisation α and [H⁺] of 0.10 M acetic acid alone, and of 0.10 M acetic acid that also contains 0.10 M sodium acetate?
options: A) Alone: α ≈ 1.34 × 10⁻² (1.34 %), [H⁺] ≈ 1.34 × 10⁻³ M; with acetate: α ≈ 1.8 × 10⁻⁴ (0.018 %), [H⁺] ≈ 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ M, because the added acetate ion shifts the equilibrium CH₃COOH ⇌ H⁺ + CH₃COO⁻ to the left
B) Alone: α = 1.8 × 10⁻⁴; with acetate: α = 1.34 × 10⁻²
C) α is the same in both, because Ka does not change
D) With acetate, α increases to 0.5 because acetate is a strong electrolyte
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) α falls from about 1.34 % to 0.018 %; [H⁺] falls from 1.34 × 10⁻³ M to 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ M.
Concept: The common ion effect is the suppression of the ionisation of a weak electrolyte by adding a strong electrolyte that supplies one of its ions. For a weak acid HA of concentration c, Ka = cα²/(1 − α) ≈ cα² when α is small, so α = √(Ka/c). Sodium acetate is fully ionised, so it adds a large concentration of CH₃COO⁻; by Le Chatelier's principle the equilibrium CH₃COOH ⇌ H⁺ + CH₃COO⁻ shifts to the left, and [CH₃COO⁻] is essentially the salt concentration. Then Ka = [H⁺][CH₃COO⁻]/[CH₃COOH] ≈ [H⁺](0.10)/(0.10), so [H⁺] ≈ Ka. Ka itself is unchanged at constant temperature; only the position of equilibrium moves.
Given: Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵; c(acid) = 0.10 M; c(salt) = 0.10 M.
Formula/Principle: Alone α = √(Ka/c); with common ion α = Ka/[A⁻].
Step 1: Alone: α = √(1.8 × 10⁻⁴) = 1.34 × 10⁻²; [H⁺] = cα = 1.34 × 10⁻³ M.
Step 2: With salt: [H⁺] = Ka × 0.10/0.10 = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ M.
Step 3: α = [H⁺]/c = 1.8 × 10⁻⁴, about 75 times smaller.
Why: The extra acetate ions force the ionisation equilibrium backwards, so far fewer acid molecules ionise.
Why not the others: (B) The two values are swapped. (C) Ka is fixed but α depends on [A⁻]. (D) A common ion suppresses ionisation.
Key point: Common ion effect: α = Ka/[common ion], much smaller than √(Ka/c).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Converting Kc to Kp using Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn for reactions with positive, zero and negative Δn
questions.question: For PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g), Kc = 0.040 mol L⁻¹ at 500 K. What is Kp (R = 0.0831 L bar K⁻¹ mol⁻¹), and how are Kp and Kc related for H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g) and N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)?
options: A) Kp = 0.040 bar; Kp = Kc for all three reactions
B) Kp = 4.8 × 10⁻⁴ bar; for HI Kp = Kc(RT)²
C) Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn with Δn = +1, so Kp = 0.040 × 0.0831 × 500 ≈ 1.66 bar; for HI Δn = 0 so Kp = Kc; for NH₃ Δn = −2 so Kp = Kc(RT)⁻², smaller than Kc at this temperature
D) Kp = 1.66 bar; for NH₃ Kp = Kc(RT)²
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Kp ≈ 1.66 bar; Kp = Kc for HI; Kp = Kc(RT)⁻² for NH₃.
Concept: For a gaseous reaction, partial pressure and molar concentration are related by p = (n/V)RT = cRT. Writing the equilibrium constant in partial pressures and substituting p = cRT for every species gives Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn, where Δn = (moles of gaseous products) − (moles of gaseous reactants) in the balanced equation. When R is taken as 0.0831 L bar K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, pressures are in bar and concentrations in mol L⁻¹. If Δn = 0 the RT terms cancel and Kp = Kc; if Δn is negative, Kp is smaller than Kc whenever RT > 1.
Given: Kc = 0.040 mol L⁻¹; T = 500 K; R = 0.0831 L bar K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
Formula/Principle: Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn.
Step 1: PCl₅: Δn = 2 − 1 = +1.
Step 2: RT = 0.0831 × 500 = 41.55; Kp = 0.040 × 41.55 = 1.66 bar.
Step 3: HI: Δn = 2 − 2 = 0; NH₃: Δn = 2 − 4 = −2.
Why: Each mole of gas contributes a factor RT when concentrations are converted to pressures, so only the net change in gas moles matters.
Why not the others: (A) Ignores Δn. (B) Divides by RT; HI has Δn = 0. (D) Sign of Δn for NH₃ is wrong.
Key point: Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn; Δn counts gaseous moles only.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Organic Chemistry: Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.sub_topic: Assigning IUPAC names to compounds with a principal functional group, substituents and multiple bonds by choosing the parent chain and lowest locants
questions.question: Which set of IUPAC names is correct for (i) CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH₂–CO–CH₃, (ii) CH₂=CH–CH₂–OH, (iii) HOOC–CH₂–CH₂–COOH and (iv) CH₃–CHCl–CH(CH₃)–CH₂–CH₃?
options: A) (i) 2-methylpentan-4-one; (ii) prop-1-en-3-ol; (iii) butane-1,4-dioic acid; (iv) 3-methyl-2-chloropentane
B) (i) 4-methylpentan-2-one; (ii) prop-2-en-1-ol; (iii) butanedioic acid; (iv) 2-chloro-3-methylpentane
C) (i) isobutyl methyl ketone only; (ii) allyl alcohol only; (iii) succinic acid only; (iv) sec-butyl chloride
D) (i) 4-methylpentanal; (ii) propenol; (iii) ethane-1,2-dicarboxylic acid; (iv) 4-chloro-3-methylpentane
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 4-methylpentan-2-one; prop-2-en-1-ol; butanedioic acid; 2-chloro-3-methylpentane.
Concept: In IUPAC nomenclature, the longest carbon chain containing the principal functional group is selected as the parent chain, and it is numbered so that the principal functional group gets the lowest locant; multiple bonds come next and then substituents. The principal group appears as a suffix (-one for ketones, -ol for alcohols, -oic acid for carboxylic acids), a double bond changes -ane to -ene, and halogens and alkyl groups are written as prefixes in alphabetical order. When the carbon of a –COOH group is part of the chain, it is counted in the parent name, so HOOC–CH₂–CH₂–COOH is a four-carbon dioic acid and needs no locants because the carboxyl carbons must be at the ends. If two numberings give the same lowest locants to the principal group, the first point of difference among substituents decides, and prefixes are listed alphabetically (chloro before methyl).
Step 1: (i) Five-carbon chain numbered from the ketone end: C=O at C-2, methyl at C-4.
Step 2: (ii) –OH gets locant 1, so the double bond is at C-2: prop-2-en-1-ol.
Step 3: (iii) Four carbons including both –COOH: butanedioic acid; (iv) numbering from the Cl end gives 2,3; alphabetical order: chloro, methyl.
Why: The principal group fixes both the suffix and the direction of numbering; substituents follow alphabetical order.
Why not the others: (A) Principal groups given higher locants; prefixes not alphabetical. (C) Common names, and (iv) is not sec-butyl chloride. (D) (i) is a ketone, not an aldehyde; (iv) locants not lowest.
Key point: Principal group lowest locant; prefixes alphabetical; carboxyl carbons included in the chain.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Identifying which alkenes show geometrical isomerism, comparing properties of cis and trans isomers, and preparing each isomer from an alkyne
questions.question: Among but-1-ene, but-2-ene, 2-methylpropene, pent-2-ene, 1,1-dichloroethene and 1,2-dichloroethene, how many show geometrical isomerism, and which statement about cis and trans isomers is correct?
options: A) 5; cis isomers always have higher melting points
B) 2; trans-but-2-ene is made from but-2-yne with Lindlar's catalyst
C) 6; 2-methylpropene shows geometrical isomerism because it has a double bond

D) 3 (but-2-ene, pent-2-ene, 1,2-dichloroethene); cis-but-2-ene, being polar, has the higher boiling point, while the more symmetrical trans isomer packs better and has the higher melting point; partial hydrogenation of but-2-yne with Lindlar's catalyst (Pd on CaCO₃ poisoned with sulphur compounds or quinoline) gives cis-but-2-ene, while sodium in liquid ammonia gives trans-but-2-ene
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Three show geometrical isomerism; cis has higher bp, trans higher mp; Lindlar → cis, Na/liquid NH₃ → trans.
Concept: Restricted rotation about the C=C double bond means that when each doubly bonded carbon carries two different groups, two spatial arrangements exist: cis (similar groups on the same side) and trans (on opposite sides). If either carbon carries two identical groups, as in but-1-ene (=CH₂), 2-methylpropene ((CH₃)₂C=) and 1,1-dichloroethene, no geometrical isomers exist. Cis isomers of compounds like but-2-ene and 1,2-dichloroethene are polar because the bond dipoles do not cancel, giving them higher boiling points; trans isomers are less polar or non-polar but more symmetrical, so they fit better into the crystal lattice and have higher melting points. Alkynes on partial reduction with calculated hydrogen in the presence of palladised charcoal partially deactivated with poisons like sulphur compounds or quinoline (Lindlar's catalyst) give cis alkenes; reduction with sodium in liquid ammonia forms trans alkenes.
Given: Six alkenes.
Formula/Principle: Geometrical isomerism needs two different groups on each doubly bonded carbon.
Step 1: But-1-ene, 2-methylpropene, 1,1-dichloroethene have two identical groups on one carbon ⇒ no.
Step 2: But-2-ene, pent-2-ene, 1,2-dichloroethene ⇒ yes; count = 3.
Step 3: Lindlar adds H₂ to one face (syn) ⇒ cis; Na/NH₃ gives trans.
Why: Restricted rotation plus two different groups at each end of C=C creates distinct, non-interconverting isomers.
Why not the others: (A) Count wrong; trans usually melts higher. (B) Count wrong; Lindlar gives cis. (C) A double bond alone is not enough.
Key point: Two different groups on each C=C carbon; Lindlar → cis, Na/liq. NH₃ → trans.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Explaining Markovnikov addition of HBr to propene and the anti-Markovnikov (peroxide) effect, and why the peroxide effect is not seen with HCl or HI
questions.question: Propene reacts with HBr in the dark without peroxide, and separately with HBr in the presence of benzoyl peroxide. Which explanation is correct?
options: A) Both reactions give 2-bromopropane by the same ionic mechanism

B) Without peroxide, H⁺ adds first to give the more stable secondary carbocation, so 2-bromopropane forms (Markovnikov); with peroxide, Br• radicals add first at the terminal carbon to give the more stable secondary free radical, so 1-bromopropane forms (anti-Markovnikov, Kharash effect); the effect is not seen with HCl because the H–Cl bond is too strong to be broken homolytically by the radicals, nor with HI because the H–I bond is weak and iodine atoms combine to form I₂ instead of adding
C) With peroxide, Br⁻ adds first to the carbon with more hydrogens
D) The peroxide effect works for HCl, HBr and HI equally
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Ionic route via secondary carbocation → 2-bromopropane; radical route via secondary radical → 1-bromopropane; not with HCl or HI.
Concept: Markovnikov's rule states that the negative part of the addendum gets attached to that carbon atom which possesses the lesser number of hydrogen atoms. Mechanistically, HBr provides an electrophile H⁺ which attacks the double bond; of the two possible carbocations, the secondary carbocation (CH₃–C⁺H–CH₃) is more stable than the primary one (CH₃CH₂C⁺H₂) and is formed faster, so Br⁻ attacks it to give 2-bromopropane. In the presence of peroxide, addition of HBr to unsymmetrical alkenes like propene takes place contrary to Markovnikov's rule; this happens only with HBr and not with HCl and HI. This reaction is known as the peroxide or Kharash effect: peroxide gives free radicals, which abstract H from HBr to form Br•; Br• adds to the CH₂ end of propene to give the more stable secondary radical CH₃–C•H–CH₂Br, which then takes H from HBr to give 1-bromopropane. The H–Cl bond (430.5 kJ mol⁻¹) is stronger than H–Br (363.7 kJ mol⁻¹) and is not cleaved by the free radical, whereas the H–I bond is weaker (296.8 kJ mol⁻¹) and iodine free radicals combine to form iodine molecules instead of adding to the double bond.
Why: Both pathways form the more stable intermediate — a secondary carbocation in the ionic route and a secondary radical in the radical route — but the attacking species that adds first differs (H⁺ versus Br•).
Why not the others: (A) Peroxide changes the mechanism and the product. (C) The radical Br•, not Br⁻, adds first. (D) Only HBr shows the effect.
Key point: Markovnikov via carbocation; anti-Markovnikov (peroxide) via radical, only with HBr.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Calculating molarity, molality, mass percentage and mole fraction of a solution prepared in the laboratory from mass and density data, and their temperature dependence
questions.question: A student dissolves 4.9 g of H₂SO₄ (M = 98 g mol⁻¹) in water and makes the volume up to 250 mL. The solution's density is 1.06 g mL⁻¹. What are the molarity, molality, mass percentage and mole fraction of H₂SO₄, and which concentration changes on heating?
options: A) Molarity 0.20 M; molality ≈ 0.192 m (mass of solution 265 g, water 260.1 g); mass percentage ≈ 1.85 %; mole fraction ≈ 3.45 × 10⁻³; molarity changes with temperature because volume changes, while molality, mass percentage and mole fraction, based on masses, do not
B) Molarity 0.020 M; molality 0.20 m; molality changes with temperature
C) Molarity 0.20 M; molality 0.20 m exactly, because the solution is dilute
D) Molarity 0.05 M; mass percentage 4.9 %; none depend on temperature
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 0.20 M; 0.192 m; 1.85 %; x ≈ 3.45 × 10⁻³; molarity is temperature dependent.
Concept: Molarity (M) is the number of moles of solute dissolved in one litre of solution; molality (m) is the number of moles of solute per kilogram of solvent; mass percentage is (mass of component/total mass of solution) × 100; mole fraction is moles of a component divided by total moles of all components. Molarity depends on volume, which changes with temperature, so molarity changes on heating; molality, mass percentage and mole fraction are based on masses, which do not change with temperature. To convert, the density gives the mass of solution, and subtracting the solute mass gives the solvent mass.
Given: m(solute) = 4.9 g; M = 98 g mol⁻¹; V = 250 mL; d = 1.06 g mL⁻¹.
Formula/Principle: M = n/V(L); m = n/kg solvent; x = n(solute)/n(total).
Step 1: n = 4.9/98 = 0.050 mol; M = 0.050/0.250 = 0.20 M.
Step 2: Mass of solution = 250 × 1.06 = 265 g; water = 260.1 g; m = 0.050/0.2601 = 0.192 m; mass % = 4.9/265 × 100 = 1.85 %.
Step 3: n(water) = 260.1/18 = 14.45 mol; x = 0.050/14.50 = 3.45 × 10⁻³.
Why: Volume-based concentrations shift as liquids expand, whereas mass-based ones are fixed by the amounts weighed out.
Why not the others: (B) Volume not converted to litres; molality is temperature-independent. (C) Molality differs because solvent mass is not 250 g. (D) Moles not 0.05 per litre; mass % uses solution mass.
Key point: Molarity (per L solution, T-dependent); molality (per kg solvent, T-independent).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Using Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions to find the limiting molar conductivity of acetic acid, then its degree of dissociation and dissociation constant
questions.question: At 298 K, Λ°m(HCl) = 425.9, Λ°m(CH₃COONa) = 91.0 and Λ°m(NaCl) = 126.4 S cm² mol⁻¹. A 1.0 × 10⁻³ M acetic acid solution has Λm = 39.05 S cm² mol⁻¹. What are Λ°m(CH₃COOH), α and Ka?
options: B) Λ°m = 39.05 S cm² mol⁻¹; α = 1; Ka cannot be found
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Λ°m = 390.5 S cm² mol⁻¹; α = 0.100; Ka ≈ 1.1 × 10⁻⁵.
Concept: Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions states that the limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte can be represented as the sum of the individual contributions of the anion and cation of the electrolyte. For a weak electrolyte like acetic acid, Λ°m cannot be obtained by extrapolating Λm to zero concentration because Λm rises steeply at low concentration; instead it is obtained by combining Λ°m values of strong electrolytes: Λ°m(CH₃COOH) = λ°(H⁺) + λ°(CH₃COO⁻) = Λ°m(HCl) + Λ°m(CH₃COONa) − Λ°m(NaCl). For a weak electrolyte the degree of dissociation at concentration c is α = Λm/Λ°m, and its dissociation constant is Ka = cα²/(1 − α).
Given: Λ°m(HCl) = 425.9, Λ°m(CH₃COONa) = 91.0, Λ°m(NaCl) = 126.4; c = 1.0 × 10⁻³ M; Λm = 39.05.
Formula/Principle: Λ°m(HA) = Λ°m(HCl) + Λ°m(NaA) − Λ°m(NaCl); α = Λm/Λ°m; Ka = cα²/(1 − α).
Step 1: Λ°m = 425.9 + 91.0 − 126.4 = 390.5 S cm² mol⁻¹.
Step 2: α = 39.05/390.5 = 0.100.
Step 3: Ka = (1.0 × 10⁻³)(0.0100)/0.900 = 1.11 × 10⁻⁵.
Why: Ions migrate independently at infinite dilution, so their contributions can be added and subtracted between salts.
Why not the others: (A) Adds NaCl instead of subtracting. (B) Λm at finite concentration is not Λ°m. (C) Subtracts HCl instead of adding.
Key point: Λ°m(HA) = Λ°m(HCl) + Λ°m(NaA) − Λ°m(NaCl); α = Λm/Λ°m.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Determining the order with respect to each reactant, the rate constant and its units from initial-rate data, and distinguishing order from molecularity
questions.question:
For A + B → products, initial rates at 298 K are:

[A] (mol L⁻¹) | [B] (mol L⁻¹) | Rate (mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹)
0.10 | 0.10 | 2.0 × 10⁻³
0.20 | 0.10 | 8.0 × 10⁻³
0.10 | 0.20 | 4.0 × 10⁻³

What are the orders, the rate constant and the rate when [A] = 0.30 M and [B] = 0.20 M?
options: A) First order in A, second in B; k = 2.0 s⁻¹; rate = 0.012 mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹
B) Overall order 2; k = 0.20 L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹; rate = 0.012 mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹

C) Second order in A, first order in B, overall third order; k = 2.0 L² mol⁻² s⁻¹; rate = 2.0 × (0.30)² × 0.20 = 3.6 × 10⁻² mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹; order is found experimentally and can be zero or fractional, while molecularity applies only to elementary reactions and is a whole number
D) Order equals the stoichiometric coefficients, so first in each; k = 0.20 L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Rate = k[A]²[B]; k = 2.0 L² mol⁻² s⁻¹; rate = 3.6 × 10⁻² mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹.
Concept: The rate law expresses the rate in terms of molar concentrations of reactants, each raised to some power that may or may not equal its stoichiometric coefficient; these powers are determined experimentally, for instance by the initial-rate method, where one concentration is changed while the others are kept constant. The sum of the powers is the overall order, which may be zero, fractional or whole. The units of k for an nth-order reaction are (mol L⁻¹)¹⁻ⁿ s⁻¹. Molecularity is the number of reacting species taking part in an elementary reaction which must collide simultaneously to bring about a chemical reaction; it is applicable only to elementary reactions, cannot be zero or fractional, and for complex reactions order is given by the slowest step.
Given: Three experiments; target [A] = 0.30, [B] = 0.20.
Formula/Principle: Rate = k[A]ˣ[B]ʸ; ratio of rates gives each order.
Step 1: Exp 2/1: [A] × 2, rate × 4 ⇒ x = 2; Exp 3/1: [B] × 2, rate × 2 ⇒ y = 1.
Step 2: k = 2.0 × 10⁻³/[(0.10)²(0.10)] = 2.0 L² mol⁻² s⁻¹.
Step 3: Rate = 2.0 × 0.090 × 0.20 = 3.6 × 10⁻² mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹.
Why: Doubling a concentration multiplies the rate by 2ⁿ, so the rate ratios reveal each order directly.
Why not the others: (A) Orders swapped. (B) Wrong overall order and k. (D) Orders are not taken from coefficients.
Key point: Orders from rate ratios; k units (mol L⁻¹)¹⁻ⁿ s⁻¹; molecularity only for elementary steps.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Explaining trends in ionisation enthalpy, atomic radii, enthalpy of atomisation and metallic character across the first transition series
questions.question: Which explanation of properties of the 3d series (Sc to Zn) is correct?
options: A) Chromium and copper have unusually high second ionisation enthalpies because removal of the second electron disturbs the stable 3d⁵ and 3d¹⁰ configurations; atomic radii decrease from Sc to about Cr and then remain nearly constant because the increased nuclear charge is largely offset by the shielding of the added 3d electrons; zinc has the lowest enthalpy of atomisation of the series because it has no unpaired d electrons for metallic bonding, while metals in the middle of the series, with the most unpaired electrons, have strong interatomic bonding and high melting points
B) Atomic radii increase steadily from Sc to Zn because electrons are added
C) Zinc has the highest enthalpy of atomisation because its d orbitals are full
D) First ionisation enthalpies decrease regularly across the series
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) High IE₂ for Cr and Cu (d⁵, d¹⁰); radii decrease then level off; Zn lowest enthalpy of atomisation.
Concept: Due to an increase in nuclear charge which accompanies the filling of the inner d orbitals, there is an increase in ionisation enthalpy along each series of transition elements from left to right, but many small variations occur. The irregular trend arises because removal of one electron alters the relative energies of 4s and 3d orbitals. The high values for Cr and Cu for the second ionisation enthalpy are due to the fact that the second electron is removed from stable d⁵ and d¹⁰ configurations of Cr⁺ and Cu⁺ respectively; the value of Zn is higher because it represents ionisation from the 4s level. In general, ions of the same charge in a given series show a progressive decrease in radius with increasing atomic number, because the new electron enters a d orbital each time the nuclear charge increases by unity; the shielding effect of a d electron is not that effective, so the net electrostatic attraction increases and the radius decreases — but the variation within a series is small. The transition elements exhibit high enthalpies of atomisation; the maxima at about the middle of each series indicate that one unpaired electron per d orbital is particularly favourable for strong interatomic interaction; in general, greater the number of valence electrons, stronger is the resultant bonding; Zn, with no unpaired electrons (3d¹⁰4s²), has the lowest enthalpy of atomisation and is relatively soft.
Why: Electronic configurations — half-filled and filled d subshells, and the number of unpaired d electrons — control ionisation energies and metallic bonding strength.
Why not the others: (B) Radii decrease and then level off. (C) Zn has the lowest value. (D) First IEs generally increase, irregularly.
Key point: Cr⁺ (d⁵), Cu⁺ (d¹⁰) → high IE₂; Zn weakest metallic bonding.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Deducing the formulae and IUPAC names of cobalt ammine complexes from the number of moles of AgCl precipitated and from molar conductivity, and predicting isomerism
questions.question: One mole each of CoCl₃·5NH₃ and CoCl₃·4NH₃ is treated with excess AgNO₃ solution at room temperature; 2 mol and 1 mol of AgCl precipitate respectively. Which formulae, names and properties are correct?
options: A) [Co(NH₃)₅]Cl₃ and [Co(NH₃)₄]Cl₃; both are triamminecobalt chlorides

B) [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]Cl₂, pentaamminechloridocobalt(III) chloride, giving 3 ions per formula unit; and [Co(NH₃)₄Cl₂]Cl, tetraamminedichloridocobalt(III) chloride, giving 2 ions, which exists as cis and trans geometrical isomers
C) [Co(NH₃)₅Cl₂]Cl and [Co(NH₃)₄Cl₃]; both give no ions in solution
D) [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]Cl₂ named chloropentaamminecobalt(II) chloride; it shows cis–trans isomerism
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]Cl₂ (pentaamminechloridocobalt(III) chloride, 3 ions); [Co(NH₃)₄Cl₂]Cl (tetraamminedichloridocobalt(III) chloride, 2 ions, cis/trans).
Concept: In Werner's experiments, only chloride ions outside the coordination sphere (counter ions) are precipitated as AgCl by AgNO₃; chloride ligands bonded to the metal are not. Molar conductivity measurements give the number of ions produced in solution, confirming the formula. Cobalt(III) forms octahedral complexes with coordination number 6. In naming, the cation is named first; ligands are named in alphabetical order before the metal (ammine before chlorido), with prefixes di-, tri-, tetra- etc. not counted for alphabetical order; the oxidation state of the metal is given in Roman numerals in parentheses. An octahedral complex of type [MA₄B₂] shows geometrical isomerism: the two B ligands can be adjacent (cis) or opposite (trans).
Given: 2 mol AgCl from CoCl₃·5NH₃; 1 mol AgCl from CoCl₃·4NH₃.
Formula/Principle: Precipitated Cl⁻ = ionisable counter ions; coordination number 6.
Step 1: 5NH₃ + 1Cl inside ⇒ [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]²⁺ + 2Cl⁻ ⇒ 3 ions.
Step 2: 4NH₃ + 2Cl inside ⇒ [Co(NH₃)₄Cl₂]⁺ + Cl⁻ ⇒ 2 ions.
Step 3: [MA₄B₂] octahedral ⇒ cis and trans.
Why: Only free chloride ions react with silver nitrate, so the precipitate count reveals how many chlorides lie outside the coordination sphere.
Why not the others: (A) Coordination number would be 5 or 4 and all Cl would precipitate. (C) Coordination number 7; ion counts wrong. (D) Co is +3; [MA₅B] has no geometrical isomers.
Key point: AgCl precipitated = counter Cl⁻; [Co(NH₃)₄Cl₂]⁺ shows cis/trans.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Explaining the order of acidity of ethanol, phenol and substituted phenols in terms of resonance stabilisation of the phenoxide ion and substituent effects
questions.question: Which order of acid strength and explanation is correct for ethanol, phenol, 4-methylphenol, 4-nitrophenol and 2,4,6-trinitrophenol?
options: A) Ethanol > phenol > 4-nitrophenol, because the alkyl group in ethanol releases electrons
B) 4-Methylphenol > phenol because the methyl group stabilises the phenoxide ion
C) All phenols have the same acidity, because the –OH group is the same

D) 2,4,6-Trinitrophenol (pKa ≈ 0.7) > 4-nitrophenol (≈ 7.1) > phenol (≈ 10.0) > 4-methylphenol (≈ 10.2) > ethanol (≈ 15.9); the phenoxide ion is stabilised by delocalisation of its negative charge into the ring, while the ethoxide ion's charge is localised; electron-withdrawing nitro groups at ortho and para positions delocalise the charge further and increase acidity, whereas the electron-releasing methyl group destabilises the phenoxide ion; so phenol reacts with aqueous NaOH but ethanol does not
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Picric acid > 4-nitrophenol > phenol > 4-methylphenol > ethanol; resonance and substituent effects.
Concept: The reactions of phenol with metals (e.g. sodium) and with sodium hydroxide indicate its acidic nature; the hydroxyl group in phenol is attached to an sp² hybridised carbon of the benzene ring, which acts as an electron-withdrawing group, so the charge distribution in the phenol molecule makes the oxygen positive. The phenoxide ion formed on ionisation is stabilised by the delocalisation of negative charge due to resonance, whereas in the alkoxide ion the negative charge is localised on oxygen; hence phenols are more acidic than alcohols. In substituted phenols, the presence of electron-withdrawing groups such as the nitro group enhances the acidic strength of phenol; this effect is more pronounced when such a group is present at ortho and para positions, due to the effective delocalisation of the negative charge in the phenoxide ion. On the other hand, electron-releasing groups, such as alkyl groups, in general, do not favour the formation of the phenoxide ion, resulting in a decrease in acid strength; cresols, for example, are less acidic than phenol. The greater the pKa value, the weaker the acid.
Why: Acidity depends on the stability of the conjugate base; groups that spread the negative charge strengthen the acid, groups that concentrate it weaken the acid.
Why not the others: (A) Alcohols are weaker acids than phenols. (B) Methyl decreases acidity. (C) Ring substituents change acidity strongly.
Key point: Phenoxide resonance; –NO₂ (o/p) increases acidity; –CH₃ decreases it; alcohols weakest.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Calculating masses of products and reagents in bromination of phenol and in Reimer–Tiemann and Kolbe reactions, and the activating effect of the –OH group
questions.question: 9.4 g of phenol (M = 94 g mol⁻¹) is treated with excess bromine water. In a separate experiment, 9.4 g of phenol undergoes the Reimer–Tiemann reaction with 60 % yield. What mass of 2,4,6-tribromophenol (M = 331) forms at 100 % yield, how much Br₂ (M = 160) is consumed, what mass of the Reimer–Tiemann product (M = 122) forms, and which statement is correct?
options: A) 33.1 g; 16 g Br₂; 12.2 g salicylic acid; the –OH group deactivates the ring
B) 11.0 g; 48 g Br₂; 7.32 g benzaldehyde; bromine water gives only 4-bromophenol

C) 33.1 g of 2,4,6-tribromophenol; 48 g Br₂ (0.3 mol, one Br₂ per substitution); 7.32 g of salicylaldehyde (2-hydroxybenzaldehyde) from CHCl₃ and NaOH; the –OH group strongly activates the ring towards ortho and para substitution, so phenol reacts with bromine water without a Lewis acid, while Kolbe's reaction (sodium phenoxide + CO₂, then acid) gives salicylic acid
D) 33.1 g; 48 g Br₂; 12.2 g salicylaldehyde; a Lewis acid is needed for bromination
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 33.1 g tribromophenol; 48 g Br₂; 7.32 g salicylaldehyde; –OH activates o/p.
Concept: The –OH group attached to the benzene ring activates it towards electrophilic substitution and directs the incoming group to ortho and para positions, because the ring is highly electron-rich due to resonance. When phenol is treated with bromine water, 2,4,6-tribromophenol is formed as a white precipitate; in solvents of low polarity such as CHCl₃ or CS₂ at low temperature, monobromophenols are formed instead. Each substitution uses one Br₂ molecule and releases one HBr. On treating phenol with chloroform in the presence of sodium hydroxide, a –CHO group is introduced at the ortho position of the benzene ring; this reaction is known as the Reimer–Tiemann reaction, and the intermediate substituted benzal chloride is hydrolysed in the presence of alkali to produce salicylaldehyde. In Kolbe's reaction, the phenoxide ion generated by treating phenol with sodium hydroxide is even more reactive than phenol towards electrophilic aromatic substitution and undergoes reaction with carbon dioxide, a weak electrophile; ortho-hydroxybenzoic acid (salicylic acid) is formed as the main product.
Given: 9.4 g phenol (0.10 mol); M: C₆H₂Br₃OH = 331, Br₂ = 160, salicylaldehyde = 122; 60 % yield.
Formula/Principle: C₆H₅OH + 3Br₂ → C₆H₂Br₃OH + 3HBr; 1 phenol → 1 salicylaldehyde.
Step 1: n(phenol) = 9.4/94 = 0.10 mol ⇒ tribromophenol = 0.10 × 331 = 33.1 g.
Step 2: Br₂ = 0.30 mol × 160 = 48 g.
Step 3: Salicylaldehyde = 0.10 × 0.60 × 122 = 7.32 g.
Why: The strongly activating –OH group allows three rapid substitutions without a catalyst, and named reactions introduce –CHO or –COOH at the ortho position.
Why not the others: (A) Br₂ mass for one substitution; –OH activates. (B) Wrong product mass and products. (D) Ignores 60 % yield; no Lewis acid needed.
Key point: Phenol + bromine water → 2,4,6-tribromophenol (3 Br₂); Reimer–Tiemann → salicylaldehyde; Kolbe → salicylic acid.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Calculating masses of silver from Tollens' test and of iodoform from the haloform reaction, and the reduction products of aldehydes and ketones, to distinguish propanal from propanone
questions.question: 1.16 g of propanal and 1.16 g of propanone (both M = 58 g mol⁻¹) are tested separately. What mass of silver (M = 108) does propanal give with excess Tollens' reagent, what mass of iodoform (CHI₃, M = 394) does propanone give with excess I₂/NaOH, and which statement about the reduction of these compounds is correct?
options: A) Propanal gives 4.32 g Ag (2 mol Ag per mol aldehyde) and no iodoform; propanone gives 7.88 g CHI₃ (it has a CH₃CO– group) and no silver mirror; NaBH₄ reduces propanal to propan-1-ol and propanone to propan-2-ol, while Clemmensen reduction (Zn–Hg/conc. HCl) or Wolff–Kishner reduction converts propanone to propane
B) Propanal gives 2.16 g Ag; propanone also gives a silver mirror
C) Both give 7.88 g CHI₃
D) Propanal gives 4.32 g Ag; Clemmensen reduction converts propanone to propan-2-ol
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 4.32 g Ag from propanal; 7.88 g CHI₃ from propanone; NaBH₄ gives alcohols; Clemmensen/Wolff–Kishner give the alkane.
Concept: Aldehydes differ from ketones in their oxidation reactions: aldehydes are easily oxidised to carboxylic acids by mild oxidising agents. On warming an aldehyde with freshly prepared ammoniacal silver nitrate solution (Tollens' reagent), a bright silver mirror is produced due to the formation of silver metal: RCHO + 2[Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ + 3OH⁻ → RCOO⁻ + 2Ag + 2H₂O + 4NH₃; ketones generally do not give this test. Aldehydes and ketones having at least one methyl group linked to the carbonyl carbon atom (methyl ketones) are oxidised by sodium hypohalite to sodium salts of the corresponding carboxylic acids having one carbon atom less than the carbonyl compound; the methyl group is converted to haloform; iodoform reaction with sodium hypoiodite is used for detection of the CH₃CO group. Aldehydes and ketones are reduced to primary and secondary alcohols respectively by sodium borohydride (NaBH₄) or lithium aluminium hydride (LiAlH₄) as well as by catalytic hydrogenation; the carbonyl group of aldehydes and ketones is reduced to a CH₂ group on treatment with zinc amalgam and concentrated hydrochloric acid (Clemmensen reduction) or with hydrazine followed by heating with sodium or potassium hydroxide in high boiling solvent such as ethylene glycol (Wolff–Kishner reduction).
Given: 1.16 g each; M = 58; Ag = 108; CHI₃ = 394.
Formula/Principle: 1 mol RCHO → 2 mol Ag; 1 mol CH₃COR → 1 mol CHI₃.
Step 1: n = 1.16/58 = 0.020 mol.
Step 2: Ag = 0.040 × 108 = 4.32 g.
Step 3: CHI₃ = 0.020 × 394 = 7.88 g.
Why: Aldehydes have an oxidisable C–H on the carbonyl carbon, while only methyl ketones (and ethanal) carry the CH₃CO– needed for the haloform reaction.
Why not the others: (B) Uses 1:1 Ag ratio; ketones do not reduce Tollens' reagent. (C) Propanal (CH₃CH₂CHO) lacks CH₃CO–. (D) Clemmensen reduces C=O to CH₂.
Key point: Tollens: 2Ag per CHO; iodoform needs CH₃CO–; NaBH₄ → alcohol, Clemmensen → alkane.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Arranging haloacetic acids and substituted benzoic acids in order of acid strength using inductive and resonance effects of substituents
questions.question: Which order of acid strength and explanation is correct?
options: A) CH₃COOH > ClCH₂COOH > FCH₂COOH, because larger halogens withdraw electrons more strongly
B) 4-Methoxybenzoic acid > benzoic acid > 4-nitrobenzoic acid
C) Carboxylic acids are weaker acids than phenols because the carboxylate ion has no resonance

D) FCH₂COOH (pKa ≈ 2.66) > ClCH₂COOH (2.86) > BrCH₂COOH (2.90) > CH₃COOH (4.76), and 4-nitrobenzoic acid (3.41) > benzoic acid (4.19) > 4-methoxybenzoic acid (4.46); electron-withdrawing groups stabilise the carboxylate anion by delocalising its negative charge and so increase acidity, the effect falling with decreasing electronegativity of the halogen, while electron-donating groups destabilise it; carboxylic acids are stronger than phenols because the carboxylate's charge is shared equally between two electronegative oxygen atoms
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) F > Cl > Br haloacetic acids > acetic acid; 4-nitro > benzoic > 4-methoxy; carboxylic acids stronger than phenols.
Concept: Carboxylic acids are weaker than mineral acids but stronger than alcohols and many simple phenols; the higher acidity of carboxylic acids as compared to phenols can be understood on the basis of the conjugate base: the carboxylate ion is stabilised by two equivalent resonance structures in which the negative charge is at the more electronegative oxygen atom, whereas in the phenoxide ion the charge is partly on less electronegative carbon atoms. Electron-withdrawing groups (EWG) increase the acidity of carboxylic acids by stabilising the conjugate base through delocalisation of the negative charge by inductive and/or resonance effects; conversely, electron-donating groups decrease the acidity by destabilising the conjugate base. The effect of the following groups in increasing acidity order is Ph < I < Br < Cl < F < CN < NO₂ < CF₃; thus FCH₂COOH > ClCH₂COOH > BrCH₂COOH. Direct attachment of groups such as phenyl or vinyl to the carboxylic acid increases its acidity due to the greater electronegativity of the sp² carbon; electron-withdrawing groups on the phenyl of aromatic carboxylic acids increase their acidity, while electron-donating groups decrease it.
Why: The more the negative charge of the carboxylate is spread out, the more stable the anion and the stronger the acid.
Why not the others: (A) Order reversed; F is most electronegative. (B) Order reversed; –NO₂ withdraws, –OCH₃ donates by resonance. (C) Carboxylate has two equivalent resonance forms.
Key point: EWG ↑ acidity (F > Cl > Br); EDG ↓ acidity; RCOOH > phenol.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Comparing numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in nuclides and ions to identify isotopes, isobars and isotones, and the comparison of neutron-to-proton ratios
questions.question: Consider ¹⁴₆C, ¹⁴₇N, ¹⁶₈O, ¹⁸₈O, ⁴⁰₁₈Ar and ⁴⁰₂₀Ca. How many pairs of isobars, isotopes and isotones (same number of neutrons) are present, and which nuclide has the highest neutron-to-proton ratio?
options: A) 1 isobar pair, 2 isotope pairs, 0 isotone pairs; ⁴⁰Ca has the highest n/p

B) 2 isobar pairs (¹⁴C–¹⁴N, ⁴⁰Ar–⁴⁰Ca), 1 isotope pair (¹⁶O–¹⁸O), 1 isotone pair (¹⁴C and ¹⁶O, 8 neutrons each); ¹⁴C has the highest n/p (8/6 ≈ 1.33, above ¹⁸O at 1.25 and ⁴⁰Ar at 1.22); isotopes have the same atomic number and chemical properties but different mass numbers, while isobars have the same mass number but different atomic numbers and chemical properties
C) 3 isobar pairs; 1 isotope pair; ¹⁸O has the highest n/p
D) 2 isobar pairs; 0 isotope pairs; ¹⁴N has the highest n/p
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 2 isobar pairs, 1 isotope pair, 1 isotone pair; ¹⁴C has the highest n/p ≈ 1.33.
Concept: The number of protons present in the nucleus is equal to the atomic number (Z); protons and neutrons present in the nucleus are collectively known as nucleons, and the total number of nucleons is termed the mass number (A); number of neutrons (n) = A − Z. Atoms with identical atomic number but different atomic mass number are known as isotopes; chemical properties of atoms are controlled by the number of electrons, which are determined by the number of protons in the nucleus, so all the isotopes of a given element show the same chemical behaviour. Atoms with the same mass number but different atomic number are called isobars, for example ¹⁴₆C and ¹⁴₇N. Nuclides with the same number of neutrons are called isotones. The neutron-to-proton ratio n/Z is found for each nuclide; among stable nuclides it is about 1 for light elements and rises for heavier ones, but neutron-rich light nuclides such as radioactive ¹⁴C can exceed it.
Given: Six nuclides with A and Z.
Formula/Principle: n = A − Z; isotopes same Z; isobars same A; isotones same n.
Step 1: n: ¹⁴C 8, ¹⁴N 7, ¹⁶O 8, ¹⁸O 10, ⁴⁰Ar 22, ⁴⁰Ca 20.
Step 2: Same A: (¹⁴C, ¹⁴N), (⁴⁰Ar, ⁴⁰Ca) ⇒ 2; same Z: (¹⁶O, ¹⁸O) ⇒ 1; same n: (¹⁴C, ¹⁶O) ⇒ 1.
Step 3: n/p: ¹⁴C 8/6 = 1.33, ¹⁸O 10/8 = 1.25, ⁴⁰Ar 22/18 = 1.22, ⁴⁰Ca 1.00, ¹⁶O 1.00, ¹⁴N 1.00 ⇒ ¹⁴C highest.
Why: Each label depends on a different count — Z for isotopes, A for isobars, n for isotones.
Why not the others: (A) Undercounts isobars, overcounts isotopes. (C) Only two pairs share A. (D) ¹⁶O and ¹⁸O are isotopes.
Key point: Isotopes same Z; isobars same A; isotones same n = A − Z.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity; s and p block trends
questions.sub_topic: Identifying the group of an element from its successive ionisation enthalpies and explaining irregularities in first ionisation enthalpy across period 2
questions.question: Successive ionisation enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹) of two elements are X: 738, 1451, 7733, 10540 and Y: 496, 4562, 6910, 9543. Which conclusion is correct?
options: A) X belongs to group 1 and Y to group 2
B) Both belong to group 13 because they have four ionisation enthalpies

C) X belongs to group 2 (the large jump after the second electron shows two valence electrons, as in Mg) and Y to group 1 (jump after the first, as in Na); across period 2, the first ionisation enthalpy of boron is lower than that of beryllium because the 2p electron is less penetrating and more shielded than a 2s electron, and that of oxygen is lower than nitrogen because removing one of the paired 2p electrons is easier owing to electron–electron repulsion, while nitrogen has a stable half-filled 2p³ configuration
D) The ionisation enthalpy always decreases from one electron to the next
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) X group 2 (Mg), Y group 1 (Na); B < Be and O < N explained by penetration and pairing.
Concept: Ionisation enthalpy is the energy required to remove an electron from an isolated gaseous atom in its ground state; the second ionisation enthalpy is always higher than the first because it is more difficult to remove an electron from a positively charged ion than from a neutral atom, and successive values increase. A very large jump occurs when an electron must be removed from a new, inner (noble-gas core) shell, so the number of electrons removed before the big jump equals the number of valence electrons. The first ionisation enthalpy of boron (Z = 5) is slightly less than that of beryllium (Z = 4) even though the former has a greater nuclear charge: when we consider the same principal quantum level, an s-electron is attracted to the nucleus more than a p-electron; in beryllium the electron removed is an s-electron, whereas in boron it is a p-electron, which is shielded from the nucleus by the inner core of electrons and the 2s electrons. Similarly, the first ionisation enthalpy of oxygen is smaller than that of nitrogen: in nitrogen, the three 2p electrons reside in different atomic orbitals (Hund's rule), whereas in oxygen two of the four 2p electrons must occupy the same 2p orbital, resulting in increased electron–electron repulsion; consequently, it is easier to remove the fourth 2p electron from oxygen than one of the three 2p electrons from nitrogen.
Given: X: jump between IE₂ (1451) and IE₃ (7733); Y: jump between IE₁ (496) and IE₂ (4562).
Formula/Principle: Number of electrons removed before the largest jump = number of valence electrons.
Step 1: X: IE₃/IE₂ ≈ 5.3 ⇒ 2 valence electrons ⇒ group 2.
Step 2: Y: IE₂/IE₁ ≈ 9.2 ⇒ 1 valence electron ⇒ group 1.
Step 3: Period 2 anomalies: Be > B (2s vs 2p); N > O (half-filled vs paired).
Why: A huge jump signals that the next electron comes from the stable inner core, so successive ionisation data reveal the valence shell.
Why not the others: (A) Groups swapped. (B) Number of values listed does not set the group. (D) Successive ionisation enthalpies increase.
Key point: Big jump after n electrons ⇒ group with n valence electrons; B < Be, O < N.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Reading a table of electron configurations in molecular orbital theory to compare bond order, bond length, bond enthalpy and magnetic behaviour of O₂ and its ions and other diatomics
questions.question:
A table gives bonding and antibonding electrons for some species.

Species | Bonding electrons | Antibonding electrons
O₂⁺ | 10 | 5
O₂ | 10 | 6
O₂⁻ | 10 | 7
O₂²⁻ | 10 | 8
N₂ | 10 | 4
B₂ | 6 | 4

Which reading of this table is correct?
options: A) O₂²⁻ has the shortest bond and O₂⁺ the longest

B) Bond orders are O₂⁺ 2.5, O₂ 2, O₂⁻ 1.5, O₂²⁻ 1, N₂ 3, B₂ 1; bond length increases O₂⁺ < O₂ < O₂⁻ < O₂²⁻ while bond enthalpy decreases in the same order; O₂, O₂⁺, O₂⁻ and B₂ have unpaired electrons and are paramagnetic, while N₂ and O₂²⁻ are diamagnetic
C) N₂ is paramagnetic because it has 14 electrons
D) All species with an even number of electrons are diamagnetic, so O₂ is diamagnetic
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Bond orders 2.5, 2, 1.5, 1, 3, 1; length O₂⁺ < O₂ < O₂⁻ < O₂²⁻; O₂, O₂⁺, O₂⁻, B₂ paramagnetic.
Concept: Bond order is defined as one half the difference between the number of electrons present in the bonding and the antibonding orbitals: bond order = ½(Nb − Na). A positive bond order means a stable molecule; integral values of 1, 2 or 3 correspond to single, double or triple bonds. Bond order gives an approximate measure of bond length: bond length decreases as bond order increases, and bond enthalpy increases with bond order. If all the molecular orbitals in a molecule are doubly occupied, the substance is diamagnetic (repelled by a magnetic field); if one or more molecular orbitals are singly occupied, it is paramagnetic. In O₂, the two electrons in π*2px and π*2py are unpaired (Hund's rule), making O₂ paramagnetic — a fact that valence bond theory could not explain. B₂ has two unpaired electrons in the π2p orbitals (because σ2pz lies above π2p for B₂, C₂ and N₂), so it is paramagnetic; N₂ has all electrons paired.
Given: Nb and Na for each species.
Formula/Principle: Bond order = ½(Nb − Na).
Step 1: O₂⁺ ½(5) = 2.5; O₂ 2; O₂⁻ 1.5; O₂²⁻ 1.
Step 2: N₂ ½(6) = 3; B₂ ½(2) = 1.
Step 3: Unpaired: O₂ (2), O₂⁺ (1), O₂⁻ (1), B₂ (2) ⇒ paramagnetic; N₂, O₂²⁻ ⇒ diamagnetic.
Why: Adding electrons to antibonding π* orbitals weakens and lengthens the O–O bond, and unpaired π or π* electrons give paramagnetism.
Why not the others: (A) Order reversed. (C) N₂ electrons all paired. (D) O₂ has two unpaired electrons.
Key point: Bond order ½(Nb − Na); higher order ⇒ shorter, stronger bond; unpaired ⇒ paramagnetic.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Linking intermolecular and intramolecular hydrogen bonding to boiling points, volatility and density in nitrophenols, hydrogen halides and water
questions.question: Which set of observations is correctly explained by hydrogen bonding?
options: A) o-Nitrophenol is steam volatile and has a lower boiling point than p-nitrophenol because it forms an intramolecular hydrogen bond, while p-nitrophenol forms intermolecular hydrogen bonds and associates; HF boils higher than HCl because HF molecules are linked by strong intermolecular F–H···F hydrogen bonds; ice is less dense than liquid water because each molecule is hydrogen-bonded tetrahedrally to four others in an open cage-like structure
B) p-Nitrophenol is steam volatile because it forms intramolecular hydrogen bonds
C) HCl boils higher than HF because chlorine is larger
D) Ice is denser than water because hydrogen bonds pull molecules closer in the solid
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Intramolecular H-bond in o-nitrophenol; intermolecular H-bonds in p-nitrophenol, HF and ice.
Concept: When hydrogen is bonded to a strongly electronegative atom such as F, O or N, the electron pair of the covalent bond is displaced towards the more electronegative atom; the partially positive hydrogen atom then forms a bond with another electronegative atom, called a hydrogen bond, which is weaker than a covalent bond. Hydrogen bonds are of two types: intermolecular, formed between two different molecules of the same or different compounds (e.g. HF, water), and intramolecular, formed when a hydrogen atom lies in between two highly electronegative atoms within the same molecule (e.g. o-nitrophenol, where the hydrogen is between two oxygen atoms). Intermolecular hydrogen bonding leads to association of molecules and raises boiling points; intramolecular hydrogen bonding prevents association, so o-nitrophenol is more volatile (steam volatile) than p-nitrophenol. In ice, each water molecule is surrounded tetrahedrally by four other molecules through hydrogen bonds, giving a highly ordered, open three-dimensional structure; this is why the density of ice is less than that of water, and ice floats.
Why: Hydrogen bonds between molecules require extra energy to break on boiling, whereas internal hydrogen bonds use up the donor and acceptor and leave molecules unassociated.
Why not the others: (B) Para isomer bonds intermolecularly. (C) HF has hydrogen bonding; HCl does not significantly. (D) Hydrogen bonding makes ice open and less dense.
Key point: Intramolecular H-bond ⇒ volatile (o-nitrophenol); intermolecular ⇒ high bp (HF, H₂O); ice open, less dense.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Applying the combined gas law, ideal gas equation and Dalton's law of partial pressures to a gas sample that is heated and compressed and then mixed with another gas
questions.question: A sample of nitrogen occupies 10.0 L at 27 °C and 2.00 bar. It is heated to 127 °C and compressed to 5.00 L. It is then pumped into a rigid 5.00 L vessel already containing oxygen at 3.00 bar and 127 °C. What are the pressure after compression, the moles of nitrogen (R = 0.0831 L bar K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) and the total pressure in the vessel?
options: A) 2.67 bar; 8.02 mol; 5.67 bar
B) 9.41 bar; 0.80 mol; 12.4 bar
C) 4.00 bar; 0.40 mol; 7.00 bar

D) 5.33 bar (P₂ = 2.00 × (400/300) × (10.0/5.00)); n = PV/RT = (2.00 × 10.0)/(0.0831 × 300) ≈ 0.802 mol; total pressure = 5.33 + 3.00 = 8.33 bar, since by Dalton's law each gas exerts its own partial pressure in the same volume at the same temperature
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 5.33 bar; 0.802 mol; 8.33 bar.
Concept: Boyle's law (P ∝ 1/V at constant T and n) and Charles' law (V ∝ T at constant P and n), with temperatures in kelvin, combine into the combined gas law P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂ for a fixed amount of gas. Including Avogadro's law gives the ideal gas equation PV = nRT. Dalton's law of partial pressures states that the total pressure exerted by a mixture of non-reactive gases is equal to the sum of the partial pressures of the individual gases, i.e. the pressures these gases would exert if they were enclosed separately in the same volume and under the same conditions of temperature.
Given: V₁ = 10.0 L, T₁ = 300 K, P₁ = 2.00 bar; V₂ = 5.00 L, T₂ = 400 K; p(O₂) = 3.00 bar in 5.00 L at 400 K.
Formula/Principle: P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂; PV = nRT; P(total) = Σp.
Step 1: P₂ = 2.00 × (10.0/5.00) × (400/300) = 5.33 bar.
Step 2: n = (2.00 × 10.0)/(0.0831 × 300) = 20.0/24.93 = 0.802 mol.
Step 3: In the 5.00 L vessel at 400 K, p(N₂) = 5.33 bar ⇒ total = 8.33 bar.
Why: Pressure rises both because the gas is squeezed into half the volume and because it is heated; in a mixture each gas behaves as if alone.
Why not the others: (A) Volume ratio inverted; n wrong by 10. (B) Celsius temperatures used. (C) Temperature change ignored.
Key point: Use kelvin; P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂; partial pressures add.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Explaining positive and negative deviations of real gases from ideal behaviour using the compressibility factor, intermolecular attraction, molecular volume and the Boyle temperature
questions.question: At 273 K, a plot of compressibility factor Z = PV/nRT against pressure shows that Z for H₂ and He is greater than 1 at all pressures, while Z for CO₂ first falls below 1 and then rises above 1 at high pressure. Which explanation is correct?
options: A) H₂ and He have strong intermolecular attractions, which make Z exceed 1
B) CO₂ behaves ideally at low pressure because its molecules are large

C) Z < 1 means attractive forces dominate, making the gas more compressible than an ideal gas, as for CO₂ at moderate pressures; Z > 1 means the finite volume of molecules (repulsive effects) dominates, making it less compressible, as for all gases at very high pressure; H₂ and He show Z > 1 at all pressures at 273 K because this is above their Boyle temperature, where attraction is weak; in the van der Waals equation (P + an²/V²)(V − nb) = nRT, a corrects for attraction and b for molecular volume, and real gases approach ideal behaviour at low pressure and high temperature
D) All gases have Z = 1 at all pressures if the temperature is 273 K
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Z < 1: attraction dominates; Z > 1: molecular volume dominates; H₂, He above Boyle temperature; van der Waals a and b.
Concept: Real gases deviate from ideal behaviour because two assumptions of the kinetic theory fail: (i) there is no force of attraction between molecules, and (ii) the volume of molecules is negligible compared with the volume of the gas. At high pressure molecules interact, and attractive forces reduce the pressure exerted on the walls, so the observed pressure is less than ideal; the correction term is an²/V². At very high pressure molecules are close together, and the volume occupied by molecules themselves becomes significant, so the free volume is V − nb. The deviation is measured by the compressibility factor Z = PV/nRT; for an ideal gas Z = 1 at all pressures. For gases with Z < 1, attractive forces are dominant and the gas is more compressible (negative deviation); for Z > 1 the gas is less compressible (positive deviation) because repulsive forces dominate. The temperature at which a real gas obeys the ideal gas law over an appreciable range of pressure is called the Boyle temperature or Boyle point; above it real gases show positive deviation, below it they first show negative deviation. Gases show ideal behaviour when the volume occupied is large, i.e. at low pressure and high temperature.
Why: Whether a gas is more or less compressible than ideal depends on whether attraction or molecular size has the larger effect under the given conditions.
Why not the others: (A) H₂ and He have very weak attractions. (B) CO₂ deviates strongly because of strong attractions. (D) Z depends on pressure for real gases.
Key point: Z < 1 attraction; Z > 1 molecular volume; ideal at low P, high T.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Recovering n and r from given values of nPr and nCr using nPr = r!·nCr, and using nCr = nC(n−r)
questions.question: If \({}^nP_r=720\) and \({}^nC_r=120\), what are \(n\) and \(r\)? Also, if \({}^mC_8={}^mC_6\), what is \({}^mC_2\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(n=10,\ r=3;\ {}^{14}C_2=91\)
Given: \({}^nP_r=720,\ {}^nC_r=120,\ {}^mC_8={}^mC_6\)
Formula/Principle: \({}^nP_r=r!\,{}^nC_r;\ {}^mC_a={}^mC_b,\ a\ne b\Rightarrow a+b=m\)
Step 1: \(r!=\dfrac{720}{120}=6\Rightarrow r=3\)
Step 2: \(n(n-1)(n-2)=720=10\cdot9\cdot8\Rightarrow n=10\)
Step 3: \(m=8+6=14,\ {}^{14}C_2=\dfrac{14\cdot13}{2}=91\)
Worked derivation: \[{}^nP_r=\frac{n!}{(n-r)!}=r!\cdot\frac{n!}{r!(n-r)!}=r!\,{}^nC_r\]
Check: \[{}^{10}P_3=720,\ {}^{10}C_3=\frac{720}{6}=120\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{arrangements count each selection }r!\text{ times, so the ratio gives }r!\)
Why not the others: (A) \({}^6P_3=120\ne720\); (C) \({}^{10}P_6\ne720\) and \(m\) is wrong; (D) \({}^9P_3=504\).
Key point: \({}^nP_r/{}^nC_r=r!;\ {}^mC_a={}^mC_b\Rightarrow m=a+b\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Using the general term of a binomial expansion with negative powers to find the term independent of x, a specific coefficient and the middle terms
questions.question: In the expansion of \(\left(x^2-\dfrac{2}{x}\right)^9\), what is the term independent of \(x\), the coefficient of \(x^9\), and which terms are the middle terms?
options: A) \(-5376;\ 672;\) only the 5th term
B) \(84;\ -84;\) the 5th term only
C) \(5376;\ 672;\) the 4th and 5th terms
D) \(5376;\ -672;\) the 5th and 6th terms
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(5376;\ -672;\ T_5\text{ and }T_6\)
Given: \(n=9,\ a=x^2,\ b=-\dfrac2x\)
Formula/Principle: \(T_{r+1}={}^9C_r\,(x^2)^{9-r}\left(-\dfrac2x\right)^r={}^9C_r(-2)^r x^{18-3r}\)
Step 1: \(18-3r=0\Rightarrow r=6:\ {}^9C_6\cdot64=84\cdot64=5376\)
Step 2: \(18-3r=9\Rightarrow r=3:\ {}^9C_3(-8)=84(-8)=-672\)
Step 3: \(n+1=10\text{ terms}\Rightarrow\text{ middle terms }T_5,\ T_6\)
Worked derivation: \[T_7={}^9C_6(x^2)^3\left(-\tfrac2x\right)^6=84\cdot x^6\cdot\frac{64}{x^6}=5376\]
Check: \[T_4={}^9C_3(x^2)^6\left(-\tfrac2x\right)^3=84\cdot(-8)\,x^{9}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the power of }x\text{ in the general term fixes which }r\text{ gives the required term, and the sign comes from }(-2)^r\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{signs reversed; odd }n\text{ has two middle terms}\); (B) \(\text{omits the factor }(-2)^r\); (C) \(\text{sign of }x^9\text{ coefficient and middle terms wrong}\).
Key point: \(T_{r+1}={}^nC_r a^{n-r}b^r;\ \text{odd }n\Rightarrow\text{two middle terms}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding a circle that touches both axes and a given line, and then a second circle touching both axes and externally touching the first
questions.question: A circle in the first quadrant touches both coordinate axes and the line \(3x+4y=12\), and lies inside the triangle they form. A second, larger circle also touches both axes and touches the first circle externally. What are the first circle's equation and the second circle's radius?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \((x-1)^2+(y-1)^2=1;\ r_2=3+2\sqrt2\)
Given: \(\text{centre }(r,r);\ \text{line }3x+4y=12;\ \text{second centre }(a,a)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{distance from centre to tangent line}=\text{radius};\ \text{external touch: }C_1C_2=r_1+r_2\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{|3r+4r-12|}{5}=r\Rightarrow 12-7r=5r\Rightarrow r=1\text{ (inside the triangle)}\)
Step 2: \(\text{first circle: }(x-1)^2+(y-1)^2=1\)
Step 3: \(\sqrt2(a-1)=a+1\Rightarrow a=\dfrac{\sqrt2+1}{\sqrt2-1}=3+2\sqrt2\)
Worked derivation: \[a(\sqrt2-1)=\sqrt2+1\Rightarrow a=\frac{(\sqrt2+1)^2}{2-1}=3+2\sqrt2\]
Check: \[r=1=\frac{3+4-5}{2}\ (\text{inradius of the }3\text{–}4\text{–}5\text{ triangle})\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{touching both axes puts the centre on }y=x\text{, and each tangency gives one equation}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(r=2\text{ is not tangent to the line}\); (C) \(\text{second radius solves }\sqrt2 a=a+1\text{ instead}\); (D) \(r=3\text{ lies outside; }3-2\sqrt2\text{ is the smaller touching circle}\).
Key point: \(\text{touches both axes}\Rightarrow\text{centre }(r,r);\ C_1C_2=r_1+r_2\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Applying the product, quotient and chain rules to find a tangent slope, the derivative of a composite function from tabulated values, and a quotient derivative at a point
questions.question: What is the slope of the tangent to \(y=x\sqrt{1+x^2}\) at \(x=\sqrt3\); the value of \(h'(1)\) where \(h=f\circ g\), \(g(1)=2,\ g'(1)=3,\ f'(2)=-1\); and the derivative of \(\dfrac{\sin x}{x}\) at \(x=\pi\)?
options: A) \(\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2};\ 3;\ \dfrac1\pi\)
C) \(\dfrac72;\ -3;\ -\dfrac1\pi\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\dfrac72;\ -3;\ -\dfrac1\pi\)
Given: \(y=x\sqrt{1+x^2};\ g(1)=2,\ g'(1)=3,\ f'(2)=-1;\ u=\dfrac{\sin x}{x}\)
Formula/Principle: \((uv)'=u'v+uv';\ (f\circ g)'(x)=f'(g(x))\,g'(x);\ \left(\dfrac uv\right)'=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}\)
Step 1: \(y'=\sqrt{1+x^2}+\dfrac{x^2}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}=\dfrac{1+2x^2}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}=\dfrac{7}{2}\text{ at }x=\sqrt3\)
Step 2: \(h'(1)=f'(2)\cdot g'(1)=(-1)(3)=-3\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\dfrac{\sin x}{x}=\dfrac{x\cos x-\sin x}{x^2}=\dfrac{-\pi}{\pi^2}=-\dfrac1\pi\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{d}{dx}\sqrt{1+x^2}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1+x^2}}\cdot2x=\frac{x}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}\]
Check: \[x=\sqrt3:\ \frac{1+6}{\sqrt4}=\frac72\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{each rule handles one way functions are combined: product, composition, quotient}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{omits a term of the product rule and the minus signs}\); (B) \(\text{uses }f'\text{ alone and }\sin\pi=0\text{ for the whole derivative}\); (D) \(\text{multiplies by }g(1)\text{ and drops }x^2\).
Key point: \((f\circ g)'=f'(g)\,g'\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding two unknown observations from a given mean and variance, and the effect of a linear transformation on mean and variance
questions.question: The six observations \(2,4,6,8,a,b\) have mean \(5\) and variance \(\dfrac{14}{3}\). What are \(a\) and \(b\), and what are the mean and variance after each observation is multiplied by \(3\) and then increased by \(2\)?
options: A) \(\{a,b\}=\{3,7\};\ \text{mean }17,\ \text{variance }42\)
B) \(\{a,b\}=\{4,6\};\ \text{mean }17,\ \text{variance }14\)
C) \(\{a,b\}=\{3,7\};\ \text{mean }15,\ \text{variance }44\)
D) \(\{a,b\}=\{1,9\};\ \text{mean }17,\ \text{variance }42\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(a,b=3,7;\ \text{new mean }17,\ \text{new variance }42\)
Given: \(n=6,\ \bar x=5,\ \sigma^2=\dfrac{14}{3}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\sigma^2=\dfrac{\sum x_i^2}{n}-\bar x^2;\ y=px+q\Rightarrow\bar y=p\bar x+q,\ \sigma_y^2=p^2\sigma_x^2\)
Step 1: \(20+a+b=30\Rightarrow a+b=10\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{120+a^2+b^2}{6}-25=\dfrac{14}{3}\Rightarrow a^2+b^2=58\)
Step 3: \(ab=\dfrac{100-58}{2}=21\Rightarrow\{a,b\}=\{3,7\};\ \bar y=17,\ \sigma_y^2=9\cdot\dfrac{14}{3}=42\)
Worked derivation: \[120+a^2+b^2=6\left(25+\tfrac{14}{3}\right)=178\Rightarrow a^2+b^2=58\]
Check: \[\frac{(9+1+1+9+4+4)}{6}=\frac{28}{6}=\frac{14}{3}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the mean fixes }a+b\text{ and the variance fixes }a^2+b^2\text{; adding a constant shifts the mean but not the spread}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(4,6\text{ give variance }\tfrac{11}{3}\text{; scaling by }3\text{ multiplies variance by }9\); (C) \(\text{omits the }+2\text{ and adds }2\text{ to variance}\); (D) \(1,9\text{ give }a^2+b^2=82\).
Key point: \(\sigma^2(px+q)=p^2\sigma^2(x)\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding P(B) from P(A∪B) when A and B are independent or mutually exclusive, and the possible range of P(A∩B) in general
questions.question: \(P(A)=0.4\) and \(P(A\cup B)=0.6\). What is \(P(B)\) if \(A\) and \(B\) are independent, and if they are mutually exclusive? For \(P(A)=0.4,\ P(B)=\tfrac13\) in general, what values can \(P(A\cap B)\) take?
options: B) \(\tfrac13\text{ in both cases};\ \{0\}\)
C) \(0.5\text{ and }0.2;\ \left[\tfrac{2}{15},\tfrac13\right]\)
D) \(\tfrac13\text{ and }0.2;\ \left[0,\tfrac13\right]\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\tfrac13;\ 0.2;\ 0\le P(A\cap B)\le\tfrac13\)
Given: \(P(A)=0.4,\ P(A\cup B)=0.6\)
Formula/Principle: \(P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B);\ \text{independent: }P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)\)
Step 1: \(\text{Independent: }0.4+x-0.4x=0.6\Rightarrow0.6x=0.2\Rightarrow x=\tfrac13\)
Step 2: \(\text{Mutually exclusive: }0.4+x=0.6\Rightarrow x=0.2\)
Step 3: \(\max(0,\,0.4+\tfrac13-1)\le P(A\cap B)\le\min(0.4,\tfrac13)\Rightarrow\left[0,\tfrac13\right]\)
Worked derivation: \[P(A\cap B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cup B)\ge P(A)+P(B)-1=-\tfrac{4}{15}\Rightarrow\text{lower limit }0\]
Check: \[\text{independent: }0.4+\tfrac13-\tfrac{2}{15}=\tfrac{6+5-2}{15}=0.6\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the multiplication theorem for independent events and the empty intersection for exclusive events give different }P(B)\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{cases swapped; upper limit is }\min(P(A),P(B))\); (B) \(\text{exclusive case differs}\); (C) \(0.5\text{ fails the union; }\tfrac2{15}\text{ is only the independent value}\).
Key point: \(\text{independent: }P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B);\ \text{exclusive: }P(A\cap B)=0\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Applying the theorem of total probability over three machines, then Bayes' theorem to find which machine probably produced a defective item
questions.question: Machines \(X,Y,Z\) produce \(50\%,30\%,20\%\) of a factory's bolts, with defective rates \(1\%,2\%,3\%\). A bolt is chosen at random. What is the probability it is defective, and given that it is defective, the probability it came from \(Z\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(P(D)=0.017;\ P(Z\mid D)=\tfrac{6}{17}\)
Given: \(P(X)=0.5,\ P(Y)=0.3,\ P(Z)=0.2;\ P(D\mid X)=0.01,\ P(D\mid Y)=0.02,\ P(D\mid Z)=0.03\)
Formula/Principle: \(P(D)=\sum P(E_i)P(D\mid E_i);\ P(E_i\mid D)=\dfrac{P(E_i)P(D\mid E_i)}{P(D)}\)
Step 1: \(P(D)=0.005+0.006+0.006=0.017\)
Step 2: \(P(Z\mid D)=\dfrac{0.006}{0.017}=\dfrac{6}{17}\)
Step 3: \(P(X\mid D)=\tfrac{5}{17},\ P(Y\mid D)=\tfrac{6}{17}\)
Worked derivation: \[P(Z\mid D)=\frac{0.2\times0.03}{0.5\times0.01+0.3\times0.02+0.2\times0.03}=\frac{6}{17}\]
Check: \[\tfrac{5}{17}+\tfrac{6}{17}+\tfrac{6}{17}=1\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the machines partition the sample space, so their weighted defect rates add to give }P(D)\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{averages the defect rates without weights}\); (C) \(\text{adds rates; ignores Bayes}\); (D) \(\tfrac{5}{17}\text{ is }P(X\mid D)\).
Key point: \(\text{total probability then Bayes}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Recovering a matrix from its symmetric and skew-symmetric parts, and properties of skew-symmetric matrices
questions.question: A square matrix \(A\) satisfies \(A+A^{T}=\begin{pmatrix}4&6\\6&10\end{pmatrix}\) and \(A-A^{T}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-2\\2&0\end{pmatrix}\). What is \(A\), what is \(\det A\), and which statement is true?
options: A) \(A=\begin{pmatrix}4&4\\8&10\end{pmatrix};\ \det A=8;\ \text{every skew-symmetric matrix is invertible}\)
B) \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&4\\2&5\end{pmatrix};\ \det A=2;\ \text{the diagonal of a skew-symmetric matrix is }1\)
C) \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\4&5\end{pmatrix};\ \det A=2;\ \text{every skew-symmetric matrix of odd order has determinant }0\)
D) \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&3\\3&5\end{pmatrix};\ \det A=1;\ A\text{ is symmetric}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\4&5\end{pmatrix};\ \det A=2;\ \text{odd-order skew-symmetric}\Rightarrow\det=0\)
Given: \(S=A+A^T,\ K=A-A^T\)
Formula/Principle: \(A=\tfrac12(A+A^T)+\tfrac12(A-A^T)\)
Step 1: \(\tfrac12 S=\begin{pmatrix}2&3\\3&5\end{pmatrix},\ \tfrac12K=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\)
Step 2: \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\4&5\end{pmatrix}\)
Step 3: \(\det A=10-8=2\)
Worked derivation: \[K^T=-K\Rightarrow\det K=\det(-K)=(-1)^n\det K\Rightarrow\det K=0\text{ for odd }n\]
Check: \[A^T=\begin{pmatrix}2&4\\2&5\end{pmatrix},\ A+A^T=\begin{pmatrix}4&6\\6&10\end{pmatrix}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{every square matrix splits uniquely into symmetric and skew-symmetric parts}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{forgets the }\tfrac12\text{; odd-order skew matrices are singular}\); (B) \(\text{this is }A^T\text{; skew diagonal entries are }0\); (D) \(\text{only the symmetric part}\).
Key point: \(A=\tfrac12(A+A^T)+\tfrac12(A-A^T)\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Showing with 2×2 matrices that AB can be zero with A, B non-zero, that AB ≠ BA, and that the binomial square formula fails for matrices
questions.question: Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\) and \(B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\). Which statement is correct?
options: A) \(AB=BA=O\), so matrices always commute
B) \(AB=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\) and \(BA=O\)
D) \(AB=O\) but \(BA=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}=A\ne O\); \(A^2=O\); and \((A+B)^2=A^2+AB+BA+B^2=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\ne A^2+2AB+B^2=B\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(AB=O,\ BA=A,\ A^2=O,\ (A+B)^2=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\)
Given: \(A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\ B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\)
Formula/Principle: \((A+B)^2=A^2+AB+BA+B^2\text{, which equals }A^2+2AB+B^2\text{ only if }AB=BA\)
Step 1: \(AB=\begin{pmatrix}0\cdot1+1\cdot0&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}=O\)
Step 2: \(BA=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}=A;\ A^2=O;\ B^2=B\)
Step 3: \((A+B)^2=O+O+A+B=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\)
Worked derivation: \[(A+B)^2=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\]
Check: \[A^2+2AB+B^2=O+O+B=B\ne(A+B)^2\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{matrix multiplication is not commutative, so products of non-zero matrices can vanish and binomial identities fail}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(BA\ne O\); (B) \(\text{products swapped}\); (C) \(\text{binomial formula invalid here}\).
Key point: \(AB=O\not\Rightarrow A=O\text{ or }B=O;\ AB\ne BA\text{ in general}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Choosing constants so that a piecewise function is continuous and differentiable at the joining point, and contrasting continuity with differentiability for |x − 2| and x|x|
questions.question: \(f(x)=\begin{cases}ax+b,&x<1\\x^2,&x\ge1\end{cases}\) is differentiable at \(x=1\). What are \(a\) and \(b\), and which statement about \(g(x)=|x-2|\) and \(h(x)=x|x|\) is correct?
options: A) \(a=2,\ b=-1;\ g\text{ is continuous but not differentiable at }2;\ h\text{ is differentiable at }0\text{ with }h'(0)=0\)
B) \(a=1,\ b=0;\ g\text{ is differentiable at }2\)
C) \(a=2,\ b=1;\ h\text{ is not differentiable at }0\)
D) \(a=-1,\ b=2;\ g\text{ is not continuous at }2\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(a=2,\ b=-1;\ g\text{ continuous, not differentiable at }2;\ h'(0)=0\)
Given: \(\text{pieces }ax+b\text{ and }x^2\text{ meet at }x=1\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{continuity: equal limits; differentiability: equal left and right derivatives}\)
Step 1: \(\text{Continuity: }a+b=1\)
Step 2: \(\text{Derivatives: }a=2\cdot1=2\Rightarrow b=-1\)
Step 3: \(g:\ \text{LHD}=-1,\ \text{RHD}=1;\ h:\ \lim_{t\to0}\dfrac{t|t|}{t}=\lim_{t\to0}|t|=0\)
Worked derivation: \[h'(0)=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{h(t)-h(0)}{t}=\lim_{t\to0}|t|=0\]
Check: \[x=1:\ 2(1)-1=1=1^2;\ \text{slopes }2=2\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{differentiability implies continuity, but a corner like }|x-2|\text{ is continuous without a derivative}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{slopes }1\ne2;\ g\text{ has a corner}\); (C) \(a+b=3\ne1\); (D) \(\text{slope }-1\ne2;\ g\text{ is continuous}\).
Key point: \(\text{differentiable}\Rightarrow\text{continuous, not conversely}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding dy/dx by implicit differentiation for a folium-type cubic curve at a point, and simplifying an inverse-trigonometric function with a half-angle identity before differentiating
questions.question: For the curve \(x^3+y^3=6xy\), what is \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) at \((3,3)\)? And for \(0<x<\pi\), what is \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\tan^{-1}\!\sqrt{\dfrac{1-\cos x}{1+\cos x}}\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(-1;\ \dfrac12\)
Given: \(x^3+y^3=6xy,\ (3,3);\ 0<x<\pi\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{differentiate both sides with }y=y(x);\ \dfrac{1-\cos x}{1+\cos x}=\tan^2\dfrac x2\)
Step 1: \(3x^2+3y^2y'=6y+6xy'\Rightarrow y'=\dfrac{2y-x^2}{y^2-2x}\)
Step 2: \(\text{At }(3,3):\ y'=\dfrac{6-9}{9-6}=-1\)
Step 3: \(0<\tfrac x2<\tfrac\pi2\Rightarrow\sqrt{\tan^2\tfrac x2}=\tan\tfrac x2\Rightarrow\tan^{-1}\left(\tan\tfrac x2\right)=\tfrac x2\Rightarrow\dfrac12\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{1-\cos x}{1+\cos x}=\frac{2\sin^2(x/2)}{2\cos^2(x/2)}=\tan^2\frac x2\]
Check: \[27+27=54=6\cdot3\cdot3\ \text{so }(3,3)\text{ lies on the curve}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{implicit differentiation avoids solving the cubic for }y\text{, and the half-angle identity reduces the inverse tangent to a linear function}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{sign lost}\); (B) \(\text{uses }\tan x\text{ instead of }\tan\tfrac x2\); (D) \(\text{numerator and sign wrong}\).
Key point: \(\tan^{-1}(\tan\theta)=\theta\text{ for }|\theta|<\tfrac\pi2\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Counting critical points and finding absolute maximum and minimum values of a cubic on a closed interval by comparing critical and end-point values
questions.question: For \(f(x)=2x^3-9x^2+12x+1\) on \([0,3]\), how many critical points lie in the interval, and what are the absolute maximum and minimum values?
options: B) \(2\ (x=1,2);\ \text{absolute max }10\text{ at }x=3,\ \text{absolute min }1\text{ at }x=0\)
C) \(2;\ \max 6\text{ at }x=1,\ \min 5\text{ at }x=2\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(2;\ \max f=10\ (x=3),\ \min f=1\ (x=0)\)
Given: \(f(x)=2x^3-9x^2+12x+1,\ [0,3]\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{absolute extrema on }[a,b]\text{ occur at critical points or end points}\)
Step 1: \(f'(x)=6x^2-18x+12=6(x-1)(x-2)=0\Rightarrow x=1,2\)
Step 2: \(f(0)=1,\ f(1)=6,\ f(2)=5,\ f(3)=10\)
Step 3: \(\text{largest }10,\ \text{smallest }1\)
Worked derivation: \[f(3)=54-81+36+1=10,\ f(2)=16-36+24+1=5\]
Check: \[f''(1)=-6<0\ (\text{local max }6),\ f''(2)=6>0\ (\text{local min }5)\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{local extrema need not be absolute; the end points must also be compared}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{misses }x=2\text{ and }x=3\); (C) \(\text{local, not absolute, values}\); (D) \(\text{only two critical points; }1<5\).
Key point: \(\text{compare }f\text{ at critical points and end points}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Integrating rational functions by partial fractions with distinct linear factors, including a definite integral
questions.question: What are \(\displaystyle\int\frac{x\,dx}{(x-1)(x-2)}\) and \(\displaystyle\int_2^3\frac{dx}{(x-1)(x+2)}\)?
options: A) \(\ln|x-1|+2\ln|x-2|+C;\ \tfrac13\ln\tfrac58\)
C) \(2\ln|x-1|-\ln|x-2|+C;\ \tfrac13\ln\tfrac85\)
D) \(-\ln|x-1|+2\ln|x-2|+C;\ \tfrac13\ln\tfrac85\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(-\ln|x-1|+2\ln|x-2|+C;\ \tfrac13\ln\tfrac85\)
Given: \(\dfrac{x}{(x-1)(x-2)},\ \dfrac{1}{(x-1)(x+2)}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac{px+q}{(x-a)(x-b)}=\dfrac{A}{x-a}+\dfrac{B}{x-b}\)
Step 1: \(x=A(x-2)+B(x-1):\ x=1\Rightarrow A=-1;\ x=2\Rightarrow B=2\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{1}{(x-1)(x+2)}=\dfrac13\left(\dfrac{1}{x-1}-\dfrac{1}{x+2}\right)\)
Step 3: \(\tfrac13\left[\ln\dfrac{x-1}{x+2}\right]_2^3=\tfrac13\left(\ln\tfrac25-\ln\tfrac14\right)=\tfrac13\ln\tfrac85\)
Worked derivation: \[\int\frac{x\,dx}{(x-1)(x-2)}=\int\left(\frac{-1}{x-1}+\frac{2}{x-2}\right)dx=-\ln|x-1|+2\ln|x-2|+C\]
Check: \[\frac{-1}{x-1}+\frac{2}{x-2}=\frac{-(x-2)+2(x-1)}{(x-1)(x-2)}=\frac{x}{(x-1)(x-2)}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{splitting into simple fractions turns each piece into a logarithm}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{sign of }A\text{ wrong; limits reversed}\); (B) \(\text{signs wrong; factor }\tfrac13\text{ lost}\); (C) \(A,B\text{ swapped}\).
Key point: \(\text{cover-up: }A=\left.\dfrac{px+q}{x-b}\right|_{x=a}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the area between an ellipse and its auxiliary circle in the first quadrant, and the area of the sector of a circle bounded by the lines y = |x|
questions.question: What is the area of the first-quadrant region lying between the ellipse \(\dfrac{x^2}{16}+\dfrac{y^2}{9}=1\) and its auxiliary circle \(x^2+y^2=16\), and the area of the region above both lines \(y=x\) and \(y=-x\) and inside the circle \(x^2+y^2=9\)?
options: C) \(\dfrac\pi4;\ \dfrac{9\pi}{4}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\pi;\ \dfrac{9\pi}{4}\)
Given: \(a=4,\ b=3;\ \text{circle }r=3;\ \text{lines }y=\pm x\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{quarter ellipse}=\tfrac14\pi ab;\ \text{quarter circle}=\tfrac14\pi a^2;\ \text{sector}=\tfrac12r^2\theta\)
Step 1: \(\text{quarter circle}=\tfrac14\pi(16)=4\pi;\ \text{quarter ellipse}=\tfrac14\pi(4)(3)=3\pi\)
Step 2: \(\text{region between them}=4\pi-3\pi=\pi\)
Step 3: \(\text{lines }y=\pm x\text{ make a right angle above the origin}\Rightarrow\theta=\tfrac\pi2;\ \text{sector}=\tfrac12(9)\left(\tfrac\pi2\right)=\tfrac{9\pi}{4}\)
Worked derivation: \[\int_0^4\left(\sqrt{16-x^2}-\tfrac34\sqrt{16-x^2}\right)dx=\tfrac14\int_0^4\sqrt{16-x^2}\,dx=\tfrac14(4\pi)=\pi\]
Check: \[\tfrac{9\pi}{4}=\tfrac14(9\pi)\ (\text{a quarter of the disc})\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the ellipse lies inside its auxiliary circle, so the region between them is the difference of two quarter areas}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{gives the quarter circle and a half disc}\); (C) \(\text{divides by 4 twice}\); (D) \(\text{quarter ellipse alone; sector angle halved}\).
Key point: \(\text{ellipse area }\pi ab;\ \text{sector }\tfrac12r^2\theta\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Solving a homogeneous first-order differential equation with an initial condition by the substitution y = vx, and studying where the solution decreases and its minimum
questions.question: Solve \(x\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x+y\) for \(x>0\) with \(y(1)=1\). Where is the solution decreasing, and what is its minimum value?
options: A) \(y=x\ln x;\ \text{decreasing on }(0,e^{-1});\ \min=-e^{-1}\)
B) \(y=x(\ln x+1);\ \text{decreasing on }(0,e^{-2});\ \min=-e^{-2}\text{ at }x=e^{-2}\)
C) \(y=x+\ln x;\ \text{increasing everywhere};\ \text{no minimum}\)
D) \(y=x(\ln x+1);\ \text{decreasing on }(e^{-2},\infty);\ \text{maximum }e^{-2}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(y=x(\ln x+1);\ \text{decreasing on }(0,e^{-2});\ \min=-e^{-2}\)
Given: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=1+\dfrac yx,\ y(1)=1\)
Formula/Principle: \(y=vx\Rightarrow\dfrac{dy}{dx}=v+x\dfrac{dv}{dx}\)
Step 1: \(v+xv'=1+v\Rightarrow dv=\dfrac{dx}{x}\Rightarrow v=\ln x+C\)
Step 2: \(y=x(\ln x+C);\ y(1)=1\Rightarrow C=1\)
Step 3: \(y'=\ln x+2<0\iff x<e^{-2};\ y(e^{-2})=e^{-2}(-2+1)=-e^{-2}\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{dy}{dx}=\ln x+1+1=\ln x+2,\ \frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac1x>0\]
Check: \[x\,y'=x\ln x+2x,\ x+y=x+x\ln x+x\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a homogeneous equation reduces to separable form with }v=y/x\)
Why not the others: (A) \(C\text{ omitted, so }y(1)\ne1\); (C) \(\text{not a solution}\); (D) \(\text{monotonicity reversed}\).
Key point: \(\text{homogeneous DE: put }y=vx\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Using the inclusion–exclusion principle for three sets to find the union and the numbers belonging to exactly one, exactly two and all three sets
questions.question: In a survey, \(n(A)=40,\ n(B)=50,\ n(C)=60,\ n(A\cap B)=20,\ n(B\cap C)=25,\ n(A\cap C)=15,\ n(A\cap B\cap C)=10\). How many are in at least one set, exactly one set and exactly two sets?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(100;\ 60;\ 30\)
Given: \(\text{the seven counts above}\)
Formula/Principle: \(n(A\cup B\cup C)=\sum n(A)-\sum n(A\cap B)+n(A\cap B\cap C)\)
Step 1: \(150-60+10=100\)
Step 2: \(\text{only }A=40-20-15+10=15,\ \text{only }B=15,\ \text{only }C=30\Rightarrow60\)
Step 3: \(\text{exactly two}=(20-10)+(25-10)+(15-10)=30\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{only }C=60-15-25+10=30\]
Check: \[60+30+10=100\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{each pairwise overlap counts the triple region once too often, so it is removed before splitting the union}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{no subtraction of overlaps}\); (B) \(\text{forgets to add back the triple}\); (D) \(\text{mixes exactly two with at least two}\).
Key point: \(\text{inclusion–exclusion; regions add to the union}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Counting all relations, reflexive relations, symmetric relations and relations that are both reflexive and symmetric on a three-element set
questions.question: On \(A=\{1,2,3\}\), how many relations, reflexive relations, symmetric relations, and relations that are both reflexive and symmetric are there?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(2^9=512;\ 2^6=64;\ 2^6=64;\ 2^3=8\)
Given: \(n=3,\ |A\times A|=9\)
