Formula/Principle: \(\text{a relation is any subset of }A\times A;\ \text{count free choices}\)
Step 1: \(\text{all relations}=2^{9}=512\)
Step 2: \(\text{reflexive: 3 diagonal pairs forced, 6 others free}\Rightarrow2^6=64\)
Step 3: \(\text{symmetric: 3 diagonal + 3 unordered pairs free}\Rightarrow2^6=64;\ \text{both: only 3 unordered pairs free}\Rightarrow2^3=8\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{reflexive: }2^{n^2-n};\ \text{symmetric: }2^{n(n+1)/2};\ \text{both: }2^{n(n-1)/2}\]
Check: \[n=3:\ 2^6,\ 2^6,\ 2^3\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{each condition removes or ties together some of the pairs that could be chosen freely}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{reflexive count wrong}\); (C) \(\text{counts pairs, not subsets}\); (D) \(\text{wrong powers}\).
Key point: \(\text{relations on an }n\text{-set: }2^{n^2}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Using sum-to-product formulae on given values of sin A + sin B and cos A + cos B to find tan((A+B)/2), cos(A+B) and cos(A−B)
questions.question: If \(\sin A+\sin B=\dfrac12\) and \(\cos A+\cos B=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\), what are \(\tan\dfrac{A+B}{2}\), \(\cos(A+B)\) and \(\cos(A-B)\)?
options: A) \(\sqrt3;\ -\dfrac12;\ \dfrac12\)
B) \(\dfrac1{\sqrt3};\ \dfrac12;\ \dfrac12\)
C) \(\dfrac1{\sqrt3};\ -\dfrac12;\ -\dfrac12\)
D) \(\dfrac1{\sqrt3};\ \dfrac12;\ -\dfrac12\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\dfrac1{\sqrt3};\ \dfrac12;\ -\dfrac12\)
Given: \(\sin A+\sin B=\tfrac12,\ \cos A+\cos B=\tfrac{\sqrt3}2\)
Formula/Principle: \(\sin A+\sin B=2\sin\tfrac{A+B}2\cos\tfrac{A-B}2;\ \cos A+\cos B=2\cos\tfrac{A+B}2\cos\tfrac{A-B}2\)
Step 1: \(\text{divide: }\tan\tfrac{A+B}{2}=\dfrac{1/2}{\sqrt3/2}=\dfrac1{\sqrt3}\)
Step 2: \(\cos(A+B)=\dfrac{1-\tan^2\frac{A+B}2}{1+\tan^2\frac{A+B}2}=\dfrac{1-\frac13}{1+\frac13}=\dfrac12\)
Step 3: \(\text{square and add: }2+2\cos(A-B)=\tfrac14+\tfrac34=1\Rightarrow\cos(A-B)=-\tfrac12\)
Worked derivation: \[(\sin A+\sin B)^2+(\cos A+\cos B)^2=2+2(\cos A\cos B+\sin A\sin B)=2+2\cos(A-B)\]
Check: \[\cos\tfrac{A-B}2=\pm\tfrac12\Rightarrow\cos(A-B)=2\cdot\tfrac14-1=-\tfrac12\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{both sums share the factor }2\cos\tfrac{A-B}2\text{, so their ratio isolates the half-sum angle}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{ratio inverted}\); (B) \(\text{sign of }\cos(A-B)\text{ wrong}\); (C) \(\cos(A+B)\text{ sign wrong}\).
Key point: \(\dfrac{\sin A+\sin B}{\cos A+\cos B}=\tan\dfrac{A+B}{2}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Using the discriminant, the product of roots and the sign of f(1) to find parameter values for equal roots, roots of opposite sign, and 1 lying between the roots of a quadratic
questions.question: For \(f(x)=x^2-2kx+(k+6)\), for which \(k\) are the roots of \(f(x)=0\) equal, for which are they of opposite sign, and for which does \(1\) lie strictly between them?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(k=3\text{ or }-2;\ k<-6;\ k>7\)
Given: \(a=1,\ b=-2k,\ c=k+6\)
Formula/Principle: \(D=0\text{ for equal roots};\ \alpha\beta<0\text{ for opposite signs};\ a\,f(1)<0\text{ for }1\text{ between the roots}\)
Step 1: \(\tfrac D4=k^2-k-6=(k-3)(k+2)=0\Rightarrow k=3,-2\)
Step 2: \(\alpha\beta=k+6<0\Rightarrow k<-6\)
Step 3: \(f(1)=1-2k+k+6=7-k<0\Rightarrow k>7\)
Worked derivation: \[a=1>0,\ f(1)<0\Rightarrow\text{the upward parabola is below the axis at }x=1\Rightarrow\alpha<1<\beta\]
Check: \[k=8:\ x^2-16x+14,\ f(1)=-1<0\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a negative product or a negative value at a point forces the parabola to cross the axis on both sides, so real roots are guaranteed}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{inequalities reversed}\); (B) \(\text{factorisation signs wrong}\); (D) \(\text{wrong product and }f(1)\).
Key point: \(af(p)<0\iff p\text{ lies between the roots}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the values of a parameter for which a cubic has three, two or one distinct real roots by comparing the parameter with the local extreme values
questions.question: For \(x^3-3x+k=0\), for which \(k\) are there three distinct real roots, and for which \(k\) exactly two distinct real roots?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(-2<k<2;\ k=\pm2\)
Given: \(g(x)=x^3-3x,\ \text{roots where }g(x)=-k\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{a horizontal line }y=-k\text{ meets the graph of }g\text{ three times between its local extreme values}\)
Step 1: \(g'(x)=3x^2-3=0\Rightarrow x=\pm1\)
Step 2: \(g(-1)=2\ (\text{local max}),\ g(1)=-2\ (\text{local min})\)
Step 3: \(-2<-k<2\iff|k|<2\Rightarrow\text{three roots};\ -k=\pm2\Rightarrow\text{a double root}\Rightarrow\text{two distinct roots}\)
Worked derivation: \[k=2:\ x^3-3x+2=(x-1)^2(x+2)\]
Check: \[k=-2:\ x^3-3x-2=(x+1)^2(x-2)\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the number of crossings depends on where the line lies relative to the turning values}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(|k|>2\text{ gives one root}\); (C) \(k=\pm2\text{ give a repeated root}\); (D) \(k>2\text{ gives one root}\).
Key point: \(\text{three real roots}\iff f(\text{local max})\cdot f(\text{local min})<0\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Predicting the nature, power and focal length of a combination of a convex and a concave lens in contact, and the magnification of a lens system
questions.question: A thin convex lens of focal length \(20\text{ cm}\) is placed in contact with a thin concave lens of focal length \(30\text{ cm}\). What is the combination's power and nature, and which statement about lens combinations is correct?
options: A) \(P=-8.3\text{ D}\); diverging, because the concave lens always dominates
B) \(P=+8.3\text{ D}\); converging with focal length \(12\text{ cm}\)

C) \(P=+1.67\text{ D}\); converging with focal length \(60\text{ cm}\); powers of thin lenses in contact add, and the total magnification of a lens system is the product of the magnifications of the individual lenses
D) \(P=+1.67\text{ D}\); diverging; the total magnification is the sum of the individual magnifications
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(P=+1.67\text{ D},\ f=+60\text{ cm}\), converging; \(m=m_1m_2\)
Given: \(f_1=+0.20\text{ m},\ f_2=-0.30\text{ m}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac1F=\dfrac1{f_1}+\dfrac1{f_2};\ P=P_1+P_2;\ m=m_1m_2\cdots\)
Step 1: \(P_1=\dfrac{1}{0.20}=+5\text{ D},\ P_2=\dfrac{1}{-0.30}=-3.33\text{ D}\)
Step 2: \(P=5-3.33=+1.67\text{ D}\)
Step 3: \(F=\dfrac{1}{1.67}\text{ m}=0.60\text{ m}=60\text{ cm}>0\Rightarrow\text{converging}\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac1F=\frac1{20}-\frac1{30}=\frac{3-2}{60}=\frac1{60}\Rightarrow F=60\text{ cm}\]
Check: \[|f_{\text{convex}}|<|f_{\text{concave}}|\Rightarrow\text{the convex lens is stronger}\Rightarrow F>0\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the stronger lens (shorter focal length) decides the nature of a thin-lens pair, since powers add}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{the concave lens is weaker here}\); (B) \(\text{adds magnitudes, ignoring sign}\); (D) \(\text{positive power means converging; magnifications multiply}\).
Key point: \(P=P_1+P_2\text{ for thin lenses in contact; sign decides nature}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.sub_topic: Applying Einstein's photoelectric equation as energy conservation to find the work function, maximum kinetic energy, stopping potential and maximum speed, and the effect of intensity
questions.question: Light of wavelength \(300\text{ nm}\) falls on a metal whose threshold wavelength is \(500\text{ nm}\). Taking \(hc=1240\text{ eV nm}\), what are the work function, the stopping potential and the maximum speed of photoelectrons (\(m_e=9.1\times10^{-31}\text{ kg}\)), and what happens if the intensity is doubled?
options: A) \(\phi=2.48\text{ eV};\ V_0\approx1.65\text{ V};\ v_{\max}\approx7.6\times10^{5}\text{ m s}^{-1}\); doubling intensity doubles the photocurrent but leaves \(V_0\) unchanged
B) \(\phi=4.13\text{ eV};\ V_0=2.48\text{ V}\); doubling intensity doubles \(V_0\)
D) \(\phi=1.65\text{ eV};\ V_0=2.48\text{ V}\); intensity affects the threshold wavelength
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\phi=2.48\text{ eV},\ V_0=1.65\text{ V},\ v_{\max}\approx7.6\times10^5\text{ m s}^{-1}\); intensity changes current only
Given: \(\lambda=300\text{ nm},\ \lambda_0=500\text{ nm},\ hc=1240\text{ eV nm}\)
Formula/Principle: \(h\nu=\phi_0+K_{\max};\ K_{\max}=eV_0=\tfrac12m v_{\max}^2;\ \phi_0=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0}\)
Step 1: \(h\nu=\dfrac{1240}{300}=4.13\text{ eV};\ \phi_0=\dfrac{1240}{500}=2.48\text{ eV}\)
Step 2: \(K_{\max}=4.13-2.48=1.65\text{ eV}\Rightarrow V_0=1.65\text{ V}\)
Step 3: \(v_{\max}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2\times1.65\times1.6\times10^{-19}}{9.1\times10^{-31}}}\approx7.6\times10^{5}\text{ m s}^{-1}\)
Worked derivation: \[v_{\max}^2=\frac{5.28\times10^{-19}}{9.1\times10^{-31}}=5.8\times10^{11}\Rightarrow v_{\max}=7.6\times10^5\text{ m s}^{-1}\]
Check: \[\lambda<\lambda_0\Rightarrow h\nu>\phi_0\Rightarrow\text{emission occurs}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{each photon gives all its energy to one electron; part frees it and the rest is kinetic energy, so only frequency sets }K_{\max}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{uses photon energy as }\phi\text{; intensity does not change }V_0\); (C) \(\text{takes }V_0\text{ equal to photon energy}\); (D) \(\phi\text{ wrong; threshold is a property of the metal}\).
Key point: \(eV_0=h\nu-\phi_0;\ \text{intensity}\to\text{current, frequency}\to K_{\max}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Using the Rydberg formula to compare the longest wavelengths of the Lyman and Balmer series, the Lyman series limit, and the scaling of wavelengths with Z for hydrogen-like ions
questions.question: Using \(\dfrac1\lambda=RZ^2\left(\dfrac1{n_1^2}-\dfrac1{n_2^2}\right)\) with \(R=1.097\times10^{7}\text{ m}^{-1}\), what is the ratio of the longest Lyman wavelength to the longest Balmer wavelength in hydrogen, the shortest Lyman wavelength, and the longest Lyman wavelength of \(\text{He}^+\) if that of hydrogen is \(121.6\text{ nm}\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(\lambda_{L}/\lambda_{B}=\dfrac{5}{27};\ \lambda_{\min,L}=91.2\text{ nm};\ \lambda(\text{He}^+)=30.4\text{ nm}\)
Given: \(\text{Lyman }n_1=1;\ \text{Balmer }n_1=2;\ Z_{\text{He}^+}=2\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac1\lambda=RZ^2\left(\dfrac1{n_1^2}-\dfrac1{n_2^2}\right);\ \lambda\propto\dfrac{1}{Z^2}\)
Step 1: \(\text{Lyman longest }(2\to1):\ \dfrac1\lambda=\dfrac{3R}{4};\ \text{Balmer longest }(3\to2):\ \dfrac1\lambda=\dfrac{5R}{36}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{\lambda_L}{\lambda_B}=\dfrac{5/36}{3/4}=\dfrac{5}{27}\)
Step 3: \(\lambda_{\min,L}=\dfrac1R=91.2\text{ nm};\ \lambda(\text{He}^+)=\dfrac{121.6}{4}=30.4\text{ nm}\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{5}{36}\cdot\frac{4}{3}=\frac{20}{108}=\frac{5}{27}\]
Check: \[121.6\times\frac{27}{5}=656.6\text{ nm}\ (\text{H}_\alpha\text{ red line})\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{longest wavelength means the smallest energy gap (adjacent levels); the }Z^2\text{ factor scales all hydrogen-like lines}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{ratio inverted; }\lambda\propto1/Z^2\text{ not }1/Z\); (B) \(\text{wrong ratio; }Z\text{ scaling ignored}\); (C) \(\text{uses only the Balmer factor; Balmer limit given}\).
Key point: \(\lambda\propto\dfrac{1}{Z^2(1/n_1^2-1/n_2^2)}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting the observations of neutron-induced fission of uranium-235 and the roles of moderators, control rods and the multiplication factor in a reactor
questions.question: When uranium is bombarded with slow neutrons, barium and krypton are found among the products and more neutrons are released. In a reactor, the fast neutrons produced must be slowed down, and the reaction rate must be held steady. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) The neutrons are absorbed by the nucleus without splitting it; moderators speed up neutrons

B) \(^{235}\text{U}\) captures a slow (thermal) neutron and splits into two medium-mass fragments, such as \(^{141}\text{Ba}\) and \(^{92}\text{Kr}\), releasing on average about \(2.5\) neutrons and about \(200\text{ MeV}\) per fission; moderators such as heavy water or graphite slow fast neutrons by elastic collisions with light nuclei; control rods of cadmium or boron absorb neutrons; the reactor is kept steady with multiplication factor \(K=1\), while \(K>1\) leads to an uncontrolled chain reaction
C) Fission releases energy only if the fragments are heavier than uranium
D) Control rods slow neutrons by collisions, and moderators absorb them
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Slow-neutron fission of \(^{235}\text{U}\) into medium nuclei with \(\sim2.5\) neutrons and \(\sim200\text{ MeV}\); moderators slow, control rods absorb; \(K=1\) steady
Given: \(\text{products Ba, Kr and neutrons; fast neutrons must be slowed; steady rate required}\)
Formula/Principle: \(^{1}_{0}n+{}^{235}_{92}\text{U}\to{}^{236}_{92}\text{U}\to{}^{141}_{56}\text{Ba}+{}^{92}_{36}\text{Kr}+3\,{}^{1}_{0}n;\ K=\dfrac{\text{neutrons in one generation}}{\text{neutrons in previous generation}}\)
Step 1: \(\text{Ba }(Z=56)+\text{Kr }(Z=36)=92\Rightarrow\text{the nucleus has split}\)
Step 2: \(\text{fast neutrons lose energy fastest in collisions with nuclei of similar mass}\Rightarrow\text{light-nucleus moderators}\)
Step 3: \(\text{control rods absorb surplus neutrons to hold }K=1\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{mass number: }1+235=141+92+3=236;\ \text{charge: }92=56+36\]
Check: \[\text{neutrons released per fission}>1\Rightarrow\text{a chain reaction is possible}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{each fission releases extra neutrons, so the process can sustain itself only if neutron numbers are controlled}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{products show splitting; moderators slow neutrons}\); (C) \(\text{fragments are lighter, with higher binding energy per nucleon}\); (D) \(\text{roles swapped}\).
Key point: \(\text{moderator slows, control rod absorbs; }K=1\text{ steady}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Reading the forward and reverse I–V characteristic of a silicon p-n junction diode to identify threshold voltage, reverse saturation current and breakdown, and calculating dynamic resistance
questions.question: On the I–V graph of a silicon diode, forward current is negligible until about \(0.7\text{ V}\) and then rises steeply, passing \(10\text{ mA}\) at \(0.70\text{ V}\) and \(30\text{ mA}\) at \(0.80\text{ V}\); in reverse bias a tiny, nearly constant current of a few \(\mu\text{A}\) flows until a sudden large increase at a certain reverse voltage. What is the dynamic resistance in that forward range, and which interpretation is correct?
options: A) \(70\ \Omega\); the reverse current is due to majority carriers
B) \(0.2\ \Omega\); the diode obeys Ohm's law in forward bias
C) \(26.7\ \Omega\); breakdown occurs at the threshold voltage

D) \(r_d=\dfrac{\Delta V}{\Delta I}=\dfrac{0.10}{0.020}=5\ \Omega\); the threshold (knee) voltage, about \(0.7\text{ V}\) for Si and \(0.2\text{ V}\) for Ge, is where the barrier is overcome; the small reverse current, due to minority carriers, is nearly independent of voltage; at the breakdown voltage the reverse current rises sharply; the I–V graph is non-linear, so resistance depends on the operating point
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(r_d=5\ \Omega\); knee \(\approx0.7\text{ V}\) (Si); minority-carrier reverse current; breakdown
Given: \((0.70\text{ V},10\text{ mA}),\ (0.80\text{ V},30\text{ mA})\)
Formula/Principle: \(r_d=\dfrac{\Delta V}{\Delta I}\)
Step 1: \(\Delta V=0.80-0.70=0.10\text{ V}\)
Step 2: \(\Delta I=30-10=20\text{ mA}=0.020\text{ A}\)
Step 3: \(r_d=\dfrac{0.10}{0.020}=5\ \Omega\)
Worked derivation: \[r_d=\frac{0.10\text{ V}}{2.0\times10^{-2}\text{ A}}=5\ \Omega\]
Check: \[\text{static }V/I\text{ at }0.80\text{ V}=26.7\ \Omega\ne r_d\Rightarrow\text{non-ohmic}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{beyond the knee, a small rise in voltage lowers the barrier enough to raise current sharply, so dynamic resistance is small}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{uses }V/I\text{ at }0.70\text{ V; reverse current is minority-carrier}\); (B) \(\text{mixes units; diode is non-ohmic}\); (C) \(\text{static, not dynamic, resistance; breakdown is in reverse bias}\).
Key point: \(r_d=\Delta V/\Delta I\text{ on the steep forward part}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Analysing positions of a ball rolling from rest down an incline at equal time intervals to verify uniform acceleration, find the acceleration and predict later motion
questions.question: A ball released from rest on an incline is photographed every \(1.0\text{ s}\). Its distances from the start are \(0.10,\ 0.40,\ 0.90\) and \(1.60\text{ m}\) at \(t=1,2,3,4\text{ s}\). What are the acceleration and the speed at \(t=4\text{ s}\), and how far does it travel during the fifth second?
options: C) \(0.20\text{ m s}^{-2};\ 0.80\text{ m s}^{-1};\ 0.90\text{ m}\); the distances in successive equal intervals are in the ratio \(1:3:5:7\), confirming uniform acceleration from rest
D) \(0.20\text{ m s}^{-2};\ 0.40\text{ m s}^{-1};\ 2.5\text{ m}\); the motion is uniform
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(a=0.20\text{ m s}^{-2},\ v(4)=0.80\text{ m s}^{-1},\ s_5=0.90\text{ m}\)
Given: \(x(1)=0.10,\ x(2)=0.40,\ x(3)=0.90,\ x(4)=1.60\text{ m};\ u=0\)
Formula/Principle: \(x=\tfrac12at^2;\ v=at;\ s_n=u+\tfrac a2(2n-1)\)
Step 1: \(\text{interval distances }0.10,0.30,0.50,0.70\Rightarrow1:3:5:7\)
Step 2: \(0.10=\tfrac12a(1)^2\Rightarrow a=0.20\text{ m s}^{-2}\)
Step 3: \(v(4)=0.20\times4=0.80\text{ m s}^{-1};\ s_5=\tfrac{0.20}{2}(2\cdot5-1)=0.90\text{ m}\)
Worked derivation: \[x(5)-x(4)=\tfrac12(0.20)(25-16)=0.90\text{ m}\]
Check: \[x(4)=\tfrac12(0.20)(16)=1.60\text{ m}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(x\propto t^2\text{ from rest, so equal intervals cover distances in the ratio of odd numbers}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{uses }x=at^2\); (B) \(\text{uses }x/t^2\text{ at }t=2\text{ with a factor 2 error}\); (D) \(\text{speed and distance wrong; motion is accelerated}\).
Key point: \(\text{from rest: }s_1:s_2:s_3\ldots=1:3:5\ldots\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the centripetal acceleration and force for a car on a level curve, the minimum coefficient of friction, and the banking angle needed without friction
questions.question: A \(900\text{ kg}\) car rounds a level curve of radius \(100\text{ m}\) at \(72\text{ km h}^{-1}\) (\(g=10\text{ m s}^{-2}\)). What are the centripetal acceleration, the force needed, the minimum coefficient of static friction, and the banking angle at which no friction is needed?
options: A) \(4\text{ m s}^{-2};\ 3600\text{ N};\ \mu_{\min}=0.4;\ \tan\theta=0.4\ (\theta\approx22^\circ)\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(a_c=4\text{ m s}^{-2},\ F=3600\text{ N},\ \mu_{\min}=0.4,\ \tan\theta=0.4\)
Given: \(m=900\text{ kg},\ r=100\text{ m},\ v=72\text{ km h}^{-1}=20\text{ m s}^{-1}\)
Formula/Principle: \(a_c=\dfrac{v^2}{r};\ F=ma_c\le\mu mg;\ \tan\theta=\dfrac{v^2}{rg}\)
Step 1: \(a_c=\dfrac{400}{100}=4\text{ m s}^{-2}\)
Step 2: \(F=900\times4=3600\text{ N}\)
Step 3: \(\mu_{\min}=\dfrac{v^2}{rg}=\dfrac{400}{1000}=0.4;\ \tan\theta=0.4\)
Worked derivation: \[\mu mg\ge\frac{mv^2}{r}\Rightarrow\mu\ge\frac{v^2}{rg}\]
Check: \[\mu mg=0.4\times900\times10=3600\text{ N}=F\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{on a level road friction alone supplies the inward force; banking lets the normal force supply it instead}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{speed not converted to m s}^{-1}\); (C) \(72\text{ used directly in }v^2\); (D) \(\text{omits }g\text{ in }\mu\).
Key point: \(\mu_{\min}=\tan\theta_{\text{ideal}}=v^2/rg\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Comparing the minimum speeds at the top and bottom for a mass on a string and on a light rod in a vertical circle, and the minimum release height for a loop-the-loop track
questions.question: For a vertical circle of radius \(R\), what are the minimum speeds at the top and at the bottom for a mass on a string and for a mass on a light rigid rod, and from what minimum height must a small block be released on a frictionless track to complete a loop of radius \(0.40\text{ m}\) (block sliding, not rolling)?
options: A) \(\text{string: }0\text{ and }\sqrt{4gR};\ \text{rod: }\sqrt{gR}\text{ and }\sqrt{5gR};\ 0.80\text{ m}\)
B) \(\text{string: }\sqrt{gR}\text{ and }\sqrt{5gR};\ \text{rod: }0\text{ and }2\sqrt{gR};\ h=2.5R=1.0\text{ m}\)
C) \(\text{string: }\sqrt{2gR}\text{ and }\sqrt{6gR};\ \text{rod: }0\text{ and }\sqrt{2gR};\ 0.40\text{ m}\)
D) \(\text{both: }\sqrt{gR}\text{ and }\sqrt{5gR};\ 1.2\text{ m}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\text{string }\sqrt{gR},\sqrt{5gR};\ \text{rod }0,\ 2\sqrt{gR};\ h_{\min}=1.0\text{ m}\)
Given: \(\text{radius }R;\ \text{loop }R=0.40\text{ m};\ \text{frictionless}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{string/track: }T\ge0\text{ at top}\Rightarrow v_{\text{top}}^2\ge gR;\ \text{rod can push, so }v_{\text{top}}\ge0;\ \text{energy conservation}\)
Step 1: \(\text{string: }v_{\text{top}}=\sqrt{gR};\ v_{\text{bot}}^2=gR+4gR=5gR\)
Step 2: \(\text{rod: }v_{\text{top}}=0;\ v_{\text{bot}}^2=0+4gR\Rightarrow v_{\text{bot}}=2\sqrt{gR}\)
Step 3: \(mgh=mg(2R)+\tfrac12m(gR)\Rightarrow h=2.5R=1.0\text{ m}\)
Worked derivation: \[\tfrac12mv_{\text{bot}}^2=\tfrac12mv_{\text{top}}^2+mg(2R)\Rightarrow v_{\text{bot}}^2=v_{\text{top}}^2+4gR\]
Check: \[h=2.5\times0.40=1.0\text{ m}>2R=0.80\text{ m}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a string or track can only pull, so gravity alone must not exceed the needed centripetal force at the top; a rod can also push}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{string and rod swapped; }h=2R\text{ ignores speed at top}\); (C) \(\text{wrong top condition}\); (D) \(\text{a rod allows zero speed at the top}\).
Key point: \(\text{string: }v_{\text{top}}\ge\sqrt{gR};\ \text{rod: }v_{\text{top}}\ge0;\ h_{\min}=2.5R\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Using conservation of energy with gravitational potential energy −GMm/r to find the maximum height reached by a body projected with a fraction of escape speed, and how escape speed depends on mass, direction and planet size
questions.question: A probe is launched vertically from Earth's surface with half the escape speed. Ignoring air resistance, how high does it rise (Earth's radius \(R\)), and which statement about escape speed is correct?
options: A) \(h=\dfrac R3\); escape speed \(v_e=\sqrt{2GM/R}=\sqrt{2gR}\approx11.2\text{ km s}^{-1}\) does not depend on the probe's mass or the direction of launch; for a planet of the same density but twice Earth's radius, \(v_e\) doubles
B) \(h=\dfrac R4\), using \(h=v^2/2g\); escape speed depends on the mass of the probe
C) \(h=R\); escape speed is the same for all planets
D) \(h=\dfrac R3\); a planet of the same density but twice the radius has \(\sqrt2\) times the escape speed
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(h=R/3\); \(v_e=\sqrt{2gR}\), independent of mass and direction; \(v_e\propto R\) at fixed density
Given: \(v=\tfrac12v_e,\ v_e^2=\dfrac{2GM}{R}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\tfrac12mv^2-\dfrac{GMm}{R}=-\dfrac{GMm}{R+h}\)
Step 1: \(\tfrac12\cdot\dfrac14\cdot\dfrac{2GM}{R}=\dfrac{GM}{R}-\dfrac{GM}{R+h}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{1}{4R}=\dfrac{1}{R}-\dfrac{1}{R+h}\Rightarrow\dfrac{1}{R+h}=\dfrac{3}{4R}\)
Step 3: \(R+h=\dfrac{4R}{3}\Rightarrow h=\dfrac R3\)
Worked derivation: \[v_e=\sqrt{\frac{2G}{R}\cdot\frac43\pi R^3\rho}=R\sqrt{\frac{8\pi G\rho}{3}}\propto R\]
Check: \[h=v^2/2g=R/4<R/3\text{ because }g\text{ weakens with height}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{mechanical energy is conserved with }U=-GMm/r\text{; constant-}g\text{ formulas underestimate large heights}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{assumes constant }g\text{; mass cancels}\); (C) \(\text{height and planet dependence wrong}\); (D) \(v_e\propto R\text{ at fixed density, not }\sqrt R\).
Key point: \(v_e=\sqrt{2GM/R};\ \text{use }U=-GMm/r\text{ for large heights}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the terminal velocity of a sphere falling through oil from Stokes' law, and using energy conservation to find the rate at which heat is produced at terminal velocity
questions.question: A steel sphere of radius \(2.0\text{ mm}\) and density \(8000\text{ kg m}^{-3}\) falls through oil of density \(900\text{ kg m}^{-3}\) and viscosity \(0.50\text{ Pa s}\) (\(g=10\text{ m s}^{-2}\)). What is its terminal velocity, and at what rate is heat produced in the oil once it reaches terminal velocity?
options: A) \(0.14\text{ m s}^{-1};\ \text{zero, since kinetic energy is constant}\)

D) \(v_t=\dfrac{2r^2(\rho-\sigma)g}{9\eta}\approx0.126\text{ m s}^{-1}\); heat is produced at about \(3.0\times10^{-4}\text{ W}\), equal to the rate of loss of gravitational potential energy minus the work done against buoyancy, since kinetic energy no longer changes
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(v_t\approx0.126\text{ m s}^{-1};\ P\approx3.0\times10^{-4}\text{ W}\)
Given: \(r=2.0\times10^{-3}\text{ m},\ \rho=8000,\ \sigma=900\text{ kg m}^{-3},\ \eta=0.50\text{ Pa s}\)
Formula/Principle: \(6\pi\eta rv_t=\tfrac43\pi r^3(\rho-\sigma)g;\ P=F_{\text{drag}}v_t\)
Step 1: \(v_t=\dfrac{2(4\times10^{-6})(7100)(10)}{9(0.50)}=\dfrac{0.568}{4.5}=0.126\text{ m s}^{-1}\)
Step 2: \(V=\tfrac43\pi r^3=3.35\times10^{-8}\text{ m}^3;\ F_{\text{drag}}=V(\rho-\sigma)g=2.38\times10^{-3}\text{ N}\)
Step 3: \(P=2.38\times10^{-3}\times0.126=3.0\times10^{-4}\text{ W}\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{d}{dt}(\text{KE})=0\Rightarrow(mg-F_B)v_t=F_{\text{drag}}v_t=\text{rate of heating}\]
Check: \[6\pi(0.50)(2\times10^{-3})(0.126)=2.38\times10^{-3}\text{ N}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{at terminal velocity the net force is zero, so all the net loss of potential energy goes into heating the fluid}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{ignores buoyancy and viscous heating}\); (B) \(\text{factor of 10 error in }r^2\); (C) \(\text{omits the factor 2}\).
Key point: \(v_t=\dfrac{2r^2(\rho-\sigma)g}{9\eta};\ \text{power}=F_{\text{drag}}v_t\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Treating two rods joined end to end as thermal resistances in series to find the steady heat current and the junction temperature
questions.question: A copper rod (\(k=400\text{ W m}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\)) and a steel rod (\(k=50\text{ W m}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\)), each \(0.10\text{ m}\) long with cross-section \(1.0\times10^{-4}\text{ m}^2\), are joined end to end with lagged sides. The free copper end is at \(100^\circ\text{C}\) and the free steel end at \(0^\circ\text{C}\). What are the heat current and the junction temperature in the steady state?
options: C) \(22.5\text{ W};\ 50^\circ\text{C}\)
D) \(45\text{ W};\ 88.9^\circ\text{C}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(H\approx4.44\text{ W};\ T_J\approx88.9^\circ\text{C}\)
Given: \(L=0.10\text{ m},\ A=1.0\times10^{-4}\text{ m}^2,\ k_{\text{Cu}}=400,\ k_{\text{St}}=50\)
Formula/Principle: \(R_{th}=\dfrac{L}{kA};\ H=\dfrac{\Delta T}{R_1+R_2}\text{ (same heat current in series)}\)
Step 1: \(R_{\text{Cu}}=\dfrac{0.10}{400\times10^{-4}}=2.5\text{ K W}^{-1};\ R_{\text{St}}=20\text{ K W}^{-1}\)
Step 2: \(H=\dfrac{100}{22.5}=4.44\text{ W}\)
Step 3: \(T_J=100-HR_{\text{Cu}}=100-11.1=88.9^\circ\text{C}\)
Worked derivation: \[k_{\text{Cu}}\frac{100-T_J}{L}=k_{\text{St}}\frac{T_J-0}{L}\Rightarrow400(100-T_J)=50T_J\Rightarrow T_J=\frac{40000}{450}=88.9^\circ\text{C}\]
Check: \[H_{\text{St}}=\frac{88.9}{20}=4.44\text{ W}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{in steady state no heat accumulates at the junction, so the same current flows through both rods; the poorer conductor takes most of the temperature drop}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{drop across copper given as the junction temperature}\); (C) \(\text{total resistance taken as the current}\); (D) \(\text{conductivities added as if in parallel}\).
Key point: \(\text{series: }R=\sum L/kA,\ \text{same }H\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the net work, heat absorbed and change in internal energy over a rectangular cyclic process on a P–V diagram, and the work in each step
questions.question: A gas is taken around the cycle \(A(1\text{ L},1\times10^{5}\text{ Pa})\to B(1\text{ L},3\times10^{5}\text{ Pa})\to C(3\text{ L},3\times10^{5}\text{ Pa})\to D(3\text{ L},1\times10^{5}\text{ Pa})\to A\). What are the work done by the gas in \(BC\) and in \(DA\), the net work in one cycle, and the net heat absorbed?
options: A) \(200\text{ J},\ -600\text{ J};\ -400\text{ J};\ \text{heat released}\)
C) \(600\text{ J},\ -200\text{ J};\ 400\text{ J};\ 400\text{ J absorbed, since }\Delta U=0\text{ for a cycle}\)
D) \(600\text{ J},\ -200\text{ J};\ 400\text{ J};\ \text{zero heat, since the gas returns to its initial state}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(W_{BC}=600\text{ J},\ W_{DA}=-200\text{ J},\ W_{\text{net}}=400\text{ J},\ Q_{\text{net}}=400\text{ J}\)
Given: \(\Delta V=2\text{ L}=2\times10^{-3}\text{ m}^3;\ P_{\text{high}}=3\times10^5,\ P_{\text{low}}=1\times10^5\text{ Pa}\)
Formula/Principle: \(W=\int P\,dV;\ \text{cycle: }\Delta U=0\Rightarrow Q=W=\text{enclosed area}\)
Step 1: \(AB,\ CD:\ \Delta V=0\Rightarrow W=0\)
Step 2: \(W_{BC}=3\times10^5\times2\times10^{-3}=600\text{ J};\ W_{DA}=1\times10^5\times(-2\times10^{-3})=-200\text{ J}\)
Step 3: \(W_{\text{net}}=400\text{ J};\ Q=W=400\text{ J}\)
Worked derivation: \[W_{\text{net}}=(P_{\text{high}}-P_{\text{low}})\Delta V=(2\times10^5)(2\times10^{-3})=400\text{ J}\]
Check: \[\text{clockwise on a }P\text{–}V\text{ diagram}\Rightarrow\text{positive net work by the gas}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{internal energy is a state function, so it returns to its start, and the first law makes net heat equal net work}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{direction reversed}\); (B) \(\text{compression work in }DA\text{ is negative}\); (D) \(\text{heat is not a state function}\).
Key point: \(\text{cycle: }Q_{\text{net}}=W_{\text{net}}=\text{area; clockwise}\Rightarrow W>0\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Finding a spring constant from static extension data, then predicting the period of oscillation for a different mass, for half the spring and for two springs in series
questions.question: In a lab, a \(100\text{ g}\) mass stretches a spring by \(4.0\text{ cm}\) (\(g=10\text{ m s}^{-2}\)). What is the spring constant, the period when a \(400\text{ g}\) mass oscillates on it, and how does the period change if the spring is cut in half, or if two such springs are joined in series, with the same \(400\text{ g}\) mass?
options: A) \(k=2.5\text{ N m}^{-1};\ T=2.5\text{ s};\ \text{half spring doubles }T\)
B) \(k=25\text{ N m}^{-1};\ T=0.13\text{ s};\ \text{no change}\)
C) \(k=250\text{ N m}^{-1};\ T=0.25\text{ s};\ \text{series halves }T\)

D) \(k=25\text{ N m}^{-1};\ T=2\pi\sqrt{0.4/25}\approx0.80\text{ s}\); half spring has \(2k\), so \(T\) becomes \(T/\sqrt2\approx0.56\text{ s}\); two springs in series have \(k/2\), so \(T\) becomes \(\sqrt2\,T\approx1.12\text{ s}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(k=25\text{ N m}^{-1};\ T\approx0.80\text{ s};\ 0.56\text{ s};\ 1.12\text{ s}\)
Given: \(m_0=0.10\text{ kg},\ x=0.040\text{ m};\ m=0.40\text{ kg}\)
Formula/Principle: \(kx=m_0g;\ T=2\pi\sqrt{m/k};\ k\propto1/\text{length};\ \text{series: }k_s=\dfrac{k_1k_2}{k_1+k_2}\)
Step 1: \(k=\dfrac{0.10\times10}{0.040}=25\text{ N m}^{-1}\)
Step 2: \(T=2\pi\sqrt{0.016}=2\pi(0.126)=0.795\text{ s}\)
Step 3: \(\text{half: }k'=50\Rightarrow T/\sqrt2=0.56\text{ s};\ \text{series: }k_s=12.5\Rightarrow\sqrt2T=1.12\text{ s}\)
Worked derivation: \[T\propto\frac{1}{\sqrt k}\Rightarrow\frac{T'}{T}=\sqrt{\frac{k}{k'}}\]
Check: \[T=2\pi\sqrt{0.40/25}=2\pi\times0.1265=0.795\text{ s}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{static extension gives }k\text{, and the period depends only on }m/k\text{, not on }g\text{ or amplitude}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(k\text{ off by 10; half spring is stiffer}\); (B) \(\text{omits }2\pi\); (C) \(k\text{ off by 10; series makes it softer}\).
Key point: \(T=2\pi\sqrt{m/k};\ \text{half spring }2k,\ \text{series }k/2\)

questions.sub_topic: Using Gauss's law and symmetry to find the electric flux through faces of a cube when a point charge sits at its centre and at one corner
questions.question: A point charge \(q\) is placed (i) at the centre of a cube and (ii) at one corner of the cube. What is the flux through one face in case (i), the total flux through the cube in case (ii), and the flux through one face not touching the corner in case (ii)?
options: A) \(\dfrac{q}{6\varepsilon_0};\ \dfrac{q}{8\varepsilon_0};\ \dfrac{q}{24\varepsilon_0}\)
B) \(\dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_0};\ \dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_0};\ \dfrac{q}{6\varepsilon_0}\)
C) \(\dfrac{q}{6\varepsilon_0};\ 0;\ 0\)
D) \(\dfrac{q}{6\varepsilon_0};\ \dfrac{q}{8\varepsilon_0};\ \dfrac{q}{8\varepsilon_0}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\dfrac{q}{6\varepsilon_0};\ \dfrac{q}{8\varepsilon_0};\ \dfrac{q}{24\varepsilon_0}\)
Given: \(\text{point charge }q;\ \text{cube}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\oint\vec E\cdot d\vec A=\dfrac{q_{\text{enc}}}{\varepsilon_0}\text{ (Gauss's law) with symmetry}\)
Step 1: \(\text{centre: six equivalent faces}\Rightarrow\dfrac{q}{6\varepsilon_0}\text{ each}\)
Step 2: \(\text{corner: eight such cubes would enclose }q\Rightarrow\text{one cube receives }\dfrac{q}{8\varepsilon_0}\)
Step 3: \(\text{three faces meeting at the corner have }\vec E\parallel\text{face}\Rightarrow0;\ \text{remaining three share }\dfrac{q}{8\varepsilon_0}\Rightarrow\dfrac{q}{24\varepsilon_0}\)
Worked derivation: \[3\Phi_{\text{far}}+3(0)=\frac{q}{8\varepsilon_0}\Rightarrow\Phi_{\text{far}}=\frac{q}{24\varepsilon_0}\]
Check: \[6\times\frac{q}{6\varepsilon_0}=\frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{Gauss's law fixes total flux from enclosed charge, and symmetry divides it among equivalent surfaces}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{ignores division among faces}\); (C) \(\text{a corner charge still sends flux through the cube}\); (D) \(\text{faces at the corner carry zero flux}\).
Key point: \(\text{charge at corner: }q/8\varepsilon_0\text{ through cube, }q/24\varepsilon_0\text{ per far face}\)

questions.sub_topic: Reducing a series–parallel capacitor network to find equivalent capacitance, charge and voltage on each capacitor, and stored energy
questions.question: Capacitors of \(2\ \mu\text{F}\) and \(4\ \mu\text{F}\) are connected in parallel, and this combination is in series with a \(3\ \mu\text{F}\) capacitor across a \(90\text{ V}\) supply. What are the equivalent capacitance, the charge on the \(2\ \mu\text{F}\) capacitor, the voltage across the \(3\ \mu\text{F}\) capacitor and the total energy stored?
options: A) \(9\ \mu\text{F};\ 180\ \mu\text{C};\ 30\text{ V};\ 36.5\text{ mJ}\)
B) \(1.33\ \mu\text{F};\ 40\ \mu\text{C};\ 40\text{ V};\ 5.4\text{ mJ}\)
C) \(2\ \mu\text{F};\ 60\ \mu\text{C};\ 60\text{ V};\ 8.1\text{ mJ}\)
D) \(2\ \mu\text{F};\ 180\ \mu\text{C};\ 30\text{ V};\ 8.1\text{ mJ}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(C_{eq}=2\ \mu\text{F};\ Q_2=60\ \mu\text{C};\ V_3=60\text{ V};\ U=8.1\text{ mJ}\)
Given: \(C_1=2,\ C_2=4\ (\text{parallel}),\ C_3=3\ \mu\text{F}\ (\text{series});\ V=90\text{ V}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{parallel: }C=\sum C_i;\ \text{series: }\dfrac1C=\sum\dfrac1{C_i};\ Q=CV;\ U=\tfrac12CV^2\)
Step 1: \(C_p=6\ \mu\text{F};\ C_{eq}=\dfrac{6\times3}{9}=2\ \mu\text{F}\)
Step 2: \(Q=2\times90=180\ \mu\text{C};\ V_3=\dfrac{180}{3}=60\text{ V};\ V_p=30\text{ V}\)
Step 3: \(Q_2=2\times30=60\ \mu\text{C};\ U=\tfrac12(2\times10^{-6})(8100)=8.1\times10^{-3}\text{ J}\)
Worked derivation: \[Q_4=4\times30=120\ \mu\text{C};\ Q_2+Q_4=180\ \mu\text{C}=Q_3\]
Check: \[V_3+V_p=60+30=90\text{ V}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{series capacitors carry equal charge, and parallel ones share the same voltage, so the smaller series capacitor takes the larger voltage}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{all treated as parallel}\); (B) \(\text{all treated as series}\); (D) \(\text{total charge assigned to the }2\ \mu\text{F capacitor; voltages swapped}\).
Key point: \(\text{series: same }Q;\ \text{parallel: same }V\)

questions.sub_topic: Explaining Kirchhoff's rules as conservation laws and the conditions and properties of a balanced Wheatstone bridge and metre bridge
questions.question: Which statement about Kirchhoff's rules and the Wheatstone bridge is correct?
options: A) The junction rule expresses conservation of charge and the loop rule conservation of energy; at balance \(\dfrac PQ=\dfrac RS\) and no current flows through the galvanometer whatever its resistance, so the balance is unchanged if the galvanometer and the battery are interchanged; in a metre bridge the null point is best kept near the middle of the wire to reduce the percentage error, and end corrections arise from the resistance of connecting strips
B) At balance, maximum current flows through the galvanometer
C) Balance depends on the emf of the battery and the galvanometer's resistance
D) The loop rule follows from conservation of charge, and the junction rule from conservation of energy
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Junction rule ↔ charge, loop rule ↔ energy; balance \(P/Q=R/S\), independent of galvanometer and emf; null point near middle
Concept: Kirchhoff's junction rule states that at any junction the sum of currents entering equals the sum leaving; this follows from conservation of charge, since charge cannot accumulate at a junction in the steady state. The loop rule states that the algebraic sum of changes in potential around any closed loop is zero; this follows from conservation of energy, since potential is a single-valued function of position. A Wheatstone bridge has four resistances \(P,Q,R,S\) with a galvanometer across one diagonal and a battery across the other; it is balanced when no current flows through the galvanometer, which happens when \(P/Q=R/S\). The balance condition contains neither the galvanometer resistance nor the battery emf, and the bridge remains balanced if the battery and galvanometer are interchanged. A metre bridge is a practical form, with \(R/S=l/(100-l)\); errors are smallest when the balance length is near \(50\text{ cm}\), and end errors arise from contact resistance at the ends of the wire.
Given: \(\text{bridge }P,Q,R,S\)
Formula/Principle: \(\sum I_{\text{in}}=\sum I_{\text{out}};\ \sum\Delta V=0;\ I_g=0\iff P/Q=R/S\)
Step 1: \(I_g=0\Rightarrow\text{the two midpoints are at equal potential}\)
Step 2: \(I_1P=I_2R\text{ and }I_1Q=I_2S\Rightarrow P/Q=R/S\)
Step 3: \(\text{condition has no }G\text{ or }\varepsilon\Rightarrow\text{interchange keeps balance}\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{I_1P}{I_1Q}=\frac{I_2R}{I_2S}\Rightarrow\frac PQ=\frac RS\]
Check: \[P=Q=R=S\Rightarrow\text{symmetric bridge, midpoints at equal potential}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{at balance the galvanometer branch carries no current, so its resistance and the source cannot affect the condition}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{balance means zero galvanometer current}\); (C) \(\text{balance is independent of both}\); (D) \(\text{laws swapped}\).
Key point: \(\text{junction = charge, loop = energy; bridge balance }P/Q=R/S\)

questions.sub_topic: Applying the Biot–Savart law to find the magnetic field at the centre of a circular loop and of a circular arc, and on the axis at a distance equal to the radius
questions.question: A circular loop of radius \(10\text{ cm}\) carries \(5.0\text{ A}\) (\(\mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7}\text{ T m A}^{-1}\)). What is the field at its centre, the field at the centre of a semicircular arc of the same radius and current, and the ratio of the field on the axis at a distance equal to the radius to the field at the centre?
options: D) \(3.14\times10^{-5}\text{ T};\ 1.57\times10^{-5}\text{ T};\ \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt2}\approx0.35\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(3.14\times10^{-5}\text{ T};\ 1.57\times10^{-5}\text{ T};\ \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt2}\)
Given: \(R=0.10\text{ m},\ I=5.0\text{ A}\)
Formula/Principle: \(dB=\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{I\,dl\sin\theta}{r^2};\ B_{\text{arc}}=\dfrac{\mu_0I\phi}{4\pi R};\ B_{\text{axis}}=\dfrac{\mu_0IR^2}{2(R^2+x^2)^{3/2}}\)
Step 1: \(B_{\text{centre}}=\dfrac{\mu_0I}{2R}=\dfrac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times5}{0.20}=3.14\times10^{-5}\text{ T}\)
Step 2: \(\text{semicircle }\phi=\pi:\ B=\dfrac{\mu_0I}{4R}=1.57\times10^{-5}\text{ T}\)
Step 3: \(x=R:\ \dfrac{B_{\text{axis}}}{B_{\text{centre}}}=\dfrac{R^3}{(2R^2)^{3/2}}=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt2}\)
Worked derivation: \[B_{\text{centre}}=\int\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{I\,dl}{R^2}=\frac{\mu_0I}{4\pi R^2}(2\pi R)=\frac{\mu_0I}{2R}\]
Check: \[\frac{1}{2\sqrt2}\times3.14\times10^{-5}=1.11\times10^{-5}\text{ T}<B_{\text{centre}}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{at the centre every element is perpendicular to its radius and adds in the same direction; on the axis distance and angle reduce each contribution}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{uses }R\text{ for diameter; arc larger than loop}\); (B) \(\text{drops }\pi\text{; axial ratio wrong}\); (C) \(\text{semicircle gives half; ratio exponent wrong}\).
Key point: \(B_{\text{centre}}=\dfrac{\mu_0I}{2R};\ \text{arc: fraction }\phi/2\pi\)

questions.sub_topic: Explaining motional emf in a rod sliding on rails, the retarding force from Lenz's law, energy conservation between mechanical power and Joule heating, and the emf of a rotating rod
questions.question: A conducting rod of length \(l\) slides with constant velocity \(v\) on frictionless rails connected through a resistance \(R\), in a uniform field \(B\) perpendicular to the plane. Which explanation is correct?
options: A) No emf is induced because the field is uniform and constant
B) The induced current aids the motion, so no external force is needed

C) The emf is \(Blv\), driving current \(I=Blv/R\); by Lenz's law the force on the current-carrying rod, \(B^2l^2v/R\), opposes the motion, so an external force of this size is needed to keep \(v\) constant; the mechanical power \(B^2l^2v^2/R\) equals the Joule heat \(I^2R\), as energy conservation requires; a rod of length \(l\) rotating with angular speed \(\omega\) about one end perpendicular to \(B\) has emf \(\tfrac12B\omega l^2\)
D) The emf is \(Blv\) but the power supplied is \(Blv^2\), independent of \(R\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\varepsilon=Blv,\ F=B^2l^2v/R,\ P=B^2l^2v^2/R=I^2R;\ \text{rotating rod }\tfrac12B\omega l^2\)
Concept: When a conductor moves through a magnetic field, the magnetic force \(q\vec v\times\vec B\) on its free charges separates them, producing a motional emf; equivalently, the flux through the circuit \(\Phi=Blx\) changes at the rate \(Blv\). Lenz's law states that the induced current flows in a direction that opposes the change producing it, so the force \(IlB\) on the rod acts against its motion. To maintain constant velocity an external agent must supply power \(Fv\); this mechanical energy is converted into heat in the resistance, as conservation of energy demands. For a rod rotating about one end, different points move with speeds \(\omega r\), and integrating \(B\omega r\,dr\) from \(0\) to \(l\) gives \(\tfrac12B\omega l^2\).
Given: \(l,\ v,\ B,\ R\)
Formula/Principle: \(\varepsilon=-\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt}=Blv;\ F=IlB;\ P=Fv\)
Step 1: \(I=\dfrac{Blv}{R}\)
Step 2: \(F=IlB=\dfrac{B^2l^2v}{R}\text{ opposing }v\)
Step 3: \(P=Fv=\dfrac{B^2l^2v^2}{R}=I^2R\)
Worked derivation: \[\varepsilon_{\text{rot}}=\int_0^l B\omega r\,dr=\tfrac12B\omega l^2\]
Check: \[I^2R=\frac{B^2l^2v^2}{R^2}R=\frac{B^2l^2v^2}{R}=Fv\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{if the induced current aided the motion, energy would be created from nothing; opposition is required by energy conservation}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{the circuit area, hence flux, changes}\); (B) \(\text{violates Lenz's law}\); (D) \(\text{power depends on }R\).
Key point: \(\varepsilon=Blv;\ \text{mechanical power}=I^2R\)

questions.sub_topic: Interpreting the graph of impedance against angular frequency for a series LCR circuit to find the resonant frequency, minimum impedance, quality factor and bandwidth, and the circuit's behaviour on either side of resonance
questions.question: For a series LCR circuit with \(R=10\ \Omega,\ L=10\text{ mH},\ C=1.0\ \mu\text{F}\), a graph of impedance \(Z\) against angular frequency \(\omega\) shows a minimum. What are the resonant angular frequency, the minimum impedance, the quality factor and the bandwidth, and how does the circuit behave on either side of resonance?
options: A) \(\omega_0=10^{3}\text{ rad s}^{-1};\ Z_{\min}=0;\ Q=1\); inductive below resonance

B) \(\omega_0=1/\sqrt{LC}=10^{4}\text{ rad s}^{-1};\ Z_{\min}=R=10\ \Omega;\ Q=\omega_0L/R=10;\ \Delta\omega=R/L=10^{3}\text{ rad s}^{-1}\); below resonance \(X_C>X_L\) and the circuit is capacitive, above resonance it is inductive; a smaller \(R\) gives a sharper minimum
C) \(\omega_0=10^{4}\text{ rad s}^{-1};\ Z_{\min}=R;\ Q=0.1\); capacitive above resonance
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\omega_0=10^4\text{ rad s}^{-1},\ Z_{\min}=10\ \Omega,\ Q=10,\ \Delta\omega=10^3\text{ rad s}^{-1}\)
Given: \(R=10\ \Omega,\ L=1.0\times10^{-2}\text{ H},\ C=1.0\times10^{-6}\text{ F}\)
Formula/Principle: \(Z=\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2};\ \omega_0=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}};\ Q=\dfrac{\omega_0L}{R};\ \Delta\omega=\dfrac{\omega_0}{Q}=\dfrac RL\)
Step 1: \(\omega_0=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{10^{-8}}}=10^4\text{ rad s}^{-1};\ Z_{\min}=R=10\ \Omega\)
Step 2: \(Q=\dfrac{10^4\times10^{-2}}{10}=10\)
Step 3: \(\Delta\omega=\dfrac{10}{10^{-2}}=10^3\text{ rad s}^{-1}\)
Worked derivation: \[X_L=X_C\Rightarrow\omega_0L=\frac{1}{\omega_0C}\Rightarrow\omega_0^2=\frac{1}{LC}\]
Check: \[X_L=10^4\times10^{-2}=100\ \Omega=X_C=\frac{1}{10^4\times10^{-6}}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{at resonance the reactances cancel, leaving only }R\text{; away from it the larger reactance dominates}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{wrong }\omega_0\text{; }Z_{\min}=R\text{; capacitive below}\); (C) \(Q\text{ inverted; inductive above}\); (D) \(\text{forgets the square root}\).
Key point: \(\omega_0=1/\sqrt{LC},\ Z_{\min}=R,\ Q=\omega_0L/R\)
